A peripheral line is therefore preferential to a central line when urgent fluid resuscitation, or blood, is required.
subject: Physiology

stem:
A 35-year-old trauma patient has a computed tomography scan of the abdomen and pelvis with contrast and delayed phases performed. He is found to have a laceration of the right kidney with urinary extravasation.

What grade of injury is this?
explanation: Renal injuries are graded in accordance with the American Association for the Surgery of Trauma renal injury scale. A grade IV injury involves a laceration that extends to the renal pelvis or extravasation as in this case. The patient may have an injury to the main renal artery.
subject: Breast and endocrine surgery

stem:
A 25-year-old man is admitted to the Emergency Department with severe polytraumatic injuries following a road traffic collision. He is managed as per ATLS guidelines and undergoes damage control surgery.

Which of the following physiological responses would you expect to find within the first few hours of his injury?
explanation: In the first few hours of a traumatic injury to the body, a complex series of responses are set in motion. This is known as the ebb phase, the features of which include decreased body temperature, decreased oxygen consumption, lactic acidosis, increased stress hormone levels, decreased insulin levels, hyperglycaemia and insulin resistance, increased substrate consumption, immune activation and a hepatic acute-phase response. The following days to weeks represents the ‘flow phase’, which features increased body temperature, increased oxygen consumption, negative nitrogen balance, increased stress hormone levels, hyperglycaemia, gluconeogenesis, proteinolysis, lipolysis and immunosuppression.
subject: Emergency medicine and trauma

stem:
Various lung intravascular and extravascular pressures influence pulmonary blood flow and its distribution in the lung. This will vary depending on the activity of an individual, how unwell they may be and throughout the day.

What is the normal mean pulmonary arterial pressure?
explanation: Normal mean pulmonary arterial pressure is 15 mmHg. This is the hydrostatic pressure generated by the right ventricle and is 1/6th that of systemic arterial pressure generated by the left ventricle. The pulmonary circulation lacks high resistance arterioles and so the pressure drop between the pulmonary arteries and capillaries is minimised.
subject: Physiology

stem:
A 75 kg, 38-year-old alcoholic patient with known varices is brought to the Emergency Department by ambulance. The paramedics tell you he has had an episode of haematemesis with an estimated one litre of blood loss.

Which of the following statements is true regarding this patient?

options.text: His pulse pressure will be increased
He will have a decreased systolic pressure with a narrowed pulse pressure
He will have a normal respiratory rate
He would have a tachycardia of 110 beats/min

explanation: Patients in class 2 shock will have a tachycardia with a rate of 100–120 beats/min (although beta-blocked patients may not mount a tachycardic response).
subject: Emergency medicine and trauma

stem:
A 28-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department in haemorrhagic shock having sustained an open tibial fracture. He undergoes emergency external fixation on the trauma operating list.

Which one of the following concerning blood volume is the best answer?

options.text: It is around 2.5 litres in a 70 kg man
Plasma accounts for approximately 60% of total blood volume
Men have less blood volume than women

explanation: Plasma accounts for about 60% of total blood volume, while erythrocytes make up roughly 40%, along with leukocytes and platelets.
subject: Emergency medicine and trauma

stem:
A patient falls onto his right shoulder and is subsequently unable to internally rotate the shoulder against resistance. Other movements are relatively well preserved. X-rays taken show no bony injury.

Which of the following muscles is likely to be injured?
explanation:
The subscapularis muscle (shown in green on the anterior or thoracic aspect of the scapula) is the primary medial/internal rotator of the arm at the glenohumeral joint and inserts anteriorly onto the lesser tubercle. It is innervated by the upper and lower subscapular nerves, both branches from the posterior cord.

Original
Henry Gray (1918) Anatomy of the Human Body
Public domain
subject: Anatomy

stem:
A 45-year-old man presents to the Acute Surgical Admissions Unit with a 1-day history of worsening epigastric pain, radiating through to the back, and vomiting. He is not able to find any comfortable position and analgesia is not helpful. Clinical examination reveals generalised abdominal guarding and rigidity.

What is the most definitive investigation to confirm diagnosis?

options.text: Amylase of 450 international units is suggestive of acute pancreatitis
Computed tomography (CT) scan of the abdomen
Normal serum amylase excludes acute pancreatitis

explanation: In this context, a CT scan of the abdomen is the best investigative modality in confirming acute pancreatitis. It is also useful when the diagnosis is not clear and other conditions such as perforation and peritonitis are being considered.
subject: Upper gastrointestinal surgery

stem:
A patient with haemorrhagic shock arrives in A&E resus, and requires a fluid challenge. The nurse puts up 5% dextrose, which is the first bag they found. The consultant asks them for a different crystalloid for this patient.

How much of 1 litre of 5% dextrose infused intravenously will remain in the intravascular compartment?
explanation: One-third of total body water is extracellular and two-thirds intracellular. Of the extracellular fluid volume, only one-quarter of extracellular fluid is intravascular and therefore only one-twelfth (one-third × one-quarter) of infused 5% dextrose will remain in the intravascular space. In comparison, one-quarter of 0.9% saline will remain in the intravascular space as it contains 154 mmol/l of Na+, which is similar to the concentration of Na+ found in the extracellular compartment.
subject: Emergency medicine and trauma

stem:
You are in the general surgery clinic reviewing a 27-year-old patient referred with new unexplained rectal bleeding and you suspect colorectal carcinoma. They are subsequently referred for urgent colonoscopy.

Which one of the following statements is correct regarding colorectal carcinoma?

options.text: It is associated with a high fibre, low fat diet
It is associated primarily with Krukenberg's tumours
It is best treated by abdominal-perineal resection if the tumour is up to 15 cm from the anal canal
A Dukes C2 colorectal cancer implies nodal involvement
It is found in the rectum in 10% of cases in adults under 65 years

explanation: In 1932, the British pathologist Cuthbert Dukes (1890 – 1977) devised a classification system for colorectal cancers. An adaptation to his original classification was proposed by Americans Astler and Coller in 1954 – this further subdivided Stages B and C. Stage C2 is defined as penetrating through the muscularis propria, with lymph node involvement.
subject: Colorectal surgery

stem:
A 28-year-old presents with a left testicular lump. The lump is around 1 cm in the mid-testes, non-painful and firm.

What is the lymphatic drainage of the testes?

options.text: Drains to the pararectal lymph nodes
Drains to the prostatic lymph nodes
Drains to both para-aortic and inguinal lymph nodes
Drains to the inguinal lymph nodes
Drains to the para-aortic lymph nodes

explanation: During development, the testes descend downwards and drag with them the blood supply and lymphatic drainage. This means malignancy that spreads to local lymph nodes will be present in para-aortic nodes, relatively concealed compared with inguinal lymphadenopathy.
subject: Anatomy

stem:
You are reviewing a patient's routine biochemistry as they recover from a laparotomy. You note some abnormalities and are concerned they may have developed an acute kidney injury.

For which one of the following substances would you expect the renal clearance to be the lowest, under normal conditions?
explanation: Under normal conditions the renal clearance of glucose is zero, as glucose is completely reabsorbed in the renal tubules and not excreted. Glycosuria may be an indicator of glucose intolerance and diabetes mellitus.
subject: Physiology

stem:
You are on an Intensive Care Unit (ITU) ward round where you review a patient admitted with severe sepsis and multiorgan failure. As a result he has low urine output and peripheral oedema. He is acidotic and hyperkalaemic.

Which one of the following is correct regarding renal replacement therapy?

options.text: It can only be delivered via a central line
It is a cure for kidney disease
It may involve replacing filtered fluid in the peritoneal cavity
It should be considered first line for fluid overload
Rapid ultrafiltration of the blood cannot be undertaken

explanation: Renal replacement therapy is indicated in intractable fluid overload, hyperkalaemia, acidosis and uraemia when medical therapy has failed. It can be administered as a holding measure to cover an acute crisis or in the chronic setting. In the acute setting, such as on ITU, haemofiltration is usually used, in which the patient’s own blood pressure drives the formation of an ultrafiltrate. The advantage over haemodialysis is that the machinery involved is less complex and it can continue for many hours. In the chronic setting, in which the maintenance of a reasonable lifestyle of the patient is requisite and the process must be rapid/intermittent, haemodialysis or peritoneal dialysis is commonly used. Haemodialysis like haemofiltration involves the patient’s blood being pumped through an artificial kidney where waste products are exchanged with dialysis fluid, which surrounds the semi-permeable tubes through which the blood is passed. Often an arteriovenous fistula is formed surgically to allow easy vascular access for haemodialysis. Peritoneal dialysis involves fluid being pumped into the abdominal cavity into which waste products diffuse. The fluid must be changed episodically (often four times per day).
subject: Critical care

stem:
A 78-year-old woman is brought to the Emergency Department after she was found on her kitchen floor drowsy and in pain following a fall. She does not recall how long she was on the floor. X-rays reveal a displaced fractured neck of femur and the catheter bag shows dark urine. Her creatine kinase result is 2045 U/L (normal 24–170 U/L) with an estimate glomerular filtration rate of 12 ml/min (normal 75 ml/min).

Given the most likely diagnosis, which of the following is correct?

options.text: Compartment syndrome is not a recognised complication of rhabdomyolysis
Rhabdomyolysis can be caused by bacteria such as Streptococcus and Clostridium difficile
The condition in adults always presents with the triad of muscle spasm, myalgias and dark urine
Myoglobin leads to acute kidney failure by renal tubular obstruction only
Blood tests show raised creatine kinase and hypokalaemia

explanation: Rhabdomyolysis is a syndrome associated with skeletal muscle injury (chemical or physical) and damage leading to a massive release of muscle breakdown products in the circulation, which exert several effects such as kidney toxicity and cardiac arrhythmias; if not treated promptly, it can lead to death. Rhabdomyolysis can be hereditary and associated with metabolic conditions or acquired. Acquired causes include extreme physical activity, drug use such as ethanol, heroin and cocaine, malignant hyperthermia, infections, toxins and trauma. It was first described in patients following a crush injury. Rhabdomyolysis can be the result of infection with a range of infectious agents. Streptococcus and Clostridium difficile have been shown to cause direct muscle toxicity due to release of toxins during their infection. Legionella is also commonly associated with rhabdomyolysis in adults.
subject: Perioperative care

stem:
A 58-year-old woman with long-standing atrial fibrillation suffered an embolic stroke that causes weakness down one side of her body. She is subsequently started on warfarin and rate control of her AF.

Which option describes the brain region affected by this stroke?
explanation: The primary motor cortex is located in the dorsal part of the precentral gyrus and the anterior bank of the central sulcus. The primary motor cortex (or M1) works in association with premotor areas to plan and execute movements. M1 contains large neurons known as Betz cells, which send long axons down the spinal cord to synapse onto alpha-motor neurones, which connect to the muscles. A stroke affecting this region will result in contralateral weakness.
subject: Physiology

stem:
A 49-year-old post-menopausal woman of Southern Asian origin presents with muscle weakness. She is found to have hypocalcaemia, and an X-ray reveals two Looser’s zones in her left upper femur.

Which impaired physiological process is most likely contributing to her condition?

options.text: Absorption of calcium from the gut

explanation: The findings in this woman suggest osteomalacia, particularly the Looser's zones, and the most important reason for impaired mineralisation of bone is reduced intestinal calcium absorption and consequently vitamin D deficiency. Decreased availability of calcium to mineralise bone leads to increased osteoblastic activity (and hence increased osteoid formation).
subject: Orthopaedics

stem:
A 45-year-old man is rushed to the Emergency Department with severe abdominal pain; he was the driver of a car travelling at 70 mph that hit the central reservation. On arrival, he is anxious with a respiratory rate 35 breaths/min, heart rate of 125 bpm and blood pressure measuring 88/46 mmHg.

Which stage of haemorrhagic shock is he most likely to be in?

options.text: This patient is not in haemorrhagic shock

explanation:
This patient is in stage III haemorrhagic shock, demonstrated by his anxious state and observations. At this stage, patients are hypotensive, tachycardic and tachypneoic with a blood loss of 1500–2000 ml (30–40% of blood volume).

 — Class of haemorrhagic shock
 — I — II — III — IV
Blood loss — Up to 750 ml — 750–1500 ml — 1500–2000 ml — > 2000 ml
Blood loss (% blood volume) — Up to 15% — 15–30% — 30–40% — > 40%
Heart rate — < 100 bpm — 100–120 bpm — 120–140 bpm — > 140 bpm
Blood pressure — Normal — Normal — Decreased — Decreased
Pulse pressure — Normal/increased — Decreased — Decreased — Decreased
Respiratory rate — 14–20 breaths/min — 20–30 breaths/min — 30–40 breaths/min — > 35 breaths/min
Urine output — > 30 ml/h — 20–30 ml/h — 5–15 ml/h — Negligible
Central nervous system — Slightly anxious — Mildly anxious — Anxious, confused — Confused, lethargic
subject: Emergency medicine and trauma

stem:
A 50-year-old man is investigated due to symptoms in keeping with vasculitis. The rheumatology team send for an autoantibody screen, which shows a high titre of anti-neutrophilic cytoplasmic autoantibodies in this patient.

This would be most suggestive of which one of the following?
explanation: Anti-neutrophilic cytoplasmic autoantibodies are most commonly seen in patients with GPA (formerly called Wegener’s granulomatosis), eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (formerly called Churg–Strauss syndrome), and microscopic polyangiitis.
subject: Pathology

stem:
When requesting imaging investigations, radiation exposure should be taken into consideration.

Which of the following is correct regarding the radiation dose following imaging investigations?

options.text: The approximate increased lifetime risk of cancer in patients under 16 years of age is approximately double that of an adult
There is an increased risk of cancer of approximately half in patients ≥ 70 years of age
Average background radiation is approximately 10 mSv per year
Chest X-rays are associated with the smallest radiation exposure of all X-rays
Computed tomography (CT) head scan exposes patients to a higher radiation dose than CT abdomen and pelvis

explanation: For paediatric patients, lifetime cancer risks are approximately doubled compared with adult patients.
topic: Radiation Use And Risks (Ionising And Non-Ionising)
topicRaw: Radiation Use And Risks (Ionising And Non-Ionising)
subject: Emergency medicine and trauma

stem:
You are assisting your consultant on an elective orthopaedic theatre list and discussing the importance of surgical safety.

She asks you how many sections there are to the World Health Organisation (WHO) surgical safety checklist?
explanation:
There are three sections to the WHO surgical safety checklist.

The World Health Organisation (WHO) developed the surgical safety checklist to aide in prevention of ‘never events’. It is currently used worldwide, should be used for all operating lists and has improved surgical safety significantly. The surgical safety checklist consists of three sections; before the induction of anaesthesia, time out before skin incision, and sign out at the end of the procedure. It centres around good communication between all theatre staff (including introductions and role), correct identification of the patient, site of surgery and procedure to be performed, allows any anticipated problems to be highlighted, as well as estimated blood loss and if antibiotics are required.
subject: Perioperative care

stem:
A 63-year-old man with a history of squamous cell carcinoma re-presents with a swelling in his neck. You carry out a fine needle aspiration (FNA) for cytology.

Which one of the following statements regarding this procedure is most accurate?

options.text: It can be used in combination with other tests to diagnose metastases
If negative it can be used to exclude malignancy
It is able to differentiate invasive from in-situ carcinoma
Always need to be done under ultrasound guidance

explanation: Malignant metastatic cells (with mitotic figures, increased nuclei and decreased cellular cohesion) can be diagnosed by needle aspiration cytology.
subject: Skin and wound management

stem:
A 25-year-old man reports to the general surgery clinic for excision of lipoma over the forearm. Soon after injection of the local anaesthetic around the swelling, the patient develops shortness of breath and cyanosis. His oxygen saturations are 85% and remain the same even on oxygen inhalation at 6 litres/min. A blood sample is drawn for blood gas analysis, which is noted to be chocolate coloured.

Which of the following is most likely to cause this complication?
explanation: The patient has developed methaemoglobinaemia due to the absorption of prilocaine injection into the blood circulation. Methaemoglobin contains the ferric form of iron that has a reduced oxygen-carrying capacity. This manifests clinically with headache, light-headedness, fatigue, shortness of breath and seizures. The oxygen saturation falls below 90% and does not improve with oxygen therapy. Other features include cyanosis, tachycardia and altered mental status. The blood sample is brown or chocolate coloured.
subject: Perioperative care

stem:
You are on the High Dependency Unit reviewing a patient with severe sepsis and the anaesthetic team are initiating treatment with inotropes.

Which of the following is correct with respect to inotropic agents?

options.text: Adrenaline can reduce renal blood flow at higher doses

explanation: At higher doses of adrenaline, alpha-mediated vasoconstriction reduces renal blood flow and can cause oliguria and precipitate acute renal failure.
topic: Mode Of Action Of Drugs In Cardiology
topicRaw: Mode Of Action Of Drugs In Cardiology
subject: Pharmacology

stem:
A 56-year-old woman is noted to be positive for methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) on a wound swab. Steps are subsequently taken to minimise risk to the other patients on the ward.

What is the most appropriate infection control procedure?

options.text: All MRSA positive patients must be nursed in the same bay, away from non-infected patients
Gloves and face masks for all entering the room

explanation: Barrier nursing with apron and gloves is the current accepted method.
topic: Hospital Acquired Infections And Infection Control
topicRaw: Hospital Acquired Infections And Infection Control
subject: Critical care

stem:
A 26-year-old obese women presents to clinic with recurrent episodes of infected epidermal cysts in her groins and under her breasts. This has left her with significant scarring.

Which one of the following statements regarding hidradenitis suppurativa is correct?

options.text: It is treated with prolonged courses of systemic antibiotics
It is due to inflammation of the eccrine glands
It requires magnetic resonance imaging to confirm the diagnosis in the acute stages
When affecting the axilla may lead to limitation of shoulder abduction

explanation: Hidradenitis suppurativa (HS) is a chronic suppurative disease of the apocrine sweat glands with a predilection for the intertriginous regions such as the axilla, groin and perineum. It is manifested by recurrent abscesses, sinuses and fistulas. Bacteria may enter the apocrine system through the hair follicles, become trapped and subsequently multiply in the nutrient rich environment of the apocrine sweat glands. The glands subsequently rupture, leading to extension of infection resulting in further local inflammation, tissue destruction and skin damage. Chronic HS leads to progressive destruction of normal skin architecture, with the development of periductal and periglandular inflammation, dermal and subcutaneous fibrosis, scarring and contractures. Chronic disease of the axillary region could lead to limitation of shoulder abduction.
subject: Skin and wound management

stem:
A 25-year-old woman who weighs 60 kg is undergoing lipofilling. The consultant wants to ensure she is comfortable and administers local anaesthetic.

What is the maximum volume of 1% lidocaine with adrenaline that can be administered?
explanation: The maximum dose of lidocaine without adrenaline is 3 mg/kg, and with adrenaline this is 7 mg/kg; 1% lidocaine contains 10 mg/ml, and 2% 20 mg/ml. The maximum dose of lidocaine with adrenaline in a 60 kg patient is 420 mg, which equates to 42 ml.
subject: Perioperative care

stem:
A 6-year-old boy is brought to the Emergency Department with vomiting and severe abdominal pain. He also had two episodes of convulsions during this period. On examination, he is pale and dehydrated. The abdomen is rigid and with maximal tenderness over the right iliac fossa. Temperature is 40.2°C, blood pressure 82/64 mmHg, and pulse 172/min.

Which of the following is the most likely pathological process in this child?
explanation: The signs and symptoms in this child are suggestive of spreading/established infection in the peritoneal cavity. Bacterial peritonitis in children may occur as a result of a ruptured viscus such as ruptured appendicitis or ruptured Meckel’s diverticulitis, or as a complication of abdominal surgery. The child may present with classical signs of peritonitis such as abdominal pain, pyrexia, nausea, vomiting, tachycardia, low blood pressure and decreased urine output. High pyrexia may result in febrile convulsions. Abdominal examination may reveal a board-like rigidity, guarding and rebound tenderness. Bowel sounds are absent if the peritonitis becomes established. Plain abdominal X-rays should be performed in both supine and upright positions to identify the presence of free gas beneath the diaphragm, which suggests perforation of a viscus. The common organisms responsible for bacterial peritonitis in children include Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae and Pseudomonas species.
subject: Breast and endocrine surgery

stem:
A 28-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with a painful, swollen right calf. He underwent an intramedullary tibial nail for a closed midshaft tibial fracture 14 days ago. The calf circumference is 3.5 cm greater on this side.

What is the gold standard investigation for diagnosing a deep vein thrombosis (DVT)?
explanation: Venography remains the gold standard investigation for DVT but is used less commonly than Doppler ultrasound as it involves the use of contrast and it is invasive.
subject: Vascular surgery

stem:
A 45-year-old woman can feel a firm, non-tender, rounded subcutaneous mass, 1 cm in diameter, along the extensor surface of the forearm. Microscopically, the nodule shows an area of central necrosis surrounded by palisading epithelioid cells.

Which one of the following laboratory test findings is most likely to be positive in this woman?
explanation: This is a rheumatoid nodule, a peculiar form of granulomatous inflammation that can be seen in the soft tissues of people with rheumatoid arthritis. Rheumatoid nodules develop in about 30% of patients with rheumatoid arthritis. They consist of a central necrotic area surrounded by palisaded histiocytic macrophages, all enveloped by lymphocytes, plasma cells and fibroblasts. Nodules and vasculitis can also develop in many of the visceral organs.
subject: Orthopaedics

stem:
A 10-year-old child presents to the Emergency Department with a severe headache and paralysis of cranial nerve (CN) VI. She has recently been treated by the General Practitioner for an ear infection, which has resolved. She is not febrile. On examination, you note papilloedema.

What is the most likely cause?
explanation: Otitic hydrocephalus is a syndrome of raised intracranial pressure, most commonly in children and adolescents, during or following middle ear infection without brain abscess. The precise aetiology is unknown. Presenting signs and symptoms include headache, CN VI palsy and papilloedema.
subject: Neurosurgery

stem:
A newborn is referred from a neonatal intensive care unit after it was noticed that he has a proximal hypospadias. He is considered for reconstructive surgery.

With what other abnormalities is this developmental abnormality associated?
explanation: Similar to most developmental disorders, hypospadias is linked with many other problems. Mild, distal hypospadias carries with it a lower rate of concurrent disorder whereas proximal hypospadias has a higher rate. It is important to investigate children appropriately for other abnormalities.
subject: Paediatric surgery

stem:
A 64-year-old steel worker undergoes coronary artery bypass surgery for three-vessel disease. Post-operatively he develops a complete heart block. Ischaemia of the atrio-ventricular node is suspected.

Which branch is most likely to be the culprit vessel?
explanation: The atrioventricular node is supplied by the atrioventricular nodal branch, a branch of the posterior interventricular artery. In the vast majority of the population the posterior interventricular artery arises from the right coronary artery. The right coronary artery arises at the anterior sinus of Valsalva and descends through the atrioventricular groove down to the heart apex. Recent statistics report that the incidence of right-sided dominance is as high as 80–85% and the remaining 15–20% of the population is either left-sided dominant or co-dominant. In the left dominance the posterior interventricular artery arises from the left circumflex, which wraps around the atrioventricular groove to supply the atrioventricular node. In some rare cases the posterior interventricular artery can arise from the left anterior descending artery.
subject: Anatomy

stem:
A 58-year-old woman with type II diabetes presents to the surgical team with fever and right upper quadrant pain after having recently been treated for cholecystitis. Further investigation reveals that she has developed a liver abscess. The initial report for the blood cultures sent shows Gram-negative rods.

Which of these bacteria is most likely to be responsible?
explanation: Klebsiella pneumoniae and Escherichia coli are two of the most frequently isolated pathogens in liver abscesses. They are both Gram-negative rods.
subject: Hepatobiliary and pancreatic surgery

stem:
You are the orthopaedic CT1 on call and are asked to see a 64-year-old woman with known breast cancer and spinal metastases. She is complaining of bladder dysfunction.

Which one of the following statements is correct regarding spinal metastases?

options.text: The majority of patients with spinal metastases present with motor or sensory neurology
They are found in 10% of patients with a palliative cancer
They most commonly affect the cervical spine
Unlike spinal trauma, compression is poorly treated with high-dose corticosteroids

explanation: The clinical features of spinal metastases include pain, urinary retention, spastic paraplegia, Brown–Séquard syndrome and other neurological symptoms and signs. Approximately 90% present with back/bone pain followed by radicular pain. Sensory or motor neurology occurs in 50%. Brown–Séquard syndrome occurs when there is damage caused to one-half of the spinal cord. This results in ipsilateral loss of motor function and proprioception and contralateral loss of pain and temperature sensation below the level of the spinal lesion.
subject: Breast and endocrine surgery

stem:
A 28-year-old professional cyclist presents to the Emergency Department complaining of penile and scrotal numbness. It improves slightly on standing and lying down. He reports urinary frequency and episodes of urinary incontinence. The urine dipstick is negative.

Which nerve has most likely been injured?
explanation: The pudendal nerve is formed by the ventral rami of the sacral spinal nerves from S2, S3 and S4. It maintains voluntary urinary continence by facilitating contraction of the external urethral sphincter. It also helps to maintain voluntary faecal continence via contraction of the external anal sphincter. Damage to this nerve could result in urinary or faecal incontinence. Cyclists may develop pudendal nerve entrapment syndrome (also known as Alcock canal syndrome), which can present with various symptoms, including pain, urinary and faecal incontinence and sensory disturbances of the perineum and genitalia due to irritation, entrapment or damage of the pudendal nerve.
topic: The Urogenital Region And Perineal Pouches Regional Anatomy
topicRaw: The Urogenital Region And Perineal Pouches Regional Anatomy
subject: Anatomy

stem:
A 15-year-old boy presents with a neck mass shortly after a respiratory tract infection. On examination it is a lateral mass anterior to the sternocleidomastoid.

Which one of these is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: This scenario is most likely to represent a branchial cleft cyst, which is typically as a result of failure of obliteration of the second branchial cleft. They account for almost 20% of neck masses in children and present as a solitary painless mass previously unnoticed until infected.
subject: Anatomy

stem:
A 9-year-old boy presents to the Emergency Department with complaints of headache, vomiting and double vision. Examination reveals papilloedema and right lateral rectus palsy. A magnetic resonance imaging scan of his head shows increased lateral ventricles as well as the third ventricle but a normal-sized fourth ventricle.

Which section of the normal cerebrospinal fluid channel is most likely to be obstructed?
explanation: The patient is having obstructive hydrocephalus. This is caused by any restriction in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) circulation pathway. The aqueduct of Sylvius joins the third and fourth ventricles. The obstruction should be at the level of the cerebral aqueduct if the lateral and third ventricles are dilated and the fourth ventricle is normal size.
subject: Neurosurgery

stem:
A 58-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with a large, pulsatile abdominal mass, hypotension and back pain. She undergoes an emergency endovascular aneurysm repair.

At which vertebral level does the aorta bifurcate to give the common iliac arteries?
explanation: The aorta bifurcates into the common iliac arteries at L4. It is also the level at which the median sacral artery arises. The intercristal plane, an imaginary horizontal line between the highest points of the iliac crests, lies at the L4/5 level. The aorta bifurcates one vertebral level higher than the inferior vena cava forms (at L5).
topic: Aorta Regional Anatomy, Including Aortic Arches Embryology
topicRaw: Aorta Regional Anatomy, Including Aortic Arches Embryology
subject: Anatomy

stem:
A 21-year-old man is shot in the chest. He is diagnosed with pericardial tamponade. He undergoes an emergency thoracotomy to create a pericardial window by excising a segment of pericardium to relieve the tamponade.

Which of the following can occur as a result of an iatrogenic injury during the pericardial incision?

options.text: Damage to the parasympathetic supply to the abdomen
Paralysis of all intercostals muscles on the left hemithorax

explanation: The phrenic nerves (C3–C5) supply motor innervation to the diaphragm. They run vertically on the external surface of the cardiac pericardium, as seen below in the image. An incision over the pericardium in emergencies could lead to phrenic nerve damage and paralysis of the ipsilateral hemidiaphragm.
subject: Cardiothoracic surgery

stem:
A 67-year-old man who is an alcoholic presents to the Emergency Department with severe chest pain following prolonged episodes of vomiting. A computed tomography (CT) scan reveals oesophageal perforation with associated mediastinitis.

Which artery supplies the upper one-third of the oesophagus?
explanation: The oesophagus is divided into three concerning its blood supply. The inferior thyroid artery supplies the upper third; the middle third is supplied by direct branches from the descending thoracic aorta (oesophageal arteries); finally, the distal third is supplied by ascending branches from the left gastric artery.
subject: Anatomy

stem:
A 25-year-old man is involved in a severe road traffic collision. Computed tomography imaging shows a haemoperitoneum secondary to a ruptured spleen.

Which of the following is the most accurate regarding the spleen?

options.text: May be absent and replaced with multiple splenunculi
Will be injured by a stab wound over the left sixth rib
The splenic artery passes to the splenic hilum in the gastrosplenic ligament
Venous drainage from the spleen passes directly to the inferior vena cava

explanation: Occasionally, the spleen may be absent and is replaced with multiple splenunculi. The spleen lies in the concavity of the left hemidiaphragm with its long axis lying along the tenth rib, extending between ribs nine and eleven. It is fully invested in the peritoneum, making it a peritoneal structure. The arterial supply is the splenic artery, which reaches the spleen via the lienorenal ligament. Venous drainage is via the splenic vein into the portal vein. Occasionally, the spleen may be replaced with multiple splenunculi.
subject: Upper gastrointestinal surgery

stem:
A 68-year-old heavy smoker presents to his General Practitioner with a drooping left eyelid, ptosis and miosis. A computed tomography (CT) scan shows a Pancoast tumour invading the stellate ganglion.

Which of the following descriptions best describes the relationships of the stellate ganglion?

options.text: Anterior to the neck of the first rib
Lateral to the angle of the first rib
Posterior to the neck of the first rib

explanation: In around 80% of people the inferior cervical ganglion fuses with the first thoracic ganglion to form the stellate ganglion (otherwise known as the cervicothoracic ganglion). The stellate ganglion lies at the level of C7, in front of the neck of the first rib.
subject: Physiology

stem:
You are in the ENT clinic reviewing a patient with a midline swelling of the neck. They wish to have the lump removed, but want to be reassured this will be risk free.

The differential diagnosis includes which one of the following?
explanation: The subhyoid bursa lies between the hyoid bone and the thyrohyoid membrane. Swellings of the neck in the midline include thyroglossal cysts and neoplasms, pharyngeal pouches, plunging ranulae, subhyoid bursae, laryngoceles and lesions in the thyroid isthmus.
subject: Head and neck surgery

stem:
A 22-year-old man, not known to have diabetes, is found to have a high blood glucose concentration two hours after sustaining major trauma in a road traffic collision. He has sustained significant injuries.

Increased secretion of which of the following substances is most likely to be responsible?
explanation: Adrenaline acts most rapidly through stimulation of glycogenolysis, causing blood glucose concentration to rise. During the metabolic response to trauma, there is increased secretion of catecholamines (such as adrenaline), cortisol, glucagon and growth hormone.
subject: Emergency medicine and trauma

stem:
A 55-year-old man has smoked two packets of cigarettes a day for many years. He has had a worsening cough for the past few months. In the past couple of weeks, he has occasionally noted blood-tinged sputum. Otherwise, he has no major health problems.

Which one of the following procedures should be done first to begin the investigation of his disease?
explanation: Sputum cytology is indicated as it can detect abnormal cells and can assist in differentiation between infectious conditions such as tuberculosis and lung malignancy. If however, the patient had a chest X-ray suggestive of lung malignancy then NICE guidelines suggest contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) of the chest to diagnose and stage disease. According to the most recent NICE guideline for the diagnosis and management of lung cancer, sputum cytology is rarely indicated and is generally reserved for centrally located masses or nodules seen on X-ray.
subject: Cardiothoracic surgery

stem:
A 63-year-old woman is seen with an enlarging mass in her thyroid and difficulty swallowing. She is later diagnosed with follicular carcinoma of the thyroid.

Which one of the statements is correct regarding follicular carcinoma of the thyroid?

options.text: It can be diagnosed by fine-needle aspiration cytology (FNAC)
It can be monitored for recurrence by calcitonin levels
The most common presentation is a hoarse voice
It has a higher incidence in iodine-deficient regions of the world
It is most common at puberty

explanation: Follicular carcinoma occurs more commonly in the Caucasian population, with an incidence higher in areas of the world where there is a higher incidence of iodine deficiency.
subject: Breast and endocrine surgery

stem:
You are incising and draining a perianal abscess and the consultant asks you about the anal canal and its anatomical relations.

How would you best describe the canal?

options.text: The canal lies above the levator ani muscle
The canal has no longitudinal muscular coat
The canal has lymphatic drainage via the inguinal lymph nodes
The canal has an external sphincter innervated by sympathetic fibres from the pelvic plexus
The canal is lined by columnar epithelium below the dentate line

explanation:
Lymph from the lower anal canal drains via the superficial inguinal nodes. The levator ani forms part of the deep external anal sphincter and the canal lies below this muscle. Lymph from the lower anal canal drains via the superficial inguinal nodes. The external anal sphincter is innervated by the inferior rectal branch of the pudendal nerve (S2–S4), while the internal sphincter receives a sympathetic supply from the pelvic plexus. The upper anal canal is thrown into vertical folds called anal columns, seen below in the image. Above the dentate line, which is visible in the image as a wavy line at the level of the internal anal sphincter, the canal is lined by columnar epithelium; below this level, this changes to squamous epithelium.

The dentate line represents the border between the hindgut and ectoderm. Drainage above the level of the dentate line is therefore into the inferior mesenteric vein territory via the mesorectum.
subject: Anatomy

stem:
A 75-year-old man is listed for an elective knee replacement. The anaesthetist requests pre-operative respiratory function tests due to a history of breathlessness.

Which of the following would be most consistent with a diagnosis of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis?

options.text: Diffusion capacity decreased, FEV1/FVC increased, total lung capacity reduced
FEV1/FVC reduced, total lung capacity increased
FEV1 reduced, total lung capacity normal, diffusion capacity normal
FEV1/FVC normal, total lung capacity increased, diffusion capacity increased

explanation: Diffusion capacity and total lung capacity is characteristically decreased in restrictive lung disorders, such as idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. FEV1/FVC is either normal or slightly increased with restrictive disorders, but is always reduced in obstructive disorders.
subject: Pathology

stem:
Your consultant has asked you to prepare a presentation for his second-year medical students on the anatomy and function of the distal convoluted tubule. You produce a diagram of the kidney and begin to label it.

The distal convoluted tubule is the site of which one of the following?

options.text: Principal water reabsorption in the kidney
The primary site of action of antidiuretic hormone (ADH)

explanation: The reabsorption of sodium in this segment is regulated by aldosterone.
subject: Physiology

stem:
A 22-year-old woman is referred to the general surgical clinic by her General Practitioner with a 2-month history of lethargy, intermittent per rectal blood loss and unintentional weight loss. She has experienced episodes of abdominal pain but is currently well and pain-free. Bloods shows microcytic anaemia and a stool sample is negative for infection. She undergoes a colonoscopy and biopsies, which are diagnostic for Crohn’s disease.

Which histological feature is most in keeping with this diagnosis?

options.text: Shallow mucosal ulceration in a confluent pattern without skip lesions

explanation: Transmural inflammatoryinfiltration on colonic biopsy is pathognomic of Crohn’s disease but is not seen in ulcerative colitis. In Crohn’s disease, there is transmural granulomatous inflammation which tends to predominantly affect the terminal ileum and proximal small bowel, but patchy inflammation can occur anywhere along the gastrointestinal tract. Although differential diagnoses for this patient could include either ulcerative colitis or Crohn’s disease, the presence of transmural inflammatory infiltration would be diagnostic of Crohn’s disease.
subject: Colorectal surgery

stem:
A 71-year-old woman is brought into the Emergency Department following a fall. She has sustained a laceration to the right side of her scalp over the superior nuchal line. When you remove the dressing there is a pulsatile bleed from the wound.

Which of the following arteries is most likely to be the cause of bleeding?

options.text: Parietal branch of the superficial temporal artery

explanation: The occipital artery is a branch of the external carotid artery, branching just before the external carotid passes behind the posterior belly of the digastric. It is crossed by the hypoglossal nerve and travels posteriorly as it ascends, passing between the transverse process of the atlas and the mastoid process, then running in a groove on the temporal bone. It pierces the trapezius at its attachment to the superior nuchal line. This artery supplies the posterior scalp.
topic: Blood Supply Of The Head And Neck
topicRaw: Blood Supply Of The Head And Neck
subject: Anatomy

stem:
A 65-year-old man with acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS) is in the Preoperative Clinic being assessed for a hip replacement. His HIV status is recorded and at the subsequent WHO meeting, the surgical team are aware so that they can prepare properly.

Regarding precautions, which of the following is true during the perioperative period?

options.text: This risk of HIV seroconversion following a needle stick injury is 2%
Eye protection would be unnecessary as there is no transmission from HIV-infected blood splashes to the eye
Suture of the wound should be carried out by two surgeons
Use of standard unenforced gowns is sufficient

explanation: Double gloving is recommended to reduce the risk of transmission of HIV.
subject: Perioperative care

stem:
A pregnant woman has increased levels of serum and amniotic fluid alpha-fetoprotein. Ultrasound scan (USS) reveals that the neural tube has failed to close rostrally.

What condition will the fetus have?
explanation: Neural tube defects can be detected pre-natally. The neural tube closure begins centrally and extends rostrally on day 24 and caudally on day 26 of gestation. Failure to close rostrally results in anencephaly. Alpha-fetoprotein levels can be raised in a number of conditions, and forms part of Down’s syndrome screening, and screening for neural tube and abdominal wall defects.
subject: Anatomy

stem:
A 68-year-old woman undergoes superficial femoral artery angioplasty after developing critical lower limb ischaemia. Two days later she complains of pain and you observe a pulsatile swelling in the left groin.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The scenario describes the case of a pseudo-aneurysm occurring secondary to the puncture of the femoral arterial wall that occurred during the procedure. This is a common side-effect of femoral punctures (can occur in up to 8% of procedures). Due to the breach in the vessel wall the blood leaks through but remains contained by the adventitia. It presents as a painful, tender, pulsatile mass with or without erythema of the overlying skin. Risk of rupture of a pseudo-aneurysm is higher due to the poor wall support and therefore requires immediate treatment when identified. Ultrasound can show turbulent flow causing the ‘yin–yang sign’ indicating bidirectional flow. Other complications associated with peripheral angioplasty include: infection, dissection of the artery, distal embolization, arterial rupture or spasm and in stent re-stenosis/thrombosis.
subject: Vascular surgery

stem:
You are examining a newborn baby who has an abdominal wall defect larger than 5 cm in diameter with a sac protruding. The umbilical cord arises from the apex of the sac. Within the sac are the intestines, liver, spleen and bladder.

What is the most probable associated anomaly?
explanation:
This patient has omphalocele (exomphalos major, > 4 cm defect) a congenital defect of the abdominal wall affecting 1 in 2500 live births. During normal development of the abdominal viscera, by the 6th week of embryonic development, the rapid growth of the liver and the intestines causes the midgut to herniate through the umbilical ring. By the 10th week, the abdominal cavity has grown enough to accommodate the organs and the midgut returns into the abdomen, with rotation and fixation of the duodenum and colon.

In exomphalos (omphalocoele) there is failure of the return of the midgut in the abdominal cavity and the intestine remains herniating into the umbilical cord. The herniating sac can contain bowel and liver and is surrounded by a peritoneal membrane. Exomphalos major is associated with a > 4 cm abdominal wall defect, whereas exomphalos minor is associated with a < 4 cm defect. Exomphalos major is associated with congenital heart defects (such as tetralogy of Fallot) in 50% of cases, limb abnormalities, ectopia cordis, bladder exstrophy. Exomphalos minor is less commonly associated with associated anomalies. Diagnosis is via routine antenatal ultrasound and can be suspected with a raised maternal serum a-fetoprotein..
subject: Anatomy

stem:
A 47-year-old woman undergoes excision of a skin cancer and direct closure. She is advised on the ideal conditions for wound healing.

Which of the following nutritional factors is required for RNA and DNA synthesis?
explanation: Zinc is an essential trace element required for RNA and DNA synthesis and for the function of some 200 metalloenzymes. If a patient is in a deficient state, zinc administration accelerates healing. However, excessive zinc can interfere with copper metabolism, which plays a role in the crosslinking of collagen and elastin.
subject: Perioperative care

stem:
You are treating a 52-year-old man with renal calculi. He has already had three admissions to the Emergency Department with renal colic.

What is most likely to predispose individuals to renal tract calculi?
explanation: Stones in the renal tract occur due to an increased concentration of urinary solutes such as calcium, uric acid and oxalic acid, or due to an increased concentration of urine during dehydration. Gout is caused by high uric acid levels and patients with gout are also at an increased risk of forming uric acid stones as uric acid deposits build in the kidney.
subject: Urology

stem:
A 24-year-old woman is admitted with a ruptured ectopic pregnancy and loses a lot of blood during her treatment. She is eventually discharged, but her haemoglobin has not yet returned to normal.

Which one of the following is true in a patient with anaemia and normal lungs?

options.text: p(O2) of mixed venous blood is reduced

explanation: Although the arterial p(O2) is typically normal, the p(O2) of mixed venous blood must fall. This is because mixed venous pO2 is related to oxygen delivery to the tissues. Anaemia reduces oxygen delivery, however the extraction by the tissues is the same. This results in a lower mixed venous pO2.
subject: Emergency medicine and trauma

stem:
An individual is exercising and their heart rate begins to rise. Starling’s law of the heart describes the strength of the heart’s systolic contraction.

Which one of the following statements about Starling’s law is correct?

options.text: It describes how the cardiac output is matched to mean arterial pressure
It explains how congestion in the left or right side of the heart is prevented
It states that cardiac output is determined solely by heart rate
It describes the relationship between afterload and stroke volume
It explains the effect of sympathetic stimulation on myocardial contractility

explanation: Starling described the intrinsic response of the heart to changes in right atrial and aortic pressure. With an increase in ventricular filling during diastole there is an increase in fibre length, which results in an increase in the force of contraction and stroke volume. This is an adaptation of stroke volume to venous return. As a consequence of Starling’s law of the heart the outputs of the two ventricles are the same and so congestion is prevented in either the right or the left heart. An increase of venous return to the right heart will increase right ventricular stroke work by Starling’s law of the heart and hence prevent right-sided congestion. The increase of right ventricular stroke work will therefore increase left atrial filling (assuming no changes to the pulmonary vascular circulation) and increase left ventricular end-diastolic volume and hence systolic stroke work to prevent left-sided congestion. All this assumes that the ventricles are operating on the ‘ascending’ limb of the Starling curve, which is generally the case. With heart failure when the heart muscle pump is not functioning normally, or is overstretched and operating on the plateau or descending limb of the Starling curve, there is a risk of congestion as either or both ventricular outputs cannot match changes to preload.
subject: Physiology

stem:
A 54-year-old woman has undergone some blood tests, as part of an employment health screen. She reports she is in good health and does not have any particular symptoms. She is taking bendroflumethiazide 2.5 mg for hypertension, and her BP is 132/82 mmHg. The only abnormality is a serum calcium concentration of 2.94 mmol/l (normal 2.20–2.60 mmol/l).

Which of the following is the most likely cause?
explanation: Primary hyperparathyroidism is a common cause of hypercalcemia, especially in asymptomatic patients. It is most often caused by a single parathyroid adenoma, leading to excessive production of parathyroid hormone (PTH). This results in increased calcium resorption from bone, increased renal calcium reabsorption, and increased production of 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D3. The patient's serum calcium concentration of 2.94 mmol/L is more consistent with primary hyperparathyroidism than with the mild hypercalcemia typically caused by thiazide diuretics.
subject: Breast and endocrine surgery

stem:
Your unit has been asked to take part in a phase II clinical trial of a new chemotherapeutic agent. This product requires a detailed knowledge of the cell cycle.

In the cell cycle, which of the following statements is true?

options.text: Duplication of cellular DNA occurs during G2 phase
RNA and proteins are synthesised during the G1 phase
Mitosis occurs during the S phase
The M phase is the longest phase of the cell cycle
Cells exit the cell cycle into G0 phase from the G2 phase

explanation: RNA and protein synthesis occur during the first growth phase, G1.
subject: Pathology

stem:
An anaesthetist is giving you teaching for the MRCS. They show you an ABG with some deranged parameters.

What would shift the oxygen–haemoglobin dissociation curve to the right?
explanation: A pH of 7.31 indicates acidosis, which shifts the oxygen–haemoglobin dissociation curve to the right. This effect is a feature of the Bohr effect in metabolically active tissue, the oxygen–haemoglobin dissociation shifts to the right ie for a given partial pressure of O2, oxygen will more readily dissociate. This situation means that more oxygen is delivered into the tissues to aid aerobic respiration. Active metabolic tissue will have a decreased pH (lactic acid production), increased temperature, increased 2,3-DPG levels and increased CO2 levels. The inverse of any of these parameters will shift the curve to the left.
subject: Physiology

stem:
A man presents with dysphonia and a possible laryngeal tumour. He attends the ENT outpatient clinic where he undergoes nasendoscopy.

Which of the following statements about laryngeal tumours is true?

options.text: The commonest form of benign laryngeal tumours are papillomas
Radiotherapy is not used in treatment of laryngeal tumours
Squamous cell carcinoma is the least common histological type
Total laryngectomy is always required for glottic tumours
The subglottis is the commonest site for laryngeal carcinoma

explanation: Papillomas are the most common benign laryngeal tumour, and are caused by human papillomavirus
subject: Head and neck surgery

stem:
You are working in the transplant team and have been asked to assist your consultant with an arteriovenous fistula formation in the patient’s non-dominant antecubital fossa.

In the cubital fossa, which is the most common anatomical arrangement from lateral to medial of the median nerve, biceps tendon and brachial artery?

options.text: Median nerve – biceps tendon – brachial artery
Biceps tendon – brachial artery – median nerve
Brachial artery - median nerve - biceps tendon
Median nerve - brachial artery - biceps tendon
Biceps tendon - median nerve - brachial artery

explanation:
The (ante)cubital fossa is a triangular area formed by a line between the two epicondyles of the humerus (superior border), the lateral border of the pronator teres muscle (medial border) and the medial border of the brachioradialis (lateral border). The roof is formed by antebrachial fascia, reinforced by the bicipital aponeurosis. Its contents are shown in the image below - from lateral to medial:

the radial nerve, beneath brachioradialis laterally

the biceps tendon

the brachial artery

the median nerve.
subject: Anatomy

stem:
You are asked to record fluid levels for the next 24 hours for a surgical patient on the ward. The nurse specialist suggests a 5% dextrose intravenous infusion.

Which of the following statements is correct regarding this type of fluid?
explanation: It is an isotonic fluid on administration, however the glucose is quickly metabolised and the resulting solution is hypotonic.
topic: Fluid Balance And Fluid Replacement Therapy
topicRaw: Fluid Balance And Fluid Replacement Therapy
subject: Perioperative care

stem:
A 61-year-old man presents with a long-standing mass of his right parotid gland that he has noted has increased in size over the last 2 months. He is being discussed at the head and neck MDT.

Which other features would be suggestive of a parotid malignancy?

options.text: Involvement of the cervical branch of the facial nerve

explanation: Clinical features suggestive of malignancy in the presence of a parotid lump include skin involvement, fixation, facial nerve palsy, trismus, and metastases (neck lump). A deep-lobe parotid tumor may medialise the palatine tonsil because of their anatomical relationship. While medialisation of the palatine tonsil can occur in both benign and malignant tumors of the parotid gland, it is considered among the features suggestive of malignancy when seen alongside other suspicious signs.
subject: Anatomy

stem:
Your consultant wants to start an elderly patient on a regime of total parenteral nutrition (TPN) as they are unable to tolerate oral feeds.

Which of the following statements regarding TPN is correct?

options.text: It may lead to copper deficiency within several days of commencement
It may cause life-threatening pancytopaenia through acute folate deficiency
It should be administered via a peripheral venous catheter
It provides approximately 500 kcal per litre
It requires no monitoring of blood glucose levels

explanation: Parenteral nutrition without giving folate or vitamin B12 will lead to megaloblastic anaemia and eventually pancytopenia.
subject: Perioperative care

stem:
You are reviewing a patient in the ear, nose and throat (ENT) clinic with a painful swelling around the jaw and you suspect there is a mass in the submandibular salivary gland.

Which of the following is true regarding the submandibular gland?

options.text: Has the facial artery running in close relation to (or grooving) its posterior surface
Is supplied exclusively by the external carotid artery
Drains via Stensen's duct into the floor of the mouth
Is enclosed within the investing layer of deep cervical fascia

explanation: The facial artery arises from the external carotid artery and passes deep to the posterior belly of the digastric and stylohyoid muscles. It then grooves the posterior surface of the submandibular gland before curving around the lower border of the mandible to enter the face. The artery is intimately related to the gland but does not pass through it.
subject: Anatomy

stem:
A 54-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with severe upper abdominal pain which is constant and localised to the right upper quadrant. She is tachycardic and pyrexial, with a positive Murphy’s sign. A diagnosis of cholecystitis is made. She is treated with antibiotics and is offered a ‘hot’ cholecystectomy.

Concerning this diagnosis and its treatment, which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: The cystic duct is a boundary of the cystohepatic triangle
Ultrasound is more sensitive than computerised tomography (CT) in the diagnosis of cholecystitis
Murphy's sign is pathognomonic for common bile duct stones
The common bile duct lies anterior to the portal vein in the free edge of the lesser omentum
Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) is the first-line investigation for gallstones

explanation: The boundaries of the cystohepatic triangle (Calot’s) are the cystic duct, the common hepatic duct and the inferior surface of the liver. The triangle's contents include the right hepatic artery, cystic artery, cystic lymph node, connective tissue and lymphatics.
subject: Hepatobiliary and pancreatic surgery

stem:
A 65-year-old man with a limp attends the Vascular Clinic with progressive pain in both buttocks and thighs at rest which now wakes him up at night. Despite the best medical management, his pain worsens, and he has been booked for an axillo bi-femoral bypass.

Which of the following is most accurate in relation to the axillary artery?

options.text: The axillary artery is divided into three parts by the pectoralis minor muscle
The axillary artery begins at the medial border of the first rib as a continuation of the subclavian artery
The thoracoacromial artery is a branch of the third part of the axillary artery
The axillary vein lies lateral to the axillary artery
The long thoracic nerve passes through the axilla posterior to the axillary artery

explanation:
The axillary artery begins at the lateral border of the first rib as the continuation of the subclavian artery and ends at the inferior border of the teres major. It is divided up into three parts by pec minor, with the axillary artery and the cut edge of pec minor overlying it from above:

from the lateral border of the first rib to the medial border of the pectoralis minor
behind the pectoralis minor
from the lateral aspect of the pectoralis minor to the inferior border of teres major.

The first part has one branch (superior thoracic), the second part gives off two branches (thoracoacromial and lateral thoracic), and the third part gives off three branches (subscapular, anterior circumflex humeral and posterior circumflex humeral).
subject: Anatomy

stem:
You have been asked to see a 63-year-old woman in the follow-up Breast Clinic who is 2.5 years following her diagnosis of a 34 mm invasive lobular breast cancer. She is asking you questions about her diagnosis.

Which of the following is most likely to be correct regarding a diagnosis of breast cancer?

options.text: Lobular cancers tend to be more often multifocal than ductal cancers
In men there will be a familial tendency in the majority of cases
Paget's disease of the nipple is associated with a good prognosis
Inflammatory breast cancer typically presents as a discrete, well-defined mass
The most common type of invasive breast cancer is lobular carcinoma

explanation: Lobular invasive carcinoma is more often multifocal and bilateral at diagnosis than ductal invasive carcinoma.
subject: Breast and endocrine surgery

stem:
Inflammatory aortic aneurysms are possibly a more severe form of degenerative abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA). They can be life threatening if untreated.

Which one of the following may lead you to confirm or suspect inflammatory aortic aneurysm?

options.text: They are always associated with an elevated procalcitonin level
They can present with abdominal pain
They are diagnosed exclusively by CT angiography
They do not require surgical intervention
They are more common in women than men

explanation:
Inflammatory abdominal aortic aneurysms are a variant of AAA, forming 5–10% of all AAA cases. They are most commonly found in younger patients (presentation age 5–10 years younger than presentation of atherosclerotic AAA), in the infrarenal abdominal aorta and are symptomatic. Symptoms include abdominal and/or back pain, fevers and weight loss. Risk factors include: male gender, smoking and family history. They are commonly associated with a raised erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) (90% of cases) and inflammatory markers. They are detected with CT scans/MRI, showing a cuff of perianeurysmal tissue and inflammatory changes. These spare the posterior wall. Radiological appearances relate to thickening of the adventitia with abundant inflammatory cells (lymphocytes, macrophages, plasma cells).

Initial treatment may require smoking cessation, steroids and immunosuppressive medication but definitive treatment is via surgery (open repair or EVAR). The inflammation involves the retroperitoneum as well leading to retroperitoneal fibrosis, causing entrapment of the ureters and progressively renal failure.
subject: Anatomy

stem:
An 85-year-old woman who is unfit for general anaesthesia undergoes spinal anaesthesia for debridement of a haematoma. She comes through the anaesthetic without a complication and her pain control is good.

Which of the following is a common complication of spinal anaesthesia?
explanation: Hypotension is a common complication of spinal anaesthesia. This is due to a reduction in sympathetic tone distal to the spinal block, subsequent venous pooling and reduced venous return. It can be managed with intravenous fluids or inotropic support if refractory to fluid replacement.
topic: Risk Factors For Surgery And Scoring Systems
topicRaw: Risk Factors For Surgery And Scoring Systems
subject: Perioperative care

stem:
A 61-year-old heavy smoker presents with recurrent chest infections treated with antibiotics from the GP. A mass is seen on his chest X-ray and a bronchoscopy confirms this is malignant in nature.

Which one of the following is a contraindication to resection?

options.text: Involvement of the recurrent laryngeal nerve

explanation: A malignant pleural effusion precludes from surgery as this implies a more advanced stage of tumour. A lung tumour must be sufficiently localised to be suitable for resection. Involvement of ipsilateral hilar lymph nodes is not usually a contraindication to resection but the presence of malignant cells in a pleural effusion is a contraindication.
subject: Cardiothoracic surgery

stem:
A 75-year-old woman presents to your breast surgery clinic with progressive tingling and numbness affecting the posterior aspect of her right arm and forearm and dorsolateral aspect of her hand. She also has a wrist drop. She had previously fallen asleep with her arm draped over her chair and noticed the numbness when she awoke.

The nerve most likely to be affected by this mechanism of injury is supplied by which nerve roots?
explanation: The brachial plexus is located partly in the neck and partly in the axilla. It is formed by rami, trunks, divisions, cords, and their branches. The supraclavicular part is located in the posterior triangle of the neck, and the infraclavicular part in the axilla. The brachial plexus is formed by the union of the ventral rami of nerves C5–C8 and the greater part of the T1 ventral ramus. C5 and C6 form the superior trunk, C7 the middle trunk, and C8 and T1 the inferior trunk. The anterior divisions supply the flexor parts of the upper limb and the posterior divisions the extensor parts. This clinical palsy is often described as ‘Saturday night palsy’ and is consequent to damage to the radial nerve. Clinically, this produces a wrist drop and numbness in the dorsum of the hand and wrist. Numbness of the posterior aspect of the arm and forearm may also be seen.
subject: Anatomy

stem:
A 45-year-old man presents to the general practice surgery with complaints of occasional headaches and increasing fatigue, especially during the daytime. He mentions that his clothes are becoming tight and his hat and shoe sizes have also increased. Physical examination reveals enlarged, swollen hands and feet, and coarse facial features, with frontal bossing and an enlarged jaw.

Which of the following is the most appropriate initial step in the management of this patient?

options.text: Computed tomography (CT) scan of the head

explanation: Insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1) is recommended as the initial screening test for suspected acromegaly. It is a highly sensitive test and normal levels usually exclude acromegaly. The presence of elevated IGF-1 confirms growth hormone excess and imaging should be performed to pinpoint the source. Levels must be compared with age-appropriate normal ranges.
subject: Breast and endocrine surgery

stem:
Hip surgery makes up a major part of orthopaedic emergency and elective work. Avascular necrosis of the femoral head is a severe complication.

It is most commonly seen following which one of these injuries?

options.text: Intracapsular fracture of the femoral neck
Intertrochanteric fracture of the femoral neck

explanation: Intracapsular neck of femur fractures are associated with disruption of the vascular supply to the femoral head. The incidence of avascular necrosis (AVN) is up to 15% in non-displaced fractures and increases to nearly 90% with untreated, completely displaced fractures.
subject: Orthopaedics

stem:
You are drawing the oxygen-haemoglobin dissociation curve for the benefit of some medical students. You demonstrate that the curve can shift to the left or right depending on various parameters.

With regards to this curve, what results in a decreased affinity for oxygen?
explanation: Pyrexia causes a shift in the oxygen–haemoglobin curve to the right. This means that for a given partial pressure of oxygen, less oxygen is bound to haemoglobin ie a decreased affinity for oxygen.
subject: Physiology

stem:
A 50-year-old patient presents with renal colic, and renal calculi are seen on imaging. Testing the urine reveals it is acidic.

What type of stones are most likely to form in this patient's urine?
explanation: Cystine and urate stones form in acidic urine and urine alkalisation forms part of the treatment of these types of stones. Cystine stones are poorly radiopaque on X-ray but can usually be seen on CT.
subject: Urology

stem:
A 28-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department having sustained a stab wound to the face. He has completely lacerated the mandibular branch of the trigeminal nerve at its origin.

Which of the following muscles would remain unaffected?
explanation: The posterior belly of digastric is innervated by the digastric branch of the facial nerve.
subject: Anatomy

stem:
A 26-year-old man is involved in a road traffic collision. At the scene, he has an oral and facial injury and respiratory stridor. After the initial evaluation, becomes apparent that he requires a surgical airway.

What is the most appropriate anatomical landmark for an emergency surgical airway in this patient?
explanation: This patient needs a surgical airway and has contraindications for oral and nasal intubation due to the facial and oral trauma. The surgical airways in a trauma scenario, when oral/nasal intubation is contraindicated, are a needle or a surgical cricothyroidotomy. Needle cricothyroidotomy can provide short-term oxygenation. A surgical cricothyroidotomy t is a quick procedure and provides a large-calibre airway that can be secured – however, it is not recommended for use in children under the age of 12. A cricothyroidotomy is made through an incision in the cricothyroid membrane.
subject: Anatomy

stem:
A 54-year-old man presents with a 2-week history of sweating, headache, constipation and itchy lesions over his back. His BOP is 162/94 mmHg and pulse 102/min. 24 h urinary catecholamines, metanephrines and vanillylmandelic acid are elevated. CT and 131I-meta-iodo-benzyl-guanidine scans confirm a phaeochromocytoma. He is also has a medullary thyroid carcinoma.

Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?
explanation: Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia II (MEN II) is an autosomal-dominant disorder caused by mutations in the RET proto-oncogene. MEN II has three distinct subtypes – MEN IIA, MEN IIB, and familial medullary thyroid carcinoma only. MEN IIA describes the association of medullary thyroid carcinoma, phaeochromocytomas and parathyroid tumours. Patients with pheochromocytomas may present with hypertension, tachycardia, sweating and headaches. Cutaneous lichen amyloidosis in patients with MEN IIA manifests as multiple pruritic scaly skin lesions in the scapular area of the back.
subject: Breast and endocrine surgery

stem:
A 65-year-old man patient undergoes an upper gastrointestinal endoscopy for a follow up of Barrett’s oesophagus.

What is the most likely histology of Barrett’s oesophagus?
explanation: Barrett’s oesophagus occurs due to metaplasia of the cells in the lower portion of the oesophagus, from the stratified squamous epithelium to the simple columnar epithelium. It occurs due to prolonged reflux and is considered a precursor for the development of oesophageal carcinoma.
subject: Upper gastrointestinal surgery

stem:
A 65-year-old man undergoes transurethral resection of the prostate due to benign prostatic hypertrophy. At his follow-up appointment, he complains of numbness on the lateral side of his left leg and difficulty walking. On examination, there is paraesthesia on the lateral side of the left leg and dorsum of the foot and he is unable to dorsiflex and evert the foot.

Which nerve is most likely to be injured?
explanation:
Patients who undergo surgical procedures while placed in a lithotomy position may show the development of lower extremity neuropathies, especially if the procedure takes longer than two hours. Several patient characteristics (eg thin body habitus, smoking, diabetes, the presence of subclinical neuropathies, anatomic anomalies), surgical factors and anaesthetic techniques have been identified as possible risk factors for perioperative lower extremity neuropathies.

Among the perioperative neuropathies, common fibular (peroneal)-nerve palsy is the most common to be affected in its two components, sensory and motor. The other types of neuropathies usually affect only the sensory portion of the nerve. The common fibular (peroneal) nerve wraps superficially around the neck of the fibula before dividing into the superficial fibular (peroneal) nerve, which amasses both sensory and motor fibers and the deep fibular (peroneal) nerve within the peroneal longus muscle, which is primarily motor but does supply sensation to the first dorsal webspace.

The common fibular (peroneal) nerve is responsible for dorsiflexion and eversion of the foot plus extension of toes. Its sensory area includes the anterior and lateral leg and dorsum of the foot. It is speculated that many perioperative fibular (peroneal) nerve palsies are associated with pressure at the fibular head on the common fibular (peroneal) nerve from contact with a hard surface, eg leg support.
topic: Patient Positioning And Avoidance Of Nerve Injuries
topicRaw: Patient Positioning And Avoidance Of Nerve Injuries
subject: Anatomy

stem:
The obturator nerve enters the thigh through the obturator canal and can become impinged in the rare event of an obturator hernia.

Which of these muscles are commonly innervated by the obturator nerve?
explanation: The obturator nerve (L2, L3, L4) exits the obturator foramen and divides into anterior and posterior branches. The anterior branch innervates adductor brevis, adductor longus, and gracilis. The posterior branch innervates the obturator externus and part of the adductor magnus.
subject: Anatomy

stem:
A 63-year-old woman is seen in the General Surgery clinic after having a positive result in a faecal occult blood test. She is due to undergo colonoscopy for change in bowel habit.

Which of the following is the most common category for the development of colorectal cancers?
explanation: Around 65% of colorectal cancers are thought to be sporadic – ie the genetic mutations present within these cancers are not inherited. Important risk factors in developing sporadic colorectal cancer include age, diet rich in red meat and low in fibre, smoking and obesity. Fewer than 10% of patients have a true inherited predisposition to colorectal cancer and these cases are subdivided according to whether or not colonic polyps are a major disease manifestation.
subject: Colorectal surgery

stem:
A 48-year-old woman is found to have high serum calcium and is subsequently diagnosed with hyperparathyroidism caused by a superior parathyroid gland adenoma. She is later booked for superior parathyroidectomy surgery.

From which pharyngeal pouch do the superior parathyroid glands develop?
explanation: The 4th pharyngeal pouch forms the superior parathyroid glands and a diverticulum called the ultimobranchial body. The cells of this body migrate into the thyroid gland, differentiating into the parafollicular cells of the thyroid gland which produce calcitonin.
subject: Anatomy

stem:
A 69-year-old smoker presents with painless haematuria and weight loss. He is diagnosed with bladder cell carcinoma.

Which one of the following statements is correct with regard to this diagnosis?

options.text: The most common chromosomal abnormality is the deletion of chromosome 9
Schistosomiasis is associated with adenocarcinoma of the bladder
Transitional cell carcinoma is the least common histological type
Smoking is not a significant risk factor for bladder cancer
Painless haematuria is uncommon in bladder cancer

explanation: Deletion of chromosome 9 is the most common chromosomal abnormality, along with alterations in the tumour suppressor genes p53 and Rb.
subject: Urology

stem:
A 54-year-old man with a normally functioning right kidney is undergoing a left nephrectomy for suspected renal-cell carcinoma. Your consultant asks you about the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system.

Where is aldosterone secreted from?

options.text: Zona glomerulosa of the adrenal gland
Zona fasciculata of the adrenal gland
Zona reticularis of the adrenal gland

explanation: The zona glomerulosa is the superficial layer of the three layers of the adrenal cortex. It produces and secretes aldosterone.
subject: Physiology

stem:
A 34-year-old patient undergoes bilateral breast reduction. During the operation, her arms are placed out in supine position. The theatre assistant forgets to place a gel pad.

Which nerve is most likely at risk of compression at the level of the elbow?
explanation: Pressure point management during surgery is vitally important to prevent iatrogenic pathology, including mononeuropathies. The ulnar nerve is at risk of compression at the elbow, as it passes behind the medial epicondyle. Fractures and cubital tunnel syndrome can also cause an ulnar nerve palsy at the elbow. Symptoms would include both sensory and motor deficits in the distribution of the ulnar nerve, as such, there would likely be weakness of the intrinsic muscles of the hand as well as paresthesia in the little finger and ulnar aspect of the ring finger.
subject: Anatomy

stem:
A 1-year-old child is admitted to hospital for cleft palate repair. Shortly after the procedure, the paediatric surgical CT1 is called to see her urgently as there is bleeding from the surgical site.

Which of the following is the best initial step to take?

options.text: Observe - This is normal and it is not necessary to do anything immediately
Call for help and manage the child using ABC first principles
Insert an oropharyngeal airway and commence bag-valve-mask ventilation immediately
Commence chest compressions at a rate of 100 per minute

explanation: All such cases require management according to first principles. The most probable cause of haemorrhage at this stage is that a suture has come undone. Children can become haemodynamically unstable very quickly. The child may need to be returned to theatre as an emergency to stop the bleeding, but this decision should be made by your seniors following assessment.
subject: Head and neck surgery

stem:
A 71-year-old woman presents to the Orthopaedic Department with weakness in the medial two fingers, numbness and tingling in lateral two fingers and dorsum of the left hand. She has a history of smoker’s cough which has now worsened in terms of severity. Vital measurements show an oxygen saturation of 90% on room air. She is unable to flex the lateral two fingers and motor strength of 2/5 in the left hand.

Which of the following is the next initial best diagnostic test to be done in this patient?
