explanation: To rule out pulmonary lesions, the first imaging is a chest X-ray, which is readily available. Small nodules, however, may not show up on a chest X-ray. Pancoast tumours are lung tumours that occupy the apex of the lung and can be detected on a chest X-ray. By compressing the brachial plexus, Pancoast tumours can cause superior vena cava syndrome or thoracic outlet syndrome, resulting in motor and sensory abnormalities in the upper extremity, which is the case in this patient.
subject: Vascular surgery

stem:
Before anaesthetising a patient, staff carry out their checks to ensure that the operation is being performed safely using the World Health Organization (WHO) surgical safety checklist. This is referred to as the ‘sign in’ stage of the procedure.

Which of the following forms part of these checks?

options.text: Pulse oximeter attached to patient and in working order

explanation: This is correct and forms part of the WHO check before induction of anaesthesia. Additional checks at this stage include confirming patient identity, site, procedure, consent, site marked, anaesthesia machine, allergies, difficult airway/aspiration risk and risk of large blood loss.
subject: Perioperative care

stem: Which of the following is the most influential cytokine involved in coagulation activation?
explanation: Interleukin-6 is released by macrophages and plays a key role in activation of lymphocytes as well as playing an important role in coagulation. IL-6 together with tumour necrosis factor are the most influential cytokines involved in coagulation activation.
subject: Pathology

stem:
A 56-year-old woman presents with a right-sided lump in the groin that has been present for the last few months. As this lump has been increasing in size, it has started causing pain and she has noticed some dilated vessels around the area.

Which of the following structures lies lateral to a femoral hernia and can cause the above presentation?
explanation:
Femoral hernias are protrusions of the peritoneal sac and contents through the femoral ring and the femoral canal. They occur more commonly in women. Femoral hernias have a characteristic neck as they protrude through the femoral canal, medial to the common femoral vein. Therefore, the common femoral vein can become indented and compressed by the hernia, leading to dilation of distal collateral veins, as seen in the patient scenario.

Femoral hernias occur posterior and inferior to the inguinal canal, inferior to the inferior epigastric vessels and lateral to the pubic tubercle.

Patients with a femoral hernia can also present with medial thigh and groin pain.

Remember: FEMoral hernias occur more commonly in women.
topic: Blood And Nerve Supply Of The Abdominal Wall
topicRaw: Blood And Nerve Supply Of The Abdominal Wall
subject: Anatomy

stem:
A 68-year-old man presents 2 months following a fracture-dislocation of the right elbow with progressively worse pain in the elbow, pins and needles in the right 4th and 5th digits, as well as a weak grip. When asked to hold a piece of paper between the thumb and index finger while this is pulled, you notice flexing of the interphalangeal joint of the thumb.

Which of the following is describes the sign explained above?
explanation:
This patient has ulnar nerve entrapment syndrome, causing a weaker grip. When the patient is asked to hold a piece of paper between the thumb and index finger, while the examiner is pulling the paper away, due to the lack of strength of the adductor pollicis (which is supplied by the ulnar nerve), the patient will compensate by flexing the interphalangeal joint of the thumb using the unaffected flexor pollicis longus (supplied by the median nerve). This gives a positive Froment’s sign. The ulnar nerve arises from the medial cord of the brachial plexus (C8–T1). After running down the medial upper arm, it passes posterior to the medial epicondyle to enter the forearm, at which point it is particularly prone to injury.

Symptoms associated with ulnar nerve entrapment include pain in the medial side of the elbow and forearm, paraesthesia in the 4th and 5th digits of the hand on the affected side, tenderness with palpation of the nerve medial epicondyle. There can be hypothenar or interossei muscle wasting and loss of power in grip in more severe cases.

Incomplete paralysis of the ulnar nerve, a claw hand can form.

Muscles supplied by the ulnar nerve (MAFFIA):

M – Median two lumbricals

A – Adductor pollicis

F – Flexor carpi ulnaris

F – Flexor digitorum profundus (medial half)

I – Interossei

A – Abductor digiti minimi and hypothenar eminence
subject: Anatomy

stem:
A 17-year-old man presents with fever, malaise and severe pain with swelling around the anus. This is on a background of a six-month history of diarrhoea and weight loss.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The most common type of anorectal sepsis is a perianal abscess (60%), and it is more commonly seen in men than women. Crohn’s disease is associated with an increased incidence of anorectal sepsis.
subject: Head and neck surgery

stem:
You are treating a patient with a pituitary tumour, which is affecting the posterior portion of the gland on CT scans. They are beginning to develop systemic manifestations of the disease.

Secretion of which hormone is most likely to be affected by this tumour?
explanation: The posterior pituitary secretes oxytocin and antidiuretic hormone (ADH) into the bloodstream. Oxytocin stimulates lactation in response to suckling.
subject: Anatomy

stem:
A 46-year-old woman has had dry eyes and dry mouth for many years and is diagnosed with Sjögren syndrome.

Which one of the following would be true regarding her saliva?

options.text: Flow rate would increase during nausea
Secretion from the parotid gland would be predominantly mucous
The parotid gland produces exclusively serous secretions at rest
The sublingual gland produces predominantly serous secretions

explanation: Sjögren's syndrome is a systemic chronic inflammatory disorder characterised by lymphocytic infiltrates in exocrine organs. Most common presentation is with sicca symptoms, ie xerophthalmia (dry eyes), xerostomia (dry mouth) and parotid gland enlargement. Salivary flow increases with nausea, both in patients with and without Sjögren’s.
subject: Head and neck surgery

stem:
A patient is suspected of having compartment syndrome. Before starting the case in theatre, the consultant questions you on the different muscular compartments of the leg.

Which of the following muscles is found outside of the anterior compartment?
explanation:
The peroneus brevis is found in the lateral compartment of the leg, along with the peroneus longus. The muscles of the anterior compartment of the leg are shown below in the image. They are:

tibialis anterior
extensor hallucis longus
extensor digitorum longus
peroneus tertius (not always present).

They are all supplied by the deep peroneal nerve and receive their blood supply from the anterior tibial artery.
subject: Anatomy

stem:
A patient is seen in the surgical endocrine clinic. They have developed systemic signs and symptoms which their General Practitioner (GP) is worried about, such as weight gain and malaise.

Which one of the following hormones is secreted by the anterior pituitary?
explanation: Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) is produced by the thyrotrope cells in the anterior pituitary. The anterior pituitary gland produces six hormones.
subject: Anatomy

stem:
During an oncology department multi-disciplinary meeting the consultant oncologist mentions that a patient has a very radiosensitive tumour. The consultant, therefore, recommends radiotherapy as part of the management plan.

Which of the following tumours is this consultant most likely referring to?
explanation: Seminoma is a very radiosensitive tumour. Standard treatment for seminoma after unilateral orchidectomy is radiation therapy, usually 20-40 Gy to the para-aortic regions up to the diaphragm (a higher dose is used for patients with a nodal mass); the ipsilateral ilioinguinal region is not treated routinely. Occasionally, the mediastinum and left supraclavicular regions are also irradiated, depending on the clinical stage.
subject: Urology

stem:
Nerve gas (organophosphate) is a weapon of chemical warfare that kills by causing respiratory and cardiovascular failure.

Which of the following is the expected effect of organophosphate poisoning on the heart?

options.text: To decrease the rate of rhythmicity of the sinoatrial (SA) node by inducing hyperpolarisation
To decrease the force of myocardial contractions by potentiating the vagal tone to the ventricular muscle
To increase norepinephrine release at the neuromuscular junction
To stimulate nicotinic receptors at the motor end plate
To inhibit acetylcholinesterase at peripheral nerve endings

explanation: The toxic effects of nerve gas derive from its ability to inhibit the enzyme cholinesterase. The inhibition of this naturally occurring degradative enzyme engenders a massive accumulation of acetylcholine evoking an overstimulation of the acetylcholine receptors throughout the body. In the heart, specifically, acetylcholine released by the vagal nerve stimulates muscarinic receptors in the cells of the SA node. This results in the opening of potassium channels and hyperpolarisation of the SA node. It therefore takes longer for sodium leakage to cause the membrane potentials of these cells to reach the threshold required for an action potential. The rate of SA node firing is therefore decreased.
subject: Critical care

stem:
As a last ditch attempt to avoid extra corporeal membrane oxygenation, nitric oxide is being used to treat primary pulmonary hypertension post meconium aspiration in one of your patients.

Which one of the following is true of nitric oxide?

options.text: It causes contraction of smooth muscle
It is produced exclusively by endothelial cells
It acts via cyclic AMP as a second messenger
It has a half-life of several hours in the circulation

explanation: Nitric oxide is soluble and this allows free diffusion between cells.
subject: Cardiothoracic surgery

stem:
A 35-year-old man is brought into the Emergency Department following a skiing accident. He is unresponsive on arrival with an obvious open fracture. He is profoundly hypothermic.

Which electrocardiogram (ECG) feature is most likely to be present?
explanation: The J wave may be present on the ECG in patients with hypothermia and is an additional upward peak immediately following the QRS complex.
subject: Perioperative care

stem:
A 26-year-old man presents 4 weeks after an eversion injury of the foot while playing football, with severe pain in the lateral aspect of the foot. On palpation, there was tenderness and a bony bulge felt on the dorsolateral aspect of the foot. The pain was increased by active and passive movements of the ankle and the patient reported difficulty in walking and running. An ankle X-ray revealed a cuboid bone fracture.

Which of the following bones does the cuboid NOT articulate with?
explanation: The cuboid articulates with the lateral cuneiform.
subject: Anatomy

stem:
A 55-year-old man with a family history of abdominal aortic aneurysm is asking about screening for the condition.

When and how is screening for abdominal aortic aneurysm performed?

options.text: One-off ultrasound for all men 60 years and older
One-off ultrasound for all men 65 years and older
One-off ultrasound for all men 55 years and older
One-off ultrasound for all men 70 years and older
One-off ultrasound for all men and women 65 years and older

explanation: All men at the age of 65 years are offered an ultrasound to screen for abdominal aortic aneurysm.
subject: Anatomy

stem:
A 35-year-old man with a history of alcohol abuse presents with an upper gastrointestinal haemorrhage. He undergoes an emergency oesophagogastroduodenoscopy, banding of the bleeding oesophageal varices.

Which anatomical structure lies anterior to the origin of the hepatic portal vein?
explanation: The neck of the pancreas is anterior to the origin of the hepatic portal vein. The hepatic portal vein is formed of the confluence of the splenic and superior mesenteric veins, just posterior to the neck of the pancreas. Portal hypertension arises secondary to hepatic pathology and causes portosystemic venous shunts. This leads to the development of oesophageal varices, which can rupture and cause torrential, often fatal, haemorrhage.
subject: Anatomy

stem:
You are clerking a patient in the pre-operative assessment clinic and they have a complement activation abnormality which is hereditary. You want to optimise them for their complex surgical procedure and refer them to the tertiary immunology service.

Regarding the complement system, which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: It is not a part of the coagulation cascade
The alternative pathway can be activated by endotoxins
The classical pathway is activated by IgA
C3a and C5a are not involved in the inflammatory response
The membrane attack complex consists of C5b-C7

explanation: The complement system consists of over 20 component proteins and is involved in bacterial killing. Complement can be activated by the classical pathway, alternative pathway or via the lectin pathway. In the alternate pathway, C3 is activated directly by endotoxins, viruses, bacteria, fungi and other parasites.
subject: Perioperative care

stem: Which one of the following takes place during inspiration?

options.text: A negative pressure of 1–3 mmHg is created

explanation: This statement is correct. During inspiration, the diaphragm contracts, enlarging the thoracic cavity and reducing intra-alveolar pressure relative to atmospheric pressure. The fall in intra-alveolar pressure typically ranges from -1 to -3 mmHg, which is sufficient to draw air into the lungs. It is essential to distinguish this from intrapleural pressure, which is already more negative and may fall to around –10 cmH2O during deep inspiration. This distinction clarifies that the value given refers to intra-alveolar pressure changes, not pleural pressure changes.
subject: Critical care

stem:
A 21-year-old patient presents with pes planus. They are struggling to take part in physical activity and want consideration of surgical intervention.

Which tendon, posterior to the medial malleolus, may be responsible for this presentation?
explanation: The peroneus brevis tendon grooves the lateral malleolus; the medial malleolus by the tibialis posterior tendon. The tibialis posterior’s main function is to support the medial arch and the foot when walking. The tibialis posterior tendon is seen below dividing into two at the level of the plantar calcaneonavicular ligament, with the superficial slip inserting on to the navicular and the deeper slip inserting on to the 2nd – 4th metatarsals.
subject: Anatomy

stem:
You are seeing a patient in the joint oncology clinic who is about to start a course of radiotherapy for adjuvant treatment of breast cancer. While waiting for the oncologist she asks you questions regarding radiotherapy as a general principle.

Which of the following statements is correct regarding radiotherapy?

options.text: The most common early side effects of radiotherapy are lethargy and skin reactions
Brachytherapy is a slow duration method of administering radiotherapy for patients with significant, eg pulmonary, pathology and therefore need a more gentle regimen
Radiotherapy has no role in the management of breast cancer
External beam radiotherapy is only given after mastectomy
Radiotherapy should be avoided in patients over 70 years old

explanation: Cancer patients are treated by external beam interstitial or intracavity radiotherapy. The effects of radiotherapy depend upon the dose, the tumour size, the tumour proliferation rate, the tumour radiosensitivity and the presence of anaemia and vascular disease. Radiotherapy can be palliative or curative. Lethargy is the most common side-effect. Skin effects are becoming less common as the more advanced radiotherapy machines are able to deliver peak dose below the level of the skin.
subject: Breast and endocrine surgery

stem:
An otherwise fit and well 25-year-old patient fractured his right tibia and is being treated non-operatively in an above-knee plaster. You see him in the clinic after his admission and the check X-ray demonstrates good progress.

What is the minimum time interval required for callus to become visible on radiographs?
explanation: Callus is formed and fluffy opacity appears on X-ray. This phase is labelled as phase of callus formation, which involves formation of scaffolding for new bone.
subject: Head and neck surgery

stem:
A 64-year-old man, who is a smoker, undergoes a left hemicolectomy. He develops a deep surgical site infection and receives IV Rocephin (ceftriaxone) for three weeks. To maintain his nutritional condition, he is placed on combined enteral and parenteral nutrition.

What most likely affects the vitamin K availability in this patient?
explanation: Prolonged treatment with broad-spectrum antibiotics, especially cephalosporins, results in vitamin K deficiency and bleeding diathesis. Vitamin K quinones are both consumed in the diet and produced by the gut microbiota. Vitamin K helps in the activation of clotting factors II, VII, IX and X. In patients on prolonged antibiotic therapy, the normal bacterial flora is reduced and this leads to vitamin K deficiency. This is clinically detected by a prolonged prothrombin time and a raised international normalised ratio (INR). Cephalosporins can also inhibit vitamin K epoxide reductase, preventing the production of the active form of vitamin K.
subject: Pharmacology

stem:
A 68-year-old woman presents with symptoms of dyspepsia. She has tested positive for Helicobacter pylori infection and been started on proton pump inhibitor (PPI) and eradication therapy.

Which one of the following tests, in common usage, has the highest combined sensitivity and specificity when used to detect Helicobacter pylori infection?

options.text: Serology for H. pylori IgG antibodies

explanation: The urea breath test detects radiolabelled carbon dioxide in the breath after ingesting radiolabelled urea (sensitivity 95%, specificity 96%).
subject: Upper gastrointestinal surgery

stem:
An 89-year-old man in hospital is on total parenteral nutrition (TPN). He is of average build and is not acutely unwell.

Which of the following regarding a TPN regime for an average sized adult is correct?

options.text: Fatty acids provide 10% of the non-protein energy requirement
In a patient with liver failure fatty emulsions should be avoided
The protein requirement is approximately 0.5 g/kg/day
Trace elements are not required in TPN formulations

explanation: In patients with liver failure, fatty acids are not tolerated.
subject: Perioperative care

stem:
A 6-year-old boy is brought to the Emergency Department with a few days’ history of general malaise, lymphadenopathy and periorbital swelling. He has had a fever and complained of a sore throat. On examination, he has a low-grade fever of 37.7ºC, with erythematous throat, enlarged tonsils and splenomegaly. Blood tests show signs of a haemolytic anaemia, with spherocytes on the blood film.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
This child presents with infectious mononucleosis, caused by the Epstein–Barr (EBV) virus, a member of the herpes virus family. This is also known as glandular fever. It presents in children with the triad of fever, pharyngitis and lymphadenopathy. It is also associated with fever, palatal petechiae, lymphadenopathy, periorbital oedema and enlarged tonsils. In later stages it can cause hepatomegaly or splenomegaly, which should resolve with symptom resolution.

Diagnosis is by detection of the EBV)heterophile antibodies. Infectious mononucleosis can be associated with secondary cold agglutinin disease which can lead to autoimmune haemolytic anaemia and can be detected with spherocytosis on the blood film, as is the case in this scenario.

Management is usually conservative with analgesics and antipyretics such as paracetamol and ibuprofen. Symptoms usually resolve in 2–3 weeks.
subject: Pathology

stem:
A 23-year-old man is stabbed in the abdomen. During an emergency laparotomy, a significant liver injury is noted. The Consultant is concerned about the severity of the haemorrhage and places a clamp on the hepatoduodenal ligament.

Which vessels have been occluded?

options.text: Hepatic artery and hepatic portal vein
Right hepatic artery and hepatic portal vein
Superior mesenteric artery and hepatic portal vein
Hepatic artery and inferior vena cava
Coeliac trunk and hepatic portal vein

explanation: Following its formation by the confluence of the superior mesenteric and splenic veins at the level of L1, the hepatic portal vein ascends in the free edge of the lesser omentum (the hepatoduodenal ligament). It is posterior to the hepatic artery proper and the common bile duct, with the bile duct lateral to the artery. These three structures enter the liver at the porta hepatis. Compression of the free edge of the lesser omentum for haemostasis is known as Pringle’s manoeuvre.
subject: Anatomy

stem:
A 32-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department after a motor vehicle collision. Vital measurements reveal a heart rate of 96 bpm, blood pressure of 110/80 mmHg and breathing rate of 17 breaths per minute. On radiographic examination, she is found to have a medial tibial plateau fracture.

Which of the following structures is most likely to be damaged with this fracture?
explanation: Fractures of the proximal tibia frequently extend into the articular surface of the knee. These fractures are referred to as tibial plateau fractures. Tibial plateau fractures can develop on the lateral or medial articular surface and are frequently associated with comorbidities. Fractures of the medial tibial plateau are frequently associated with tears of the medial meniscus.
subject: Head and neck surgery

stem:
Acute hypokalaemia can lead to muscle weakness and direct renal tubular cell injury. The causes can be classified according to the presence or absence of hypertension with reference also to the plasma renin activity and urinary potassium excretion.

Which one of the following is a cause of hypokalaemia without hypertension but with high plasma renin activity?
explanation: Gitelman’s syndrome can be either autosomal recessive or dominant and is characterised by hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis and with hypocalciuria and hypomagnesaemia. Blood pressure is low or normal.
subject: Urology

stem:
A 26-year-old man reports to the Emergency Department after sustaining an injury to the face while skiing. He has a small haematoma involving the upper eyelid.

Which bone is most likely to be palpated along the supero-medial margin of the orbit?
explanation: The frontal bone forms the upper part of the medial margin of the orbit. The lower part of the medial margin is formed by the frontal process of the maxilla. The medial margin is least well defined in comparison to the other orbital margins.
subject: Anatomy

stem:
An 81-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with a grossly distended tympanic abdomen and absolute constipation. He also appears confused. A plain abdominal X-ray reveals a grossly dilated large intestine but no evidence of pneumoperitoneum.

What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Computerised tomographic scan of the abdomen and pelvis
Rigid sigmoidoscopy and flatus tube insertion

explanation: For this scenario, the differential diagnosis is pseudo-obstruction, sigmoid volvulus and carcinoma of the distal colon/rectum. Computerised tomography of the abdomen and pelvis is the best option, as it permits the diagnosis to be obtained and the correct treatment instituted. Pseudo-obstruction may be associated with an underlying precipitating condition such as renal failure, electrolyte abnormalities, myxoedema, stroke, myocardial infarction, chest infection and retroperitoneal malignancy. Medical management comprises correction of electrolyte abnormalities, treatment of the underlying cause and use of the anticholinesterase inhibitor neostigmine (with heart monitor surveillance).
subject: Head and neck surgery

stem:
A 25-year-old man was stabbed in the right supraclavicular fossa. The knife punctured the portion of the parietal pleura that extends above the first rib.

What is the name for this portion of the parietal pleura?
explanation: The cervical pleura is also known as the dome or cupola. It is important to know that the pleura extends approximately 2.5 cm above the medial one-third of the clavicle, higher on the left. Pneumothorax is a potential complicating factor in neck stabbings.
subject: Anatomy

stem:
A 67-year-old woman presents to the surgical outpatient clinic with a palpable lump in her right groin. On examination, there is a palpable smooth lump in the femoral triangle.

Which of the following statements is true of the femoral triangle?

options.text: The floor of the femoral triangle is formed by the pectineus, iliopsoas and adductor magnus muscles
Clinically, a palpable lump found within the femoral triangle with no systemic symptoms in a woman patient is most likely to be a femoral hernia
The femoral triangle is bounded laterally by the adductor longus
The femoral canal contains the femoral artery
The roof of the femoral triangle is formed by the fascia lata

explanation: Femoral hernias are palpable lumps/ bulges found within the femoral triangle and are more common in women. They are differentiated from inguinal hernias by being found below and lateral to the pubic tubercle. They are caused by herniation of abdominal contents through the femoral canal. The management is surgical in nature. Other differential diagnoses of a femoral hernia include inguinal hernia, saphena varix, lymphadenopathy, lipoma, femoral aneurysm, sarcoma, ectopic testes and obturator hernia.
subject: Head and neck surgery

stem: Regarding the cranial foramina, which of the following statements is the correct answer?

options.text: The foramen rotundum allows passage of the maxillary nerve
The foramen lacerum allows passage of the external carotid artery
The foramen ovale transmits the mandibular nerve and the accessory meningeal artery
The superior orbital fissure transmits the optic nerve
The jugular foramen transmits the facial nerve

explanation: The foramen rotundum allows passage of the maxillary nerve (V2) as well as the artery of the foramen rotundum, a small branch of the maxillary artery.
subject: Anatomy

stem:
You are discussing cases in the urology MDT. The pathologist discusses the details of some of the cancers encountered at the meeting.

Which one of the following malignancies is most commonly multi-centric?
explanation: Transitional cell carcinomas can occur anywhere in the urothelium and multi-centricity and recurrence are common.
subject: Urology

stem:
A 5-week-old boy has been brought to hospital, having been persistently vomiting for the past 10 days, and bringing up what the mother describes as ‘curdled milk’. On examination, he is tired and there is a palpable mass in the right upper quadrant. Capillary gas reveals:

Investigation	Normal Value
pH	7.35–7.45
p(O2)	10-14 kPa
p(CO2)	4.5-6 kPa
Base excess (BE)	-2 to 2 mmol/l
HCO3	22-26 mmol/l
Sodium (Na+)	135-145 mmol/l
Potassium (K+)	3.5-5 mmol/l
Cl-	95-105 mmol/l

Which of the following is most likely to resemble the capillary gas result for this patient?
explanation: This baby has pyloric stenosis, and the classical blood gas picture is a hypokalaemic, hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis, with or without respiratory compensation, depending on the duration of symptoms. When the baby vomits profusely as they do in pyloric stenosis, H+, Cl–, and volume are lost, leading to relative gain in HCO3–; the gain in HCO3– is in turn enhanced by carbonic anhydrase producing more H+/HCO3–. The kidney preserves sodium as there is less chloride for sodium to be absorbed with (because of the loss of Cl– from the vomiting), and instead exchanges Na+ for H+. This worsens the alkalosis. Then, as H+ continues to fall, Na+ exchanges with K+, leading to hypokalaemia. As described in the explanation for answer A, the hypokalaemia can take up to 3 weeks of symptoms to set in, hence the potassium only being mildly decreased.
subject: Upper gastrointestinal surgery

stem:
A 2-year-old boy presents to the Emergency Department, as he has developed a right-testicular mass. An inguinal orchidectomy is performed. On the cut section, the tumour is yellow and mucinous. The histopathology shows the presence of areas resembling primitive glomeruli. A magnetic resonance imaging scan shows a diffusely enlarged heterogeneous testis with areas of haemorrhage and necrosis.

Which tumour marker is most likely to be raised?
explanation: The areas resembling primitive glomeruli are called Schiller Duval bodies. These are perivascular tumour cell collections seen in more than 50% of yolk-sac tumours in children. The tumour marker alpha-fetoprotein is characteristically elevated in > 90% cases of yolk-sac tumours. It is the most common testicular tumour in children under three and is also known as an endodermal-sinus tumour. Macroscopically, the testis is replaced by a gelatinous mass.
subject: Surgical oncology

stem:
A 35-year-old man presents for a blood sample in the Pre-assessment Clinic. You consider how the new puncture wound you have created is going to heal.

Which of the following regarding this process is correct?

options.text: During the inflammatory phase, neutrophils are the first leukocytes to appear in the wound
The tensile strength of the wound will reach up to 100% of that of normal skin after healing
Macrophages are the predominant cells by 48 hours
Fibroblast activity begins within the first 6 hours
Collagen synthesis is maximal in the first 24 hours

explanation: The inflammatory phase is dominated initially by neutrophils that appear in the first few hours and reach a peak in 24–48 h. Their main function is phagocytosis and cleaning the wound of bacteria and foreign material.
subject: Skin and wound management

stem:
A 25-year-old HIV-positive man presents with pain, swelling and fever in the mandibular region following a tooth extraction. He is admitted under the maxillofacial surgical team for intravenous antibiotics while cultures are awaited.

Which of the following options best describes actinomycosis infection in this patient?

options.text: Is caused by aerobic Gram-negative bacilli
Is treated with a short course of oral antibiotics only

explanation: Actinomycosis bacterial infections cause pus containing sulphur granules.
subject: Clinical microbiology

stem:
One of your patients has respiratory failure. You phone the medical registrar who reviews the patient and recommends BiPAP ventilation. The medical registrar asks what you know about this type of ventilation.

What would you tell them regarding BiPAP?

options.text: It is a form of continuous positive airway pressure ventilation (CPAP)
It is suitable for type II respiratory failure
It provides a fixed positive end-expiratory pressure only
It is contraindicated in patients with COPD
It requires endotracheal intubation for delivery

explanation: BiPAP has been shown to be an effective mode of treatment in acute hypercapnic respiratory failure (type II respiratory failure), particularly if this is related to chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). Other indications for non-invasive ventilation (NIV) include: obstructive sleep apnoea, cardiogenic pulmonary oedema (CPAP more effective), acute exacerbation of COPD with respiratory acidosis, acute on chronic hypercarbic respiratory failure due to neuromuscular disease or chest wall deformities, to wean off invasive ventilation if other strategies have failed.
subject: Critical care

stem:
A 69-year-old woman presents with bright red rectal bleeding. On examination, a firm mass is palpable in the proximal rectum. A rectal biopsy confirms the presence of invasive rectal adenocarcinoma and she proceeds to abdominoperineal resection.

Which group of lymph nodes primarily drain the lower part of the anal canal?
explanation: The superficial inguinal lymph nodes run parallel to and below the inguinal ligament and vertically along the great saphenous vein. In the perineum, it drains the lower part of the anal canal and the vagina. It is also involved in the drainage of external genitalia (excluding the testes), the lower abdominal wall below the umbilicus and the lower limb. The pelvic part of the rectum and the anal canal represent different lymph drainage territories. The pectinate line separates the two territories, but communication does exist between them (i.e. the lymphatics of the anal canal communicate with the perineal and rectal lymphatics). The lymph of the perineum and the anal canal is drained to the superficial inguinal lymph nodes, whereas the lymph of the pelvic territory flows to the iliac and lumbar nodes.
subject: Anatomy

stem:
A 35-year-old woman with severe rheumatoid arthritis is reviewed by her rheumatologist. It is noted she has not responded to disease-modifying antirheumatoid drugs (DMARDs) and has been unable to tolerate infliximab. It is decided to commence tocilizumab, an interleukin-6 inhibitor.

Which one of the following cell types is responsible for predominantly releasing interleukins?
explanation: Macrophages are phagocytic white blood cells that engulf and digest foreign substances and microbes. Interleukins are released predominantly by activated macrophages into the systemic circulation and have a wide range of effects. These include stimulation of acute phase proteins, stimulation of the hypothalamus to produce fever, and they may also have direct cytotoxic properties.
subject: Pathology

stem:
You are seeing a 43-year-old patient with frank jaundice, pruritus, pale stools and dark urine. Blood tests show a pattern consistent with obstructive jaundice and an ultrasound scan shows dilated intra- and extra-hepatic ducts.

Which one of the following statements is true regarding obstructive jaundice?

options.text: Gallstones are the commonest cause of obstructive jaundice in the UK
There is an excess of urobilinogen in the urine
Pancreatic head carcinoma is the commonest cause of obstructive jaundice in the UK
Conjugated bilirubin is increased in pre-hepatic jaundice
Alkaline phosphatase is characteristically low in obstructive jaundice

explanation: Gallstones are the commonest cause of obstructive jaundice in the United Kingdom. In this patient, jaundice is caused by an obstructing stone in the common bile duct (CBD) – the pressure in the system proximal to this area leads to dilatation of intra- and extra-hepatic biliary ducts proximal to the CBD.
subject: Hepatobiliary and pancreatic surgery

stem:
A 77-year-old woman develops central, crushing chest pain two days following surgery for a ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm. Her temperature is 37.0 °C, her heart rate is 110 beats per min and her respiratory rate is 28 breaths per min. An ECG shows ST segment depression.

Other results are below:

Investigation	Result	Normal value
White blood cell count	9 × 109/l	4–11 × 109/l
Oxygen saturation	99% on room air	94–98% on room air

What is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation: In light of a triad of central, crushing chest pain, tachycardia and ST segment depression on an ECG, the most likely diagnosis in this vignette is a myocardial infarction. Elevated levels of cardiac enzymes (troponin-T) help confirm the diagnosis, but can only be detected in the blood 5–7 hours after the onset of the infarction. The other differentials presented here are important to exclude when seeing a post-op patient with new-onset chest pain.
subject: Perioperative care

stem:
A patient with a prolonged smoking history is referred to the ENT clinic with an increasingly hoarse voice. You perform a nasendoscopy and discover a lesion in the larynx.

Which of the following statements is true regarding the vocal ligaments?

options.text: Are formed by the junction of the aryepiglottic and thyroepiglottic ligaments
Are formed by the superior free edge of the conus elasticus
Are formed by the inferior free edge of the quadrangular membrane
Contain the vocalis muscle within them
Are innervated by the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve

explanation: The conus elasticus is mostly yellow, elastic tissue. It is the lateral part of the cricothyroid membrane. Superiorly, its free edge forms part of the vocal ligaments.
topic: Airways Regional Anatomy Inc. Larynx And Trachea Regional Anatomy
topicRaw: Airways Regional Anatomy Inc. Larynx And Trachea Regional Anatomy
subject: Anatomy

stem:
A 42-year-old woman admitted for elective cholecystectomy revealed that she has factor IX deficiency.

Which of the following is true of factor IX?

options.text: Is a co-factor in the coagulation cascade
Acts by hydrolysing one arginine–isoleucine bond in factor X to form factor Xa
Is a vitamin K dependent factor

explanation: When activated into factor IXa, factor IX acts by hydrolysing one arginine–isoleucine bond in factor X to form factor Xa.
subject: Physiology

stem:
A 35-year-old man is admitted to the Intensive Care Unit after being stabbed in the chest. He weighs 80 kg and is deemed stable on arrival, but a chest X-ray shows fluid sitting in the pleural cavity. When a chest drain is inserted, approximately 1 litre of blood is removed.

Which option will best describe the patient’s clinical state following the loss of 1 litre of blood?

options.text: Pulse = 100; blood pressure = 120/90; respiratory rate = 20; mental state is agitated but orientated
Pulse = 100; blood pressure = 120/80; respiratory rate = 20; mental state is normal
Pulse = 120; blood pressure = 90/60; respiratory rate = 30; mental state is confused (Class III)
Pulse = 140; blood pressure = 70/40; respiratory rate = 40; mental state is lethargic (Class IV)
Pulse = 80; blood pressure = 130/85; respiratory rate = 16; mental state is alert (Class I)

explanation:
This option is describing stage II of hypovolaemic/haemorrhagic shock. This patient has lost somewhere between 15 and 30% of their circulating volume (class II). Circulating volume is about 5 litres but it does vary with gender and weight. This patient is likely to have a circulating volume of about 6 litres.

A mnemonic to remember the classes of haemorrhage in trauma is described below. As it progresses, remember that pulse rate and respiratory rate increase, while blood pressure, pulse pressure and urine output decrease.

GCS in Class I and II is normal and reduced in III and IV:

0–15 — < 15% — less than 750 ml blood loss
15–30 — 15–30% — 750 to 1500 ml blood loss
30–40 — 30–40% — 1500 to 2000 ml blood loss
 — > 40% — > 2000 ml blood loss
subject: Emergency medicine and trauma

stem:
A 42-year-old woman undergoes a transverse rectus abdominis myocutaneous (TRAM) breast reconstruction following mastectomy for breast cancer. The anaesthetist inserts a central venous pressure (CVP) line for monitoring.

Which one of the following statements regarding CVP is correct?

options.text: In normovolaemia after administration of a 200 ml bolus of colloid intravenously there will be a fall in CVP sustained for 10 min
It can be estimated by examining the internal jugular vein
It directly measures left ventricular end-diastolic pressure
It can only be measured using a Swan-Ganz catheter
It is unaffected by positive pressure ventilation

explanation: Central venous pressure (CVP) can be estimated by examining the height of the pulsation in the internal jugular vein. The height of the pulsation (in cm) should be compared with the angle of Louis as the patient sits at 45° to the horizontal.
topic: Central And Peripheral Venous Line Insertion
topicRaw: Central And Peripheral Venous Line Insertion
subject: Breast and endocrine surgery

stem:
A 58-year-old woman undergoes an emergency laparotomy for a perforated sigmoid diverticulum. One hour after surgery she is persistently hypotensive despite fluid resuscitation and requires vasopressor support. During review, it is noted that she is peripherally vasodilated. Several intravenous infusions are running, one of which has this vasodilatory effect as its primary pharmacological action.

What is the most likely cause of the peripheral vasodilation?
explanation: Sodium nitroprusside is a potent arterial and venous vasodilator that acts by releasing nitric oxide, leading to smooth muscle relaxation. It is used to induce controlled hypotension during anaesthesia or to manage hypertensive crises. Its vasodilatory effect reduces systemic vascular resistance, which can contribute to persistent hypotension in a postoperative setting if not carefully titrated. Among the agents listed, sodium nitroprusside is the only one that directly causes widespread peripheral vasodilation as a primary pharmacological action.
topic: Mode Of Action Of Drugs In Cardiology
topicRaw: Mode Of Action Of Drugs In Cardiology
subject: Pharmacology

stem:
A 40-year-old man has been started on omeprazole due to dyspepsia. Gastric acid secretion is important for the pH of the stomach.

Which one of the following statements about gastric acid is correct?
explanation: Acetylcholine released by the enteric neurons in response to vagal nerve stimulation promotes the production of acid by the stomach.
subject: Colorectal surgery

stem:
A patient presents with a painful slowly enlarging left parotid mass and a facial nerve palsy. They are discussed at the head and neck MDT.

The most likely lesion is which one of the following?
explanation: The facial nerve involvement points to a malignant tumour and while pleomorphic adenomas have malignant potential this is usually noted by a sudden increase in size, not a facial nerve palsy. Adenoid cystic carcinomas are a rare salivary gland tumour that is high grade and can lead to a facial nerve palsy.
subject: Anatomy

stem:
During a difficult vaginal delivery, the senior house officer (SHO) on call was asked to come and make an episiotomy. She made a midline episiotomy and in doing so cut too far through the perineal body into the structure immediately posterior.

Which one of the following structures did she cut?
explanation:
An episiotomy is a perineal incision used in labour. The episiotomy has the effect of enlarging the distal birth canal – often the purpose is to prevent trauma to and damage of the perineal structures in breech or forceps delivery, in which there is a risk of this occurring.

A midline episiotomy is made from the posterior vagina through the perineal body with a risk of damage to the external anal sphincter if extended too far. The rectum can also be damaged with this procedure.

Most episiotomies are, however, posterolateral rather than midline – this procedure is safer and avoids the risk of damage to the external anal sphincter and rectum.
subject: Colorectal surgery

stem:
A 19-year-old man attends the Day Surgery for an elective open repair of a right inguinal hernia. During the procedure, the spermatic cord is encountered.

Which of the following structures is not within the contents of the spermatic cord?

options.text: Genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve
Femoral branch of the genitofemoral nerve
Lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh

explanation: The ilioinguinal nerve arises from the L1 nerve root and the iliohypogastric nerve and tends to lie on the cord but not within it.
subject: Anatomy

stem:
Commensal organisms have the potential to be pathogenic if there is a breach of the body’s defence system or when outside of their normal environment.

Which of these micro-organisms is correctly matched with where it is found as normal flora?
explanation: Diphtheroids, along with coagulase-negative staphylococci, are normal skin flora.
subject: Clinical microbiology

stem:
A 45-year-old man was referred by his GP with back pain, urinary retention and saddle paraesthesia for 10 h. On examination, he has bilateral altered sensation in his legs and reduced anal tone.

What is the next step in management?

options.text: MRI scan of the lumbar spine
Computed tomography (CT) myelogram of the lumbar spine
Plain X-ray of the lumbar spine
CT scan of the lumbar spine without contrast

explanation: This patient has classic symptoms of cauda equina syndrome. The most important next step is to confirm the diagnosis with an MRI scan to evaluate neurological compression. In patients who are unable to undergo an MRI such as those with pacemakers and claustrophobia, a CT myelogram is an alternative. Cauda equina syndrome is a complex of low back pain, bilateral or unilateral sciatica, saddle anaesthesia, motor weakness and bowel/bladder dysfunction. Studies have shown improved outcomes in bowel and bladder function and resolution of motor and sensory deficits when decompression performed within 48 h of the onset of symptoms.
subject: Orthopaedics

stem:
You are in breast clinic reviewing a patient with a lesion detected via the national screening programme. You have read a recent article regarding the need to be conscious of bias in such screening programmes.

In general, screening programmes for cancer are susceptible to which one of the following?
explanation: Results of screening programmes for cancer are limited by selection, length and lead-time bias. Lead-time bias occurs when screening advances the date at which diagnosis is made. This, therefore, lengthens the calculated survival time without necessarily altering the date of death. Length bias can also affect screening programmes. This is the tendency for screening to detect a disproportionate number of cancers that are slow-growing and have a better prognosis anyway.
subject: Breast and endocrine surgery

stem:
A man weighing 100 kg is brought to the Emergency Department after being caught in a house fire. The primary survey is unremarkable with the exception of obvious burns of both of his anterior lower limbs and both palms. You want to start immediate fluid resuscitation.

How much fluid should you give this patient over the first 8 hours (according to Advanced trauma life support (ATLS) 10th edition guidelines)?
explanation:
Patients with burns require significant fluid resuscitation, which can be calculated using the formula 2 ml × weight in kg × % burn, as per the latest version of the advanced trauma life support (ATLS) guidelines. Adult patients with deep-partial and full-thickness burns involving more than 20% total body surface area (TBSA) should receive initial fluid resuscitation of 2 ml/kg/%TBSA. In paediatric burns 3 ml/kg/%TBSA should be used, and 4 ml/kg/%TBSA used for electrical burns. The first half of the fluid should be given over the course of eight hours and the remaining half is provided over the next 16 hours.

The area of a burn can be calculated using the rule of 9s or the Lund and Browder chart. Each lower limb is 18% (9% anterior and 9% posterior). In this patient, the anterior surfaces of both lower limbs have been burnt. The palms are 1% each. Therefore, the total burn % would be 20%. Accordingly, 4000 ml should be given in 24 hours, of which 2000 ml should be given within the first eight hours.
subject: Skin and wound management

stem:
A 50-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department in the morning at 9 am due to a laceration in his right forearm. He has diabetes mellitus. He cut himself accidentally last evening at 5 pm when he broke a glass and washed the injury at home and put a dressing on it. On examination, the cut is deep, 6 cm in length, clean and without redness or warmness around its borders.

What is the most appropriate management option?
explanation:
The optimal length of time between injury and laceration repair has not been adequately defined. In patients without risk factors for a poor wound outcome, most simple lacerations that are small (eg < 5 cm in length), do not have gross contamination and are not located on the lower extremities can be closed up to 12–18 hours later with little risk of infection. By contrast, closure beyond 12 hours after injury should be avoided for large wounds (longer than 5 cm in length), contaminated wounds or lacerations in individuals with risk factors for poor outcomes.

Delayed primary closure, or tertiary intention closure, consists of initial cleaning and debridement of the wound followed by at least a 4-to-5-day waiting period prior to wound closure. This waiting period permits the host defence system to decrease bacterial load and to evacuate possible wound infection. It should be considered for uncomplicated wounds (clean, no foreign body) that present after the safe period for primary closure.

Examples of complex wounds include:

animal and human bites likely harbouring high bacterial loads, coupled with complex injuries to the soft tissue (ie crushing, avulsions and multiple perforations)
wounds older than 24 hours that were insufficiently cleansed, debrided or decontaminated
wounds older than 24 hours that present in the setting of advanced age, diabetes mellitus, renal impairment, impaired nutrition, smoking, obesity and chronic steroid use.

At the time of closure, additional debridement may be needed and excessive accumulated granulation tissue trimmed back to the wound margins.
subject: Skin and wound management

stem:
A 17-year-old man is brought to the Emergency Department following a road traffic collision and is quickly diagnosed with hypovolaemic shock. Several attempts at intravenous cannulation are unsuccessful. An incision is made anterior to the medial malleolus.

Which vessel should be cannulated?
explanation: The long (or ‘great’) saphenous vein passes anterior to the medial malleolus of the tibia before ascending up the medial aspect of the leg. It traverses the posterior aspect of the femoral medial epicondyle before ascending to penetrate the fascia lata and confluence with the femoral vein at the saphenofemoral junction. It can be accessed via an incision anterior to the medial malleolus when emergency venous access is required. Another option in this scenario would be to consider intraosseous access.
topic: Central And Peripheral Venous Line Insertion
topicRaw: Central And Peripheral Venous Line Insertion
subject: Anatomy

stem:
You take a set of arterial blood gases from a patient on 28% oxygen and discover that the oxygen saturation differs significantly from the pulse oximeter reading.

What could cause inaccuracy of the pulse oximeter reading?
explanation: Arrhythmias can affect pulse oximetry accuracy because the device relies on regular pulsatile blood flow to detect arterial oxygen saturation. In patients with irregular rhythms, such as atrial fibrillation or frequent ectopic beats, the pulse waveform may become erratic or difficult for the sensor to interpret, resulting in signal artefact or false readings. This is particularly problematic when combined with other factors like hypotension or poor perfusion.
subject: Physiology

stem:
You are reviewing a patient with a rash on their legs and a diagnosis of thrombophlebitis migrans is made. Additional investigations may be required.

With which of the following is this associated?
explanation: Thrombophlebitis migrans, also known as Trousseau’s sign of malignancy, is a migratory thrombophlebitis causing recurrent episodes of superficial thrombophlebitis in the low extremities. It has a strong association with visceral carcinoma, most commonly adenocarcinoma of the pancreas, lung, stomach and genital tract.
subject: Hepatobiliary and pancreatic surgery

stem:
A 35-year-old woman currently being treated for malignant melanoma has two first-degree relatives who have also been diagnosed (her mother and older sister). She has a young daughter and they are referred on to a genetic counselling service.

Which of the following are associated with a high risk for developing melanoma?
explanation: Familial melanoma is recognised in around 1–2% of patients when two first-degree relatives also have melanoma. Although many genetic causes are unrecognised and unstudied, many familial links have been found. BRCA1 carries with it a higher risk of melanoma, along with breast and ovarian cancer.
subject: Breast and endocrine surgery

stem:
A 22-year-old patient with a bleeding tendency was investigated and diagnosed with gray platelet syndrome (GPS). They require an emergency open reduction and internal fixation of a spiral fracture of the humerus. You seek advice from the haematologist to optimise their clotting for the procedure.

Which one of the following components is deficient in this patient’s platelets?
explanation: In GPS there is a reduction or absence of alpha granules in the platelets. GPS is a very rare inherited disorder that is characterised by thrombocytopenia, abnormally large, agranular platelets in peripheral blood smears (which appear grey), splenomegaly, and myelofibrosis. Alpha platelet granules normally serve to promote platelet adhesion and wound healing. Patients with GPS may present with prolonged bleeding following injury, nosebleeds and easy bruising.
subject: Pathology

stem:
The uterine artery is a key blood vessel in the pelvis. When ligated, other structures related to it can be injured.

Which one of the following statements concerning the uterine artery is most correct?

options.text: It lies anterior and superior to the ureter near the lateral portion of the fornix
The point at which it crosses the ureter is 4 cm superior to the ischial spine
It crosses inferior to the ureter in the broad ligament
It is a direct branch of the internal iliac artery that runs in the round ligament
It anastomoses with the inferior mesenteric artery at the cervix

explanation: The uterine artery crosses anterior and superior to the ureter near the lateral portion of the fornix. This relation is of surgical importance as the ureter is in danger of being damaged at the time of a hysterectomy.
topic: Uterus And Fallopian Tubes Regional Anatomy
topicRaw: Uterus And Fallopian Tubes Regional Anatomy
subject: Anatomy

stem:
A 65-year-old woman has been referred to the orthopaedic team with bone pain. On further investigation, she is found to have renal failure and pneumococcal pneumonia.

In this setting, a bone marrow biopsy is most likely to show numerous:
explanation: The features are suggestive of multiple myeloma. Multiple myeloma is a malignancy of plasma cells that produce monoclonal immunoglobulin and invade and destroy adjacent bone tissue. Common manifestations include bone pain, renal insufficiency, hypercalcaemia, anaemia and recurrent infections. Plasma cell clones produce a monoclonal (M) protein leading to renal failure caused by light chains or hyperviscosity. Diagnosis requires the demonstration of M-protein (sometimes present in urine and not serum) and either lytic bone lesions, light-chain proteinuria or excessive marrow plasma cells.
subject: Pathology

stem:
You are assisting the paediatric orthopaedic consultant. They ask you about likely cases you will see in the clinic.

What is the commonest pathological cause of the limping child aged 4–8 years?
explanation: Perthes’ disease is a condition in which avascular necrosis of the femoral head occurs. The incidence is approximately 1 : 10 000, the male to female ratio is 4 : 1. It presents between the ages of 4 and 8 years with a limp. The characteristic X-ray appearances may not become evident for up to 3 months after initial presentation.
subject: Paediatric surgery

stem:
An 8-year-old girl presents with right iliac fossa pain and a fever. An ultrasound is suggestive of appendicitis and she has an open appendectomy.

What is the main mechanism of heat loss during surgery?
explanation: Radiation is the transfer of heat through electromagnetic waves and heat loss through this occurs all the time. Radiation is the major source of heat loss in surgical patients contributing up to 40% of heat loss.
subject: Emergency medicine and trauma

stem:
A 12-year-old boy undergoes a diagnostic laparoscopy for right iliac fossa pain. The appendix looks normal but prominent lymph nodes are noted in the small bowel mesentery.

Which of the following best describes the small bowel mesentery?

options.text: Blood vessels traversing the small bowel supply the large bowel
Contains goblet cells in the epithelium of the duodenum only
Is attached to the posterior abdominal wall by the mesentery proper
Receives its blood supply from the inferior mesenteric artery

explanation: The small bowel mesentery contains the superior mesenteric artery, which supplies the mid-gut; this includes the large bowel as far as the distal transverse colon. The veins in the mesentery are all tributaries of the portal system. The root of the small bowel mesentery extends from a point to the left of the L2 vertebra, at the duodenojejunal junction, down to the right sacroiliac joint.
subject: Colorectal surgery

stem:
In clinical examination of the chest, accurate knowledge of the surface markings of the lungs is essential.

Which of the following corresponds to the clinical situation?

options.text: The oblique fissure of the lung corresponds to the medial border of the scapula when the arm is fully abducted
The lower border of the lung on each side corresponds to the tenth rib in the mid-axillary line
The horizontal fissure of the right lung runs along the fourth costal cartilage
The apex of the lung extends 5 cm above the medial third of the clavicle
The lower border of the lung on each side corresponds to the eighth rib in the mid-axillary line

explanation: The superior part of the right oblique fissure separates the right upper lobe from the right lower lobe and the inferior part separates the right middle lobe from the right lower lobe. Its approximate position can be marked by a curved line on the thoracic wall that begins roughly at the spinous process of the T4 level of the thoracic spine, then crosses the fifth intercostal space laterally, before following the contour of the right 6th rib anteriorly. The left oblique fissure separates the left upper lobe from the left lower lobe. Its approximate position can be marked by a curved line on the thoracic wall that begins between the spinous processes of vertebrae T3 and T4, then crosses the 5th intercostal space laterally, before following the contour of the 6th rib anteriorly. When the arms are fully abducted, the medial border of the scapula parallels the position of the oblique fissure bilaterally. This can be used as a rough guide for determining the surface projections of the superior and inferior lobes of the lung.
subject: Anatomy

stem:
A patient is referred to the Ear, Nose and Throat (ENT) clinic by their General Practitioner. On examination, there is a skin lesion in their mouth and the patient is concerned regarding cancer.

Which of the following is correct regarding leukoplakia?

options.text: It is only seen in the oral mucosa
Management includes a biopsy and regular follow-up
Surgical excision is always the first-line treatment
It is caused exclusively by tobacco use

explanation: Leukoplakia, meaning ‘white patch’, is seen primarily on the oral, vulval, or vaginal mucosa. Leukoplakia in the mouth is mostly seen in older men with a history of smoking. Ill-fitting dentures and teeth in poor state are also often associated with this condition. The lesions are elevated, sharply defined patchy areas of keratinisation and are generally lighter in colour (white to grey) than the surrounding tissue. When long-standing or chronic, the lesions may exhibit a verrucoid appearance. In smaller lesions, the treatment is generally non-operative, with lip cream, emollients or ointments. Smokers should refrain from the habit. Poorly fitting dentures are refitted and operative dentistry carried out where indicated. Management remains slightly controversial, as a recent meta-analysis has not conclusively proven that surgical excision is more effective at preventing malignant change compared to no treatment or placebo. Simple excision of the involved mucosa remains the primary form of treatment (over the lips, this procedure is called a lip shave or vermilionectomy).
subject: Head and neck surgery

stem:
A 54-year-old man underwent a right hemicolectomy. Five days post-operatively, he becomes short of breath with abdominal pain. A pulmonary embolism (PE) is suspected and he is given a treatment dose of heparin. Computed tomography pulmonary angiogram and abdomen/pelvis with contrast shows no PE but detects an anastomotic leak. The patient is booked for an emergency laparotomy.

Which of the following medications should be given in view of the recent dose of heparin?
explanation: Protamine sulphate works by binding with heparin to reverse its effects. This patient requires urgent surgery and should be discussed with the haematologist and receive protamine.
subject: Perioperative care

stem:
An obese patient with profound haemodynamic shock requires emergency intravenous access. The anaesthetic team are able to place a central line in the right subclavian vein.

Which is the least likely structure to be damaged?
explanation: Remember the thoracic duct is on the right side of the thorax, only up to the level of the sternal angle, where it crosses over to the left. The thoracic duct enters the posterior mediastinum along with the aorta as the continuation of the cisterna chyli. It ascends on the right side between the aorta and the azygos vein until the T4–T5 level (at the manubriosternal angle), where it crosses to the left, draining eventually into the junction of the left subclavian and left internal jugular veins. A right-sided subclavian line would not be at risk of damaging the thoracic duct, but a left-sided might, with the subsequent complication of chylothorax.
subject: Cardiothoracic surgery

stem:
During an elective repair of an aortic aneurysm, you are asked to identify a vessel that passes posterior to the inferior vena cava, the head of the pancreas and the duodenum.

What is the best description of this vessel?
explanation: The right renal artery usually arises slightly lower than the left. It passes posterior to the inferior vena cava (IVC), the right renal vein, the head of the pancreas and the duodenum. It divides before reaching the renal hilum and, as with the left renal artery, gives branches that supply the adrenal gland and the proximal ureter. It would not be safe to divide this vessel, although occasionally, accessory renal arteries present branching directly off the aorta.
subject: Anatomy

stem:
A 33-year-old man requires an emergency fasciotomy for left lower limb compartment syndrome. Pre-operative screening for an upcoming elective shoulder arthroscopy has found him to be a nasal carrier of Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA). He has not yet followed an MRSA eradication protocol.

Which of the following is the most appropriate course of action?

options.text: Admit the patient for the procedure as normal and ensure they undertake a standard 5-day eradication process post-operatively on a normal ward
Admit the patient for the procedure as normal, cover with appropriate antibiotic prophylaxis and ensure a side room is available post-operatively
Cancel the procedure and rebook when the patient is MRSA negative
Refuse to operate and refer to infectious diseases team
Postpone surgery for 6 weeks of decolonisation treatment

explanation: Admit the patient for the procedure as normal, cover with appropriate antibiotic prophylaxis and ensure a side room is available post-operatively. This patient’s emergency operation is the first priority. They should be covered for the procedure with appropriate antibiotics and then post-operatively be placed in a side room to reduce the risk of spreading MRSA to other patients. Ensure they undertake a standard 5-day eradication process post-operatively.
topic: Hospital Acquired Infections And Infection Control
topicRaw: Hospital Acquired Infections And Infection Control
subject: Critical care

stem: Which of the following statements regarding the anatomy of the pelvis is correct?

options.text: Ischial spines are palpable per vagina examination
The femoral canal lies medial to the lacunar ligament
The pubic symphysis is a synovial joint
The sacroiliac joint is a fibrous joint
The obturator foramen is completely closed by the obturator membrane

explanation: The ischial spines are palpable per vaginam and allow the guidance of a needle to the pudendal canal for transvaginal pudendal nerve block.
subject: Anatomy

stem:
A patient with an allergy to penicillin is given tazocin. They develop respiratory distress and exhibit angioedema. You suspect anaphylaxis with massive mast cell activation. Antigen binding to mast cells results in the release of both pre-formed and newly formed mediators.

Which of the following options is an example of newly formed mediators?
explanation: Most mediators from mast cells are pre-formed, while others include cytokines and chemokines, or are newly formed following degranulation. Thromboxane is one of the newly formed lipid mediators following mast cell degranulation. Thromboxane causes vasoconstriction, platelet aggregation and bronchoconstriction.
subject: Clinical microbiology

stem:
You are assisting in a sentinel node biopsy for a patient with known breast cancer. You have difficulty locating the sentinel node but do so with a combination of blue dye and radioisotope.

Which of the following statements about sentinel node biopsy is correct?

options.text: Lymphoscintigraphy can be performed up to one week in advance of the procedure
Blue dye is contraindicated in pregnancy
Patent blue dye can cause anaphylaxis
Sentinel node biopsy has no role in multifocal breast cancer
The sentinel node is always located in the axilla

explanation: Currently, the use of blue dye is not recommended during sentinel node biopsy in patients who are pregnant. However, this is generally due to the risk of anaphylaxis rather than the foetal exposure to methylene blue – recent research into this topic suggests that the foetal risk is minimal.
subject: Breast and endocrine surgery

stem:
A patient presents with pituitary pathology. There is a concern the disease may be related to the posterior part of the gland.

Vasopressin acts by which one of the following?

options.text: Increasing the permeability of collecting ducts to water
Enhancing sodium reabsorption in the proximal tubule
Promoting sodium reabsorption in the loop of Henle
Stimulating aldosterone release from the adrenal cortex

explanation:
Vasopressin (otherwise known as ADH) acts upon the collecting ducts. It increases reabsorption of water by increasing the permeability of the collecting ducts to water.

Fine tuning of salt and water balance is achieved in the distal and collecting tubules under the influence of aldosterone and vasopressin.
topic: Fluid Balance And Fluid Replacement Therapy
topicRaw: Fluid Balance And Fluid Replacement Therapy
subject: Perioperative care

stem:
A patient is referred with refractory hypertension. Despite basic medical treatment their blood pressure remains 180/110 mmHg.

Which one of the following is the correct investigation and diagnosis of secondary hypertension?

options.text: A phaeochromocytoma can be shown by metaiodobenzylguanidine (MIBG) scintigraphy
Renovascular disease is a rare cause of secondary hypertension
Cushing's syndrome is always caused by an adrenal adenoma
Conn's syndrome presents with hypokalaemia and metabolic acidosis
Renal artery stenosis is best diagnosed by serum creatinine alone

explanation: MIBG scintigraphy is a very specific test for detecting phaeochromocytoma. Radioactive iodine-131-metaiodobenzylguanidine is administered to the patient and localises to adrenergic tissue. In the case of a patient with a phaeochromocytoma there is a focal area in the adrenal medulla where there is very strong and prolonged uptake of the solution. MIBG scintigraphy is not considered the first line investigation to detect phaeochromocytoma. MIBG is useful in detecting extra-adrenal tumours or disease recurrence.
subject: Anatomy

stem:
A 26-year-old man with von Willebrand’s disease was admitted with a painful swollen knee due to haemarthrosis. They are referred to the orthopaedic team with a possible septic arthritis but given the underlying diagnosis, it is felt that a knee aspiration will just raise the chances of the haemarthrosis becoming infected.

What are the main coagulation abnormalities in von Willebrand’s disease?

options.text: Abnormal factor VIII with platelet dysfunction
Normal factor VIII with isolated platelet dysfunction
Normal factor VIII with prolonged bleeding time only

explanation:
Von Willebrand’s disease sufferers have platelet dysfunction and abnormal factor VIII. Von Willebrand’s factor binds factor VIII and platelets to help form a platelet plug during clotting.

Von Willebrand’s disease is the commonest inherited bleeding disorder in white populations and is usually autosomal dominant in inheritance. Affected individuals have reduced or dysfunctional von Willebrand factor (vWF), a protein normally present in platelets and endothelium. vWF stabilises factor VIII in the circulation and mediates platelet adhesion at the site of vascular injury. The associated laboratory abnormalities therefore include a prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT) (due to reduced factor VIII), a normal prothrombin time and a prolonged bleeding time (platelet adhesion defect). Clinically, affected individuals usually show a mild bleeding tendency with epistaxis, easy bruising, menorrhagia and gingival bleeding. Although factor VIII levels are characteristically reduced, levels are rarely sufficiently low to cause haemarthroses, the hallmark of haemophilia A. Preoperative management usually involves treatment with desmopressin (which liberates platelet stores of vWF) or factor replacement with either intermediate-purity factor VIII or a specific vWF concentrate.
subject: Pathology

stem:
An 11-year-old boy presents with a short history of sudden onset left testicular pain and has a scrotal exploration.

Which one of these is correct regarding the stress response in this patient?

options.text: Cortisol levels will be elevated 24 h post-operatively
There will be an increase in catecholamine levels immediately post-operatively
Blood glucose levels will decrease immediately post-operatively
Thyroid hormone levels will rise immediately post-operatively
Insulin levels will be elevated in the first 24 hours post-operatively

explanation: Catecholamine levels are significantly elevated during surgery as part of the stress response and will remain so immediately post-operatively. Over the following approximately six hours these levels will return to normal in a paediatric patient.
subject: Emergency medicine and trauma

stem:
A 4-year-old child is brought to the hospital by child protection services after she was found to have been neglected by her foster parents. She is small for her age and looks pale and lethargic. Physical examination reveals a potbelly, moon facies, pedal oedema, enlarged liver and non-specific dermatitis. Her weight for height z-score is found to be more than 3 standard deviations below the mean.

Which of the following nutritional deficiencies most probably describes this condition?
explanation: The signs and symptoms in this patient are suggestive of kwashiorkor. Kwashiorkor is caused by a lack of protein, regardless of calorie intake. Patients have fair-to-normal energy intake but inadequate protein. They present with lethargy, irritability and anorexia. The growth retardation can be milder than in marasmus. High-quality protein foods and protein caloric supplements are used as treatment.
subject: Hepatobiliary and pancreatic surgery

stem:
One of your patients on the Intensive Care Unit has a Swan–Ganz catheter in situ. The patient’s cardiac output has been calculated as 6 L/min.

Which of the following factors increases cardiac output?
explanation: Histamine causes reduced peripheral resistance (via vasodilatation and increased capillary permeability), resulting in increased cardiac output (see formula below). Systemic vascular resistance = ((mean arterial pressure – central venous pressure)/cardiac output) × 80.
subject: Physiology

stem:
A 50-year-old man has an adrenal mass noted on computed tomography (CT) scan. This is a metastasis as there is an obvious primary on the CT therefore it is not biopsied.

The most likely primary source is which of the following?
explanation: Tumours commonly metastasising to the adrenal glands are lung and breast cancers. Isolated adrenal metastases are reported in 1.6% - 3.5% of patients with primary non-small cell lung cancer who present with resectable tumours. The incidence increases to up to 40% as the clinical course of the disease progresses. Other primaries that commonly metastasise to the adrenal glands are colorectal cancer and pancreatic cancer.
subject: Urology

stem:
A 35-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department after falling 8 feet off a ladder. The patient is alert, reports back pain and difficulty moving the lower extremities.

The presence of which additional examination finding would be an indication the patient may be experiencing neurogenic shock?
explanation: Neurogenic shock is a condition that happens when there is a disruption in sympathetic tone. The slowed heart rate results from unopposed vagal tone activity.
subject: Emergency medicine and trauma

stem:
A 48-year-old man is having an elective right inguinal hernia repair. Your consultant asks you to prepare and drape the patient. You are asked by the scrub nurse what you would like to use to prepare and you decide to use chlorhexidine.

Which of the following best describes the action of chlorhexidine?
explanation: Chlorhexidine is bactericidal at high concentrations by causing bacterial cell membrane disruption. It is effective against Gram-positive organisms, with moderate activity against Gram-negative organisms.
subject: Perioperative care

stem:
A 25-year-old man with jaundice had laboratory investigations performed, which showed: total bilirubin 120 µmol/L (normal 3–17), unconjugated bilirubin 86 µmol/L (normal <3) and anaemia.

What is the most likely cause of his jaundice?
explanation: Haemolysis results in the destruction of red cells therefore anaemia. Destruction of red cells also leads to the increased production of unconjugated bilirubin.
subject: Hepatobiliary and pancreatic surgery

stem:
A 26-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department after a football match. During the match, he headed a ball several times and soon after, lost consciousness. He is drowsy with a Glasgow Coma Score of 13. A computed tomography (CT) scan demonstrates an extradural haemorrhage.

From which blood vessel is the patient most likely to be bleeding?
explanation: The middle meningeal artery is a branch of the maxillary artery which is one of the terminal branches of the external carotid artery. It is found in the middle cranial fossa after entering the skull through the foramen spinosum. It is deep to the squamous part of the temporal bone; as this is the thinnest part of the skull (the pterion), the vessel is susceptible to injury.
subject: Neurosurgery

stem:
A 10-year-old girl is admitted to the Emergency Department with an acute abdomen. She is peripherally cool and tachycardic with a normal blood pressure. You decide to administer intravenous fluids.

What is the most appropriate regimen?

options.text: Hartmann’s solution 50 ml/kg peripherally, then reassess
Hartmann's solution 20 ml/kg peripherally, then reassess

explanation: The NICE (National Institute for Health and Care Excellence) suggests 10 ml/kg of a solution containing 131–154 mmol/l of sodium over 10 min through an IV route. The safest way of giving IV fluids in this instance is peripherally. If a child needs further multiple boluses then expert help should be sought.
topic: Fluid Balance And Fluid Replacement Therapy
topicRaw: Fluid Balance And Fluid Replacement Therapy
subject: Perioperative care

stem:
A 56-year-old man is admitted for a laminectomy of L4. There was no intra- or post-operative complications and he was asymptomatic at his follow-up outpatient clinic.

Where are the laminae of each vertebra located?

options.text: Posterior to the vertebral body between it and the transverse process
Posterior to the transverse processes, between them and the spinous process
Within the vertebral canal, anterior to the spinal cord
Between the vertebral body and the posterior longitudinal ligament

explanation: The laminae lie on both sides of the vertebral arch, between the transverse and spinal processes. The pedicles complete the arch and are between the transverse processes and the body.
subject: Perioperative care

stem:
During a hemihepatectomy for hepatocellular carcinoma, the Consultant points to an H-shaped arrangement of structures on the visceral surface.

Which structures form this ‘H’ shape?

options.text: Gallbladder, IVC, ligamentum teres, ligamentum venosum, porta hepatis
Porta hepatis, IVC, gallbladder, falciform ligament
Ligamentum teres, IVC, gallbladder, falciform ligament
Gallbladder, portal vein, ligamentum teres, hepatic veins

explanation: These five structures form the ‘H’ shape that divides the visceral surface of the liver. The gall bladder can be seen to the right of the image, the inferior vena cava (IVC) superiorly and the ligamentum teres towards the lower left.
subject: Anatomy

stem:
You are seeing a 75-year-old man in the Emergency Department (ED) with gross abdominal distension and prominent superficial abdominal veins. He has shifting dullness and you diagnose ascites secondary to chronic liver disease.

Which one of the following statements is correct regarding ascites?

options.text: A high serum-ascites albumin gradient (> 1.1) indicates a transudate such as pancreatitis
A low serum-ascites albumin gradient (< 1.1) indicates an exudate such as hereditary angioedema
A high serum-ascites albumin gradient (> 1.1) indicates an exudate such as malignancy
Ascitic fluid analysis is not useful in determining the cause of ascites
A low serum-ascites albumin gradient (< 1.1) indicates a transudate such as cirrhosis

explanation: An exudate ascites is defined by a low serum-ascites albumin gradient (SAAG) < 1.1. Exudative ascites are associated with malignancy, pancreatitis and hereditary angioedema.
subject: Hepatobiliary and pancreatic surgery

stem:
A 25-year-old woman presents to her General Practitioner with pain in the right hand which is associated with a tingling sensation and weakness. On investigation, she is diagnosed with thoracic outlet syndrome.

Which of the following muscles does the likely affected neurovascular bundle run through?
explanation: The neurovascular bundle referred to is the brachial plexus, the roots of which emerge from the intervertebral foraminae of the C5-T1 vertebrae and pass between the anterior and middle scalene muscles. The brachial plexus is highlighted in the image and the roots can be seen emerging from between them.
subject: Vascular surgery

stem:
A 56-year-old golfer presents to the Orthopaedic Clinic with a painful right shoulder on abduction. Following an appropriate investigation, a diagnosis of rotator cuff syndrome is made.
