Which of the following statements is true regarding the rotator cuff mechanism?

options.text: The Long head of biceps brachii forms part of the rotator cuff mechanism
Subscapularis arises from the medial 2/3 of the costal surface of the scapula and the intermuscular septa. It acts to stabilise the shoulder
Supraspinatus initiates abduction and is active through the full range of abduction
Teres minor is responsible for internal rotation of the shoulder
Infraspinatus inserts into the lesser tuberosity of the humerus

explanation:
Subscapularis arises from the subscapular fossa on the costal surface of the scapula and inserts to the lesser tubercle of the humerus (the only rotator cuff muscle to do so – the others insert onto the greater tubercle). It is innervated by the upper and lower subscapular nerves (C5, C6, C7). It acts to rotate and adduct the arm internally, and along with the other three rotator cuff muscles, stabilises the humerus in the glenoid cavity.

Original
Henry Gray (1918) Anatomy of the Human Body
Public domain
subject: Anatomy

stem:
A 46-year-old woman has a core biopsy of a screen-detected right breast lesion. Unfortunately, she develops a large bruise, which resolves over time.

Which one of the following statements most accurately describes the process involved?

options.text: Monocytes are responsible for phagocytosing effete red blood cells
Mast cells produce antibodies that recruit phagocytic cells to the area
Neutrophils are the predominant cell type during the proliferative phase
Platelets release growth factors that inhibit fibroblast migration
Macrophages play no role in wound debridement

explanation: Following an injury, the body recruits cells such as neutrophils, monocytes and macrophages which act to phagocytose the effete material to start the process of regeneration.
subject: Skin and wound management

stem:
A patient with known cancer is noted to have high concentrations of calcium in their blood. Hypercalcaemia can be present in malignant disease secondary to the secretion of parathyroid hormone-related peptide by a tumour.

It is most frequently associated with which of the following?

options.text: Squamous cell carcinoma of the bronchus
Small cell carcinoma of the bronchus

explanation: Hypercalcaemia is a frequent complication of cancer and is most usually the result of the secretion of parathyroid hormone-related peptide (paraneoplastic syndrome). Squamous cell carcinomas are particularly frequently responsible, but hypercalcaemia is uncommon with other bronchogenic cancers.
subject: Skin and wound management

stem:
A 6-month-old boy is seen by the orthopaedic team with a clubfoot (talipes equinovarus). It is a relatively common congenital deformity of the foot.

What does this consist of?

options.text: Eversion, abduction of the forefoot relative to the hindfoot and plantarflexion
Inversion, adduction of the forefoot relative to the hindfoot and plantarflexion
Eversion, abduction of the forefoot relative to the hindfoot and dorsiflexion
Inversion, abduction of the forefoot relative to the hindfoot and dorsiflexion
Eversion, adduction of the forefoot relative to the hindfoot and plantarflexion

explanation: Clubfoot can be unilateral or bilateral and affects boys and girls equally. Treatment now consists of a series of plaster casts to slowly manipulate the foot back into the correct position (Ponsetti’s method). It is linked to prune-belly syndrome, arthrogryposis and myelomeningocele.
subject: Anatomy

stem:
A 57-year-old man undergoes an elective repair of an abdominal aortic aneurysm via an open approach. Postoperatively, he experiences complete paralysis of his legs, loss of pain and temperature sensation in the same region.

Which vessel is most likely to have been injured during the procedure?
explanation: The spinal cord receives its blood supply from the anterior and posterior spinal arteries, which are branches of the vertebral arteries. The anterior spinal arteries supply the whole of the cord (anterior to the posterior grey columns). The blood supply to the spine is reinforced by the radicular arteries, which are branches of the ascending cervical, vertebral, posterior intercostal and lumbar arteries. If the anterior spinal artery is damaged (as in this case), it can lead to loss of function in the anterior two-thirds of the spinal cord, including the descending corticospinal tract, the ascending spinothalamic tract and some autonomic fibres. The patient will complain of corresponding loss of motor function as well as loss of pain and temperature sensation.
subject: Anatomy

stem:
You are assisting in a mastectomy and a level three axillary clearance operation. The consultant permits you to undertake the axillary clearance.

Which of the following statements best describes the anatomical level to which clearance should be gained?

options.text: Between pectoralis major and pectoralis minor

explanation: Axillary node clearance is the established operative management for disease control in invasive breast cancer, obtaining prognostic information and influencing post-operative therapy including the choice of breast cancer trials. Axillary node clearance can be defined as clearing the axillary contents bounded by the axillary skin laterally, latissimus dorsi, teres major and subscapularis posteriorly, the lower border of the axillary vein superiorly, pectoralis muscles anteriorly, and the chest wall medially. Superomedial to the pectoralis minor would be defined as a level three axillary clearance operation. The levels of axillary nodes are anatomically defined as level one (inferolateral to pectoralis minor), level two (posterior to pectoralis minor) and level three (superomedial to pectoralis minor).
subject: Breast and endocrine surgery

stem:
A 55-year-old man is admitted with an extradural haemorrhage. They are known to be on a anticoagulant and the neurosurgeons recommend this be reversed as soon as possible.

Prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC) is used as a reversal agent for which anticoagulant?
explanation: PCC (eg Octaplex) is licensed for warfarin reversal. It is derived from human plasma (non-UK) and contains the clotting factors II, VII, IX and X. PCC provides immediate reversal of warfarin but the effect will begin to wear off after 6–12 h. Vitamin K can be used if the reversal of warfarin is less urgent.
subject: Perioperative care

stem:
An 88-year-old man with known chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) presents with acute shortening of breath and low oxygen saturations. An arterial blood gas is attempted using his radial artery.

Which of the following concerning the radial artery is correct?

options.text: It crosses the floor of the anatomical snuffbox
It is the larger of the two terminal branches of the brachial artery
It is a direct branch of the axillary artery
It passes through the carpal tunnel
It does not contribute to the superficial palmar arch

explanation: The radial artery crosses the floor of the anatomical snuffbox (where it can be palpated) before piercing the first dorsal interosseous muscle to form the deep palmar arch. It gives off its dorsal carpal branch in the proximal part of the snuffbox. The course of the radial artery in the forearm is shown below.
topic: Blood Supply Of The Upper Limb
topicRaw: Blood Supply Of The Upper Limb
subject: Anatomy

stem:
A 25-year-old man is brought to the Emergency Department in shock following a trauma. He is acutely unwell with obvious derangement of their vital signs.

Which part of the adrenal gland is least likely to be stimulated?
explanation: The zona reticularis is the innermost cortical layer; the zona reticularis produces androgens, mainly dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA). These are anabolic hormones and are supressed during the stress response.
subject: Emergency medicine and trauma

stem: Complex starches are mainly digested by enzymes secreted from which of the following?
explanation: Pancreatic secretion contains a large quantity of α-amylase, a digestive enzyme that hydrolyses starches, glycogen and most other carbohydrates to form disaccharides and a few trisaccharides.
subject: Hepatobiliary and pancreatic surgery

stem:
A 56-year-old man is admitted with the worst headache he has ever had and a possible subarachnoid haemorrhage is considered. A CT scan is not diagnostic so a lumbar puncture is attempted.

Where does the subarachnoid space end in a fully developed adult?
explanation: Although the spinal cord in an adult finishes in the upper lumbar vertebrae, the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) within the dura passes all the way down to the sacral vertebrae. The exact termination is variable within the sacrum.
subject: Neurosurgery

stem:
A 38-year-old builder’s labourer sustained a severe fracture of his left elbow, which damaged the ulnar nerve behind the medial epicondyle of the humerus. A month later, he still has total ulnar nerve paralysis.

Which clinical sign is most likely to be present on examination?

options.text: Ring and little fingers on the affected side are held in the claw position
Inability to grip a sheet of paper between his fingers
Loss of sensation over the lateral forearm
Inability to flex the distal interphalangeal joint of the index finger

explanation: To grip a sheet of paper requires finger adduction and the functioning of the palmar interossei muscles, which are supplied by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve.
subject: Anatomy

stem:
You have been asked to place a large-bore intravenous cannula into a trauma patient in the Emergency Department. He appears peripherally ‘shut down’, but you manage to secure intravenous access in his right antecubital fossa.

How would you describe the antecubital fossa?

options.text: The bicipitalaponeurosis forms the floor of the cubital fossa
It contains the terminal branches of the brachial artery
The radial nerve forms the lateral boundary of the cubital fossa
The median nerve is the most superficial structure in the cubital fossa
The ulnar nerve passes through the cubital fossa

explanation:
The brachial artery divides into its two terminal branches (the radial artery and the ulnar artery) in the distal aspect of the antecubital fossa, opposite the neck of the radius. The cubital fossa is described as having the following borders:

Proximally: a line connecting the medial and lateral epicondyles of the humerus
Medially: lateral border of the pronator teres
Laterally: medial border of brachioradialis
Roof: Bicipital aponeurosis, antebrachial and brachial fascia, subcutaneous fat and skin
Floor: Brachialis and supinator muscles.
subject: Anatomy

stem:
Total hip arthroplasty is a routine procedure; however, it can cause major complications. There are different techniques to complete the procedure, each with benefits and disadvantages.

Which nerve is potentially at greatest danger of iatrogenic injury during total hip arthroplasty via the posterior approach?
explanation: Sciatic nerve injury is the most common peripheral nerve injury occurring in total hip replacement (THA). Pressure and an irregular gait pattern are the most common and recurrent symptoms. Foot drop, hip external rotation and abduction contracture, equinovarus or equinus deformity, muscular weakness/atrophy and motor and sensory deficits such as paraesthesia and numbness are among the other symptoms. The most commonly used approaches for THA include the posterior approach, the direct lateral approach and the direct anterior approach.
subject: Anatomy

stem:
An 18-year-old man comes to the Rheumatology Clinic for review. He has suffered recurrent shoulder pain over the past 6 months whilst playing rugby. Previously acute episodes of pain resolved, but they are now becoming a chronic, dull ache in his shoulder joint. Right shoulder abduction is limited by pain. He has no past medical history of note.

Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Avascular necrosis of the humeral head

explanation: A Hill–Sachs lesion is a posterolateral humeral head compression fracture caused by recurrent anterior shoulder dislocation. The history of repeated painful episodes during rugby strongly suggests recurrent subluxation or dislocation events. The chronic ache now experienced is likely secondary to the bony defect and coexistent soft tissue injury, such as a Bankart lesion. This explains why this is the most likely diagnosis.
subject: Anatomy

stem:
A 7-year-old boy falls over sustaining a fractured right distal radius. On plain radiography, the fracture passes through the epiphysis into the physis with displacement of the fragment; the metaphysis is intact.

How would you classify this fracture?
explanation:
The Salter–Harris classification is a commonly used classification of epiphyseal injuries in children. There were five types originally described. The types are:

Salter–Harris I – separation of the epiphysis from the metaphysis
Salter–Harris II – fracture through the physis with a metaphyseal fragment
Salter–Harris III – fracture through the epiphysis and physis
Salter–Harris IV – fracture through the epiphysis, physis and metaphysis
Salter–Harris V – crush injury to the physis.
subject: Anatomy

stem:
A 18-year-old man presents following an injury during a football match. He sustained a tackle to the lateral side of his knee, hearing a 'pop' sound and noted immediate swelling. Since then he reports ongoing pain, and feels the knee locking and being unstable.

Concerning the injury above, which of the following is the correct answer?

options.text: Priority in treatment involves medial collateral ligament (MCL) reconstruction
The injuries involved can be described as the O’Donoghue’s triad
Isolated anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) tear is the most likely diagnosis
Surgical repair of the ACL should be performed within 24 hours
MRI is contraindicated in the acute setting

explanation: The triad of injury involving tear of the anterior cruciate ligament, medial collateral ligament and a medial meniscal tear is known as the O’Donoghue’s or the unhappy triad. This is named after DH O’Donoghue, an American orthopaedic surgeon who described it in 1950. Of note, subsequent studies into this injury have proven that lateral meniscus tears significantly out-number medial meniscus tears on arthroscopy – however, a lateral meniscal injury is not described in O’Donoghue’s initial paper.
subject: Anatomy

stem:
A 14-year-old male footballer presents with severe pain and swelling of the left ankle. Plain X-rays confirm a bimalleolar ankle fracture.

The distal tibia articulates with which bone?
explanation: The ankle joint is formed from the distal tibia and fibula, articulating with the talus – as shown below.
subject: Anatomy

stem:
A patient has been suffering from severe osteoarthritis for several years after failed conservative treatment. She is awaiting an elective total hip replacement.

Which of the following statements about the hip joint is correct?

options.text: The hip joint capsule is tight in flexion
The hip joint is a condyloid joint
The acetabular labrum reduces the stability of the hip joint
The ligament of the head of femur carries the main blood supply to the femoral head in adults

explanation: Diarthrosis (or diarthrodal joint) is another term for a synovial joint. The hip joint is a ball and socket synovial joint – its articulations are shown below.
subject: Anatomy

stem:
A 26-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department two months after an emergency open appendicectomy. She has developed lower abdominal pain accompanied by numbness and paraesthesia radiating to the groin, labia majora and inner thigh. On examination, pain is reproduced when palpated medial to the ASIS and worsens with hip extension.

This presentation is associated with damage to which of the following nerves?

options.text: Lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh

explanation:
The ilioinguinal nerve arises from T12 and L1 roots. It commences near the lateral border of psoas major and once it reaches the iliac crest, it pierces through the transversus abdominis and internal oblique muscle. It is the sensory nerve of the pubic symphysis, superior and medial femoral triangle, mons pubis and the labia majora in females.

Causes of injury include lower abdominal operations, orchidectomy, appendicectomy, hysterectomy, but it can also be idiopathic. Symptoms include numbness or paraesthesia over the inguinal ligament, inner thigh, labia majora and perineum. Symptoms are worsened with hip extension and palpation medial to the anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS). Diagnosis is clinical or by relief of symptoms with local anaesthetic infiltration of the nerve. Management is with NSAIDs, local anaesthetic ± steroid injections and physical therapy. If these prove unsuccessful, neurolysis or nerve excision are recommended.
topic: Blood And Nerve Supply Of The Abdominal Wall
topicRaw: Blood And Nerve Supply Of The Abdominal Wall
subject: Anatomy

stem:
A 34-year-old man who is a keen cyclist has been referred to the Orthopaedic Clinic with pain and tingling affecting both hands' ring and little fingers. A bilateral nerve compression of the ulnar nerve is suspected and is advised to rest, hoping for a non-surgical resolution.

How would you best describe the course of the affected nerve?

options.text: The nerve wraps around the posterior aspect of the lateral epicondyle at the level of the elbow
It enters the forearm by passing between the two heads of flexor carpi ulnaris
The nerve passes through the cubital tunnel posterior to the medial epicondyle
It is a branch of the posterior cord of the brachial plexus
It provides motor innervation to all the lumbricals of the hand

explanation: The ulnar nerve enters the forearm by winding around the posterior aspect of the medial epicondyle of the humerus and travelling between the two heads of the flexor carpi ulnaris fibro-osseous channel known as the cubital tunnel. The two heads of FCU arise from the medial epicondyle of the humerus and the olecranon/posterior ulna, respectively. These bony landmarks (medial epicondyle and olecranon) form the medial and lateral borders of the cubital tunnel, with the roof formed by the cubital tunnel retinaculum and the floor by the capsule of the elbow joint. The path of the ulnar nerve in the arm and forearm is shown in the image below. The cubital tunnel is an important site of entrapment of the ulnar nerve, with cubital tunnel syndrome being the second most common nerve entrapment of the upper limb after carpal tunnel syndrome. Symptoms include pain, paraesthesia, numbness in the ring and little fingers, weakness of the hand, and chronic compression that can lead to clawing.
subject: Anatomy

stem:
A 78-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department (ED) complaining of isolated neck pain, without neurology, following a fall from standing. A lateral X-ray of the neck reveals a retropharyngeal haematoma. The doctor in ED suspects an odontoid peg fracture.

What is the next most appropriate investigation?

options.text: A magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan of the neck
A computed tomography (CT) scan of the cervical spine
Plain X-rays of the cervical spine
Flexion-extension views of the cervical spine

explanation: In current practice a CT scan is the gold standard. Many hospitals include C-spine CT as standard with any head CT request, particularly in elderly patients. The odontoid peg (dens) is an upward projection from the axis (C2). The peg has an articular facet at its front and forms part of a joint with the anterior arch of the atlas. The atlanto-axial joint (C1–C2) allows rotation. It is a non-weight-bearing joint. It is supported by a number of ligaments – the alar ligaments (from the side of the peg to the occipital condyle), the apical ligament (from the tip of C2 to the anterior margin of the foramen magnum), and the transverse ligament (which arches across the atlas to maintain the position of the peg).
subject: Anatomy

stem:
A 33-year-old woman presents to the Hand Clinic complaining of swelling and pain in the small joints of her feet and hands. She says her hands feel most stiff when she wakes early in the morning and this gets better throughout the day. On examination, several of the small joints in her feet and hands are swollen and tender bilaterally. All blood tests are unremarkable.

Which imaging modality is going to be the most appropriate in helping establish an early diagnosis?

options.text: CT scan of the hands and feet
MRI of the hands and feet

explanation: It is most likely that this woman has early rheumatoid arthritis, given the few clinical findings and normal bloods test results. Her symptoms, though, are very typical of rheumatoid arthritis. Ultrasound is a quick, sensitive and non-invasive method of demonstrating the soft tissue changes that may appear in the small joints in early rheumatoid arthritis, before any bony changes are seen on plain radiographs. One must remember that ultrasound diagnoses are operator dependent.
subject: Orthopaedics

stem:
A 78-year-old woman presents with pain in both hands and they are dropping. Examination reveals that her middle finger proximal interphalangeal joint is fixed in flexion of approximately 30° and the distal interphalangeal (DIP) joint is fixed in hyperextension.

How would you describe this finding?
explanation: The deformity described in the vignette is characteristic of a boutonnière deformity. Boutonnière is the French word for ‘buttonhole’.
subject: Anatomy

stem:
A 34-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department following a stab wound to the right side of his neck. He reports weakness when trying to flex his neck and rotate his head to the left. Injury to the spinal accessory nerve is suspected.

Where is this nerve located on the sternocleidomastoid?
explanation: The spinal accessory nerve (cranial nerve XI) innervates the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles. As it traverses the sternocleidomastoid, it typically enters the muscle at the junction of the upper and middle thirds, most commonly in the posterior third of the muscle. Injury to the nerve at this location can impair head rotation to the contralateral side and neck flexion due to weakened sternocleidomastoid function. Given the anatomical course, a stab wound to the posterior third of the sternocleidomastoid is most likely to damage the spinal accessory nerve and result in the described clinical features.
subject: Anatomy

stem:
A 2-day-old girl is brought to the Emergency Department by her parents due to persistent vomiting and abdominal distension. On examination, she has a single palmar crease and appears slightly jaundiced. An abdominal X-ray shows a double bubble sign.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Duodenal atresia is a congenital condition where there is a complete closure or absence of a portion of the lumen of the duodenum. It is strongly associated with Down syndrome, which can present with a single palmar crease. The double bubble sign on an abdominal X-ray is characteristic of duodenal atresia, showing a distended stomach and proximal duodenum with no air beyond this point. The presence of vomiting and abdominal distension in this age group further supports this diagnosis.
subject: Upper gastrointestinal surgery

stem:
A 5-year-old boy is brought to the Emergency Department with axillary and cervical lymphadenopathy following a bite from his pet cat. He has no significant past medical history and is otherwise well.

What is the most likely causative organism responsible for his symptoms?
explanation: Bartonella henselae is the bacterium responsible for cat scratch disease, which is commonly transmitted through scratches or bites from cats. This condition often presents with regional lymphadenopathy, typically involving the axillary or cervical lymph nodes, as seen in this vignette. The organism is a gram-negative bacillus, and the disease is self-limiting in most immunocompetent individuals. Diagnosis is often clinical, supported by serological testing if needed, and treatment is usually supportive, although antibiotics +/- formal debridement may be required in severe cases.
subject: Head and neck surgery

stem:
A 55-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with sudden and severe abdominal pain radiating to his back. He has a history of a sexually transmitted infection (STI). On examination, his BP is low and there is a pulsatile abdominal mass.

What is the most likely layer of the vessel wall that has been affected?
explanation: The tunica adventitia is the outermost layer of blood vessels and provides structural support. In the case of an abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA), which is likely given the patient's presentation of sudden back pain and a pulsatile mass, the integrity of the tunica adventitia is compromised. The rupture of an AAA typically involves the adventitia, leading to haemorrhage into the retroperitoneal space, which explains the severe abdominal and back pain. The history of an STI might suggest atherosclerotic changes or vasculitis, which can weaken the vessel wall, predisposing to aneurysm formation and subsequent rupture.
topic: Aorta Regional Anatomy, Including Aortic Arches Embryology
topicRaw: Aorta Regional Anatomy, Including Aortic Arches Embryology
subject: Anatomy

stem:
A 3-day-old boy is brought to the Emergency Department with a urine leak from the umbilicus. On examination, a small stream of urine is seen emanating from the umbilical stump. Imaging reveals a patent urachal tract.

Which of the following is the embryological origin of the bladder?
explanation: The urogenital sinus is the embryological precursor to the bladder. It arises from the anterior portion of the cloaca after division by the urorectal septum. The upper part of the urogenital sinus forms most of the urinary bladder, while the lower parts give rise to portions of the urethra. This structure is distinct from the urachus or allantois and is the definitive embryological origin of the bladder in both men and women.
subject: Anatomy

stem:
A 27-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with sudden-onset severe right upper quadrant pain, fever, jaundice, dark urine, and pale stools. Blood tests show elevated bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase. Ultrasound reveals a dilated common bile duct.

What is the most likely anatomical location of the obstruction?
explanation: The Ampulla of Vater, also known as the hepatopancreatic ampulla, is the point where the common bile duct and main pancreatic duct converge and empty into the second part of the duodenum. It is a common site of obstruction by gallstones (choledocholithiasis), strictures, or tumours. Obstruction here leads to backpressure and dilation of the common bile duct, resulting in obstructive jaundice, dark urine (conjugated bilirubinuria), pale stools (lack of stercobilin), and elevated alkaline phosphatase. This clinical picture, along with the imaging finding of a dilated CBD, is most consistent with obstruction at the Ampulla of Vater.
subject: Hepatobiliary and pancreatic surgery

stem:
A 48-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department one week after superficial parotid surgery. She reports difficulty putting on her earrings due to altered sensation around her earlobe. On examination, there is reduced sensation over the lower part of the external ear.

What is the most likely nerve that has been injured during surgery?
explanation: The great auricular nerve is a sensory branch of the cervical plexus (C2–C3) that supplies the skin over the parotid region, mastoid process and external ear, particularly the lobule. It crosses the sternocleidomastoid muscle and is often encountered and at risk during parotid surgery. Injury to this nerve causes numbness or altered sensation in the region of the lower ear, which may make manipulating earrings difficult. This is a purely sensory nerve, so motor function remains intact, but patients may describe clumsiness or discomfort due to the sensory loss.
topic: Nerve Supply Of The Head And Neck
topicRaw: Nerve Supply Of The Head And Neck
subject: Critical care

stem:
A 28-year-old woman presents to her General Practitioner with a midline neck swelling that moves on tongue protrusion. She reports that it has been present for several years but has recently become painful and tender. On examination, the lesion is fluctuant and mildly erythematous. There is no associated dysphagia or dyspnoea.

What is the most likely complication that would necessitate surgical removal of this lesion?
explanation: Recurrent infections are the most common complication associated with thyroglossal cysts and represent the primary indication for surgical excision. These cysts arise from remnants of the thyroglossal duct and are prone to infection due to their connection to the oropharyngeal mucosa or through small tracts that allow bacterial entry. Infected cysts can become painful, erythematous and may form abscesses if left untreated. The Sistrunk procedure, which includes removal of the central portion of the hyoid bone along with the cyst, is the standard treatment to reduce recurrence.
subject: Head and neck surgery

stem:
A 45-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with numbness and tingling in his right middle finger. He reports that the symptoms began gradually over the past week without any associated trauma. On examination, there is no muscle weakness or atrophy, but the numbness is isolated to the middle finger.

Which nerve root is most likely affected in this patient?
explanation: The C7 nerve root primarily innervates the middle finger, and its involvement can result in sensory changes, such as numbness or tingling, in this digit. The C7 nerve root contributes to the median nerve, which provides sensation to the palmar aspect of the middle finger. Given the isolated sensory symptoms in the middle finger without motor deficits, the C7 nerve root is the most likely nerve root to be affected. In cases of cervical radiculopathy, the C7 nerve root is one of the most commonly involved nerve roots, often due to disc herniation or foraminal stenosis.
topic: Nerve Supply Of The Upper Limb

stem:
A 72-year-old man presents to his General Practitioner with worsening lower back and hip pain over the past few months. Examination reveals no palpable lymphadenopathy and no obvious joint swelling. Blood tests show a mildly raised alkaline phosphatase. Imaging demonstrates multiple osteoblastic lesions throughout the pelvis and lumbar spine.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Prostate cancer is well known for metastasising to bone with a characteristic osteoblastic pattern, as opposed to the lytic lesions seen in many other malignancies. The presence of osteoblastic lesions, particularly in the axial skeleton such as the spine and pelvis, is highly suggestive of metastatic prostate cancer in an older man. Metastases to the spine occur via the vertebral venous plexus. Lesions are often painful, and serum alkaline phosphatase levels are commonly elevated due to increased osteoblastic activity. The absence of lymphadenopathy further supports a diagnosis of bony metastases rather than a primary lymphoproliferative disorder.
subject: Urology

stem:
A 32-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with right upper quadrant pain and jaundice. He has a history of hereditary spherocytosis and has required multiple blood transfusions for haemolytic episodes. Laboratory results show anaemia and elevated unconjugated bilirubin. Abdominal ultrasound reveals multiple gallstones.

Which type of gallstone is he most likely to have?
explanation: Black pigment stones are primarily composed of calcium bilirubinate and form in sterile bile. They are strongly associated with chronic haemolytic conditions such as hereditary spherocytosis, sickle cell disease, and thalassemia. Ongoing haemolysis leads to increased unconjugated bilirubin in bile, which then precipitates into stones. These stones tend to be small, brittle, and dark in colour. Although they may contain calcium and are sometimes visible on plain X-rays, ultrasound remains the diagnostic imaging modality of choice. In this patient with hereditary spherocytosis and haemolysis, black pigment stones are the most likely finding.
subject: Hepatobiliary and pancreatic surgery

stem:
A 62-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with rectal bleeding and altered bowel habits. Imaging reveals an upper rectum tumour and he is scheduled for a low anterior resection.

During this procedure, which vessel is most likely to be ligated?
explanation: The superior rectal artery is a direct continuation of the inferior mesenteric artery (IMA) and supplies the upper part of the rectum. In the context of a low anterior resection, which is typically performed for tumours located in the upper rectum, the superior rectal artery is routinely ligated to ensure adequate removal of the tumour and its blood supply. This vessel is crucial as it provides the main arterial supply to the upper rectum. Ligation of this artery during surgery helps in achieving clear margins and reducing the risk of local recurrence. It may be ligated at its origin from the IMA during high ligation for oncological clearance.
subject: Anatomy

stem:
A 2-day-old baby boy is brought to the Emergency Department by his concerned parents due to frequent episodes of crying and turning blue. On examination, the baby is cyanosed, and a cardiac murmur is detected, and an echocardiogram reveals a patent foramen ovale.

What is the embryological origin of the foramen ovale?

options.text: Fusion of septum primum and secundum

explanation: The foramen ovale is an opening in the septum secundum that allows blood to bypass the pulmonary circulation in the fetal heart by flowing directly from the right atrium to the left atrium. During fetal development, the septum primum and septum secundum fuse to form the interatrial septum, closing the foramen ovale after birth as the pressures in the left atrium exceed those in the right atrium. In the case of a patent foramen ovale, this fusion is incomplete, allowing the foramen to remain open. The origin of the foramen ovale is specifically related to the incomplete fusion of these two septa, which is why this option is correct.
subject: Anatomy

stem:
A 12-year-old boy undergoes laparoscopic bilateral inguinal hernia repair. During the procedure, the surgeon observes two fibrous bands running inferolaterally from the umbilicus toward the pelvis, located medial to the deep inguinal rings. These are identified as the remnants of embryological structures.

What is the primary function of these structures in utero?

options.text: Transport deoxygenated blood from the foetus to the placenta
Guide the descent of the testes through the inguinal canal
Drain foetal urine from the bladder into the allantois
Form part of the future vas deferens
Supply blood to the developing bladder

explanation: The structures described are the medial umbilical ligaments, which are fibrous remnants of the umbilical arteries. In utero, the umbilical arteries arise from the foetal internal iliac arteries and travel along the anterior abdominal wall to reach the umbilical cord, through which they carry deoxygenated blood and waste products to the placenta for exchange. After birth, the intra-abdominal portions of these arteries obliterate and persist as the medial umbilical ligaments, seen as paired fibrous bands running inferolaterally from the umbilicus. These are commonly encountered during laparoscopic procedures near the internal inguinal ring and are a normal anatomical finding.
subject: Anatomy

stem:
A 25-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with severe left flank pain radiating to the groin. A CT scan reveals a left ureteric stone with associated hydronephrosis.

Which of the following arteries does not typically supply the left ureter?
explanation: The inferior mesenteric artery (IMA) primarily supplies the hindgut structures, including the descending colon, sigmoid colon, and upper rectum. It does not supply the ureter at any point along its course. The ureter is located anterior and lateral to the aorta and receives blood from arteries that are either directly adjacent to it or travel alongside it in the retroperitoneum. The IMA does not travel near the ureter, making it the least likely artery to contribute to ureteric vascularisation.
subject: Urology

stem:
A 34-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department after a fall from a height. On examination, there is clear fluid leaking from his right ear. A CT scan of the head reveals a fracture of the skull bones.

Which part of the skull is most likely to be damaged?

options.text: Petrous part of the temporal bone
Squamous part of the temporal bone

explanation: The tegmen tympani is a thin plate of bone that forms the roof of the middle ear cavity and separates it from the cranial cavity. A fracture in this area can result in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) leakage into the middle ear, which can then exit through the external auditory canal, presenting as otorrhoea. This condition is known as CSF otorrhoea and is a common complication of temporal bone fractures. The presentation of clear fluid leaking from the ear following head trauma is highly suggestive of this condition.
subject: Anatomy

stem:
A 37-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with sudden onset of abdominal pain. Imaging reveals an internal hernia through the omental (epiploic) foramen.

Which structure forms the superior border of the omental foramen?
explanation: The omental foramen, also known as the epiploic foramen or foramen of Winslow, is an important anatomical passage in the abdominal cavity. It is bordered superiorly by the caudate lobe of the liver. This foramen allows communication between the greater and lesser sacs of the peritoneal cavity. Understanding the borders of the omental foramen is crucial for surgeons, particularly in procedures involving the hepatoduodenal ligament or when addressing internal hernias.
subject: Anatomy

stem:
A 65-year-old man with a known history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) develops drowsiness and hypoventilation after receiving 20 mg of IV morphine for pain management following a minor surgical procedure. On examination, he is somnolent and has a reduced respiratory rate.

Which of the following arterial blood gas (ABG) results would be most consistent with this patient's condition?

options.text: pH 7.20 / PaO2 80 mmHg / PaCO2 60 mmHg / HCO3- 24 mmol/L / BE -2
pH 7.35 / PaO2 60 mmHg / PaCO2 50 mmHg / HCO3- 30 mmol/L / BE +4
pH 7.28 / PaO2 75 mmHg / PaCO2 70 mmHg / HCO3- 28 mmol/L / BE +3
pH 7.45 / PaO2 90 mmHg / PaCO2 40 mmHg / HCO3- 26 mmol/L / BE 0
pH 7.50 / PaO2 70 mmHg / PaCO2 30 mmHg / HCO3- 20 mmol/L / BE -5

explanation: This ABG result indicates acute-on-chronic respiratory acidosis with partial metabolic compensation, which is characteristic of a COPD patient who has developed opioid-induced hypoventilation. The elevated PaCO2 (70 mmHg) reflects impaired ventilation due to morphine’s depressant effect on the respiratory centre. The low pH (7.28) indicates acidaemia, while the elevated HCO3- (28 mmol/L) reflects renal compensation from underlying chronic CO2 retention. The base excess (BE) +3 supports a buffered, partially compensated acidosis. This is the most physiologically appropriate ABG in the setting of COPD and opioid overdose.
subject: Perioperative care

stem:
A 64-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with right-sided ptosis and miosis. He has recently been diagnosed with a Pancoast tumour affecting the apex of the right lung with radiological evidence of a T1 nerve root lesion. On neurological examination, his upper limb motor function is preserved.

Which of the following signs is most likely to be found on examination?
explanation: Anhidrosis of the face is a classical component of Horner’s syndrome, which results from disruption of the sympathetic pathway to the eye and face. A lesion affecting the T1 nerve root can interrupt the preganglionic sympathetic fibres travelling from the spinal cord to the superior cervical ganglion. This interruption leads to the triad of ptosis, miosis and anhidrosis. In the context of a Pancoast tumour compressing the T1 root, ipsilateral facial anhidrosis is a key associated symptom and helps confirm the presence of Horner’s syndrome.
subject: Head and neck surgery

stem:
A 44-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with abdominal pain and discomfort. Imaging reveals fused lower poles of the kidneys lying low in the abdomen, consistent with a horseshoe kidney.

Which of the following structures is related to the development of this condition?
explanation: The horseshoe kidney is a congenital condition where the kidneys are fused at the lower poles, typically lying lower in the abdomen than normal. During embryonic development, the ascent of the kidneys is halted by the inferior mesenteric artery (IMA), which crosses the midline and prevents the fused kidneys from rising to their usual position. This anatomical relationship is significant because it explains why horseshoe kidneys are often found lower in the abdomen. Additionally, the presence of the IMA can lead to complications such as hydronephrosis due to impaired drainage.

stem:
A 60-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with lower abdominal pain and haematuria. Imaging reveals a midline supravesical mass arising from the urachus at the dome of the bladder.

What is the most likely type of cancer that can develop from this remnant?
explanation: Adenocarcinoma is the most common type of cancer arising from urachal remnants. The urachus is a vestigial remnant of the allantois, which is present during embryonic development. It can persist as a fibrous cord between the bladder and the umbilicus. When malignancy occurs in this remnant, it typically presents as adenocarcinoma due to the glandular tissue characteristics of the urachus.
subject: Urology

stem:
A 32-year-old man presents to the General Practitioner with hearing loss and a dull, scarred tympanic membrane.

Which pharyngeal pouch gives rise to the middle ear cavity containing the tympanic membrane?
explanation: The first pharyngeal pouch develops into the tubotympanic recess, which contributes to the formation of the middle ear cavity and the auditory (Eustachian) tube. The tympanic membrane itself is formed at the junction of the first pharyngeal cleft and the first pouch, with contributions from all three germ layers. It is closely related to structures derived from the first arch, including the malleus and incus. A clear understanding of this embryology is important in recognising congenital causes of middle ear disease.
subject: Anatomy

stem:
A 41-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with a 5 cm, tender, subcutaneous nodule on the extensor aspect of her elbow. The nodule becomes inflamed intermittently but settles down only to repeat the cycle. A biopsy of the nodule reveals synovium with fibrous walls.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Rheumatoid nodules are firm, non-tender subcutaneous nodules commonly found on extensor surfaces such as the elbow. They can become inflamed and fluctuate in size, as described in the vignette. Histologically, they consist of a central area of fibrinoid necrosis surrounded by palisading histiocytes and a fibrous capsule, which aligns with the biopsy findings of synovium with fibrous walls. These nodules are associated with rheumatoid arthritis, although they can occur in patients with high rheumatoid factor titres even without joint symptoms.
subject: Anatomy

stem:
A 37-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with symptoms of fatigue, weight loss and increased thirst. Her blood glucose level is significantly elevated.

Which part of the pancreas is responsible for the production of insulin?
explanation: The pancreas is a gland with both exocrine and endocrine functions. The endocrine component consists of the Islets of Langerhans, which are scattered throughout the pancreas but are most densely located in the tail. These islets contain beta cells, which are responsible for the production of insulin. Insulin is crucial for regulating blood glucose levels by facilitating cellular glucose uptake.
subject: Physiology

stem:
A 35-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with a laceration on his forearm sustained while working with machinery. On examination, the wound is erythematous, swollen, warm, and painful. Laboratory studies show elevated markers of systemic inflammation.

Which interleukin is most likely responsible for mediating pain and vasodilation during this stage of the inflammatory response?
explanation: Interleukin-6 (IL-6) is a pro-inflammatory cytokine that plays a significant role in the acute phase response. It is known to mediate fever and the acute phase response by acting on the hypothalamus and liver, respectively. IL-6 can also cause pain and vasodilation by promoting the release of prostaglandins, which are potent mediators of inflammation. This cytokine is crucial in the early stages of wound healing as it helps recruit immune cells to the site of injury and facilitates tissue repair.
subject: Skin and wound management

stem:
A 55-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with a persistent, scaly rash on her right nipple that has been present for several months. She reports associated itching and occasional discharge but denies any palpable lumps in the breast. A biopsy of the nipple is performed and reveals Paget's disease.

What is the underlying breast pathology associated with Paget's disease of the nipple?
explanation: Paget's disease of the nipple is most commonly associated with underlying breast carcinoma, particularly invasive ductal carcinoma (IDC). IDC is the most prevalent type of breast cancer, representing approximately 70-80% of all cases. The disease often presents with nipple changes such as eczema-like rashes and is frequently associated with palpable masses in the breast, although not always. In Paget's disease, malignant cells infiltrate the epidermis of the nipple, and in many cases, an underlying IDC is identified upon further investigation.
subject: Breast and endocrine surgery

stem:
A 51-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with a painful swelling in his lower jaw. On examination, there is a dental abscess involving a mandibular premolar. Imaging suggests the infection is localised and has not yet spread to deeper cervical spaces.

Which muscle acts as a barrier, limiting the spread of this infection from the submandibular region into the neck?
explanation: The mylohyoid muscle forms a muscular diaphragm that constitutes the floor of the oral cavity, lying superior to the submandibular space and inferior to the sublingual space. It stretches from the mylohyoid line of the mandible to the hyoid bone, creating a barrier that separates infections originating above it (such as from mandibular premolars) from spreading into deeper cervical spaces. Because of this anatomical position, the mylohyoid plays a crucial role in limiting the downward spread of odontogenic infections from the oral cavity into the neck.
topic: Lymphatics Of The Head And Neck
topicRaw: Lymphatics Of The Head And Neck

stem:
A 44-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with a severe head injury following a road traffic accident. He is unconscious and requires intensive monitoring. His BP is recorded at 120/60 mmHg, and his intracranial pressure (ICP) is measured at 25 mmHg.

What is the most likely cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP)?
explanation:
CPP is calculated using the formula: CPP = Mean Arterial Pressure (MAP) - ICP.

First, calculate the MAP using the formula: MAP = Diastolic BP + 1/3(Systolic BP - Diastolic BP). With a BP of 120/60 mmHg, the MAP is 60 + 1/3(120-60) = 60 + 20 = 80 mmHg. Therefore, the CPP is 80 - 25 = 55 mmHg.

This CPP is on the lower end of the acceptable range, but it still maintains some perfusion. In neurocritical care, values < 60 mmHg often prompt interventions to either raise MAP or lower ICP. Nonetheless, this matches the calculated value precisely.
subject: Physiology

stem:
A 39-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with complaints of difficulty moving his right eye. On examination, the right eye fails to move upward and outward (superolaterally). There is no ptosis or pupillary abnormality. Neurological examination is otherwise unremarkable.

Which of the following extraocular muscles is most likely affected?
explanation: The inferior oblique muscle is responsible for elevating the eye and moving it laterally, which corresponds to the movement of the eye upwards and outwards. This muscle originates from the maxillary bone and inserts onto the sclera of the eye. It is innervated by the oculomotor nerve (cranial nerve III). Dysfunction of this muscle would lead to an inability to perform the upward and outward movement, as observed in this patient.
subject: Anatomy

stem:
A 30-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with a painless swelling in the scrotum that he has noticed gradually enlarging over the past few weeks. On examination, the swelling is soft, transilluminates with light, and is located anterior to the testis.

Which structure most likely surrounds this swelling?
explanation: The tunica vaginalis is a serous membrane that surrounds the testis and is derived from the peritoneum. It consists of two layers: a visceral layer that covers the anterior and lateral surfaces of the testis and epididymis and a parietal layer that lines the internal surface of the scrotum. A hydrocele is an accumulation of fluid between these two layers, producing a painless, fluctuant, and transilluminable scrotal swelling that is typically located anterior to the testis.
subject: Anatomy

stem:
A 52-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with confusion, diaphoresis, and tremors. Blood tests reveal significant hypoglycaemia. Further evaluation shows elevated serum insulin and C-peptide levels. Imaging studies reveal a well-defined mass within the pancreas.

Which part of the pancreas is most likely affected?
explanation: The tail of the pancreas is the most likely part affected in this scenario because it contains a higher concentration of islet cells, which produce insulin. Insulinomas, which are tumours that secrete insulin, are often found in the tail of the pancreas. The excessive production of insulin by such a tumour can lead to hypoglycaemia, as seen in this patient. Therefore, a pancreatic tumour causing hypoglycaemia is most likely to be located in the tail.
subject: Physiology

stem:
A 32-year-old man is brought to the Emergency Department by paramedics after being found unresponsive with shallow breathing. His friends report that he may have overdosed on heroin.

What is the mechanism of action of the drug used to reverse his condition?
explanation: Naloxone is an opioid antagonist that works primarily by competitively binding to mu-opioid receptors in the central nervous system. By blocking these receptors, naloxone reverses the effects of opioid overdose, such as respiratory depression and sedation. It has a higher affinity for mu receptors than opioids like heroin or morphine, which allows it to displace these substances and reverse their effects. The rapid onset of action makes naloxone highly effective in emergency situations where opioid overdose is suspected.
subject: Head and neck surgery

stem:
A 50-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with fatigue and shortness of breath. His heart rate is recorded as 72 bpm. Investigations reveal an end-diastolic volume of 150 mL and an end-systolic volume of 80 mL.

What is his cardiac output?
explanation: Cardiac output is calculated by multiplying stroke volume by heart rate. Stroke volume is the difference between the end-diastolic volume (EDV) and the end-systolic volume (ESV). In this case, stroke volume = 150 mL – 80 mL = 70 mL. Cardiac output = 70 mL × 72 bpm = 5040 mL/min, which is equivalent to 5.0 L/min when converted to litres. This value represents a normal resting cardiac output in a healthy adult and is physiologically appropriate for the values given.
subject: Physiology

stem:
A 45-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with left flank pain. A CT scan is performed to evaluate the cause of the pain.

Which muscle lies directly posterior to the inferior pole of the left kidney in the posterior abdominal wall?
explanation: The quadratus lumborum muscle is located in the posterior abdominal wall and is positioned posterior to the inferior pole of the left kidney. This muscle functions to stabilise the 12th rib during respiration and assists in lateral flexion of the vertebral column. Its anatomical position makes it directly posterior to the inferior aspect of the kidneys, particularly the left kidney. Understanding the anatomical relationships of the kidney is crucial for procedures such as percutaneous nephrolithotomy and in the assessment of retroperitoneal pathologies.

stem:
A 35-year-old man is brought to the Emergency Department after being rescued from a house fire. He is experiencing difficulty breathing and has soot around his nostrils and mouth. On examination, his respiratory rate is elevated and his GCS score is 8.

What is the most appropriate indication for intubation in this patient?
explanation: A decreased level of consciousness, as indicated by a GCS of 8, is a critical indication for intubation because it suggests a compromised airway and an inability to protect it. Patients with a GCS of 8 or less are at high risk of airway obstruction and aspiration due to reduced gag and cough reflexes. Intubation is necessary to secure the airway and ensure adequate ventilation and oxygenation. In the context of smoke inhalation, the risk of airway compromise is further increased due to potential thermal injury and inhalation of toxic gases.
subject: Critical care

stem:
A 49-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with persistent cough and right-sided chest pain. A chest X-ray reveals a suspicious lesion in the right middle lobe. A biopsy of the middle lobe is due to be performed.

What is the most appropriate location to access the right middle lobe for a biopsy?
explanation: The right middle lobe of the lung is anatomically positioned anteriorly and is best accessed through the right fifth midclavicular space. This location allows for direct access to the middle lobe without interference from other lobes. It is important to avoid the ribs and major vessels, and the 5th intercostal space provides a relatively safe passage. Additionally, this space is commonly used for procedures involving the right middle lobe due to its accessibility and reduced risk of complications.
subject: Cardiothoracic surgery

stem:
A 35-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with lower back pain and bilateral leg weakness. Neurological examination reveals decreased sensation in the perineal region and reduced ankle reflexes.

At what vertebral level does the dural sac end in adults?
explanation: In adults, the dural sac, which is the membranous sheath surrounding the spinal cord and the cauda equina, typically terminates at the level of the second sacral vertebra (S2). This is a critical anatomical landmark as it signifies the end of the cerebrospinal fluid-filled space where the cauda equina resides. Beyond this point, the dura mater continues as the filum terminale, which attaches to the coccyx. Understanding the termination of the dural sac is essential for procedures such as lumbar punctures and epidural anaesthesia to avoid injury to neural structures.
topic: Spinal Cord Surface Anatomy Inc. Spinal Levels
topicRaw: Spinal Cord Surface Anatomy Inc. Spinal Levels
subject: Anatomy

stem:
A 29-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department following a fall from a ladder onto his face. On examination, his vision is blurred with double vision. CT imaging reveals an orbital floor fracture with entrapment of a muscle.

Which direction of eye movement is most likely limited due to the trapped muscle?
explanation: An orbital floor fracture often results in entrapment of the inferior rectus muscle, which normally depresses the eye when it is abducted. However, when this muscle becomes trapped in the fracture site, it prevents the eye from elevating due to mechanical restriction and tethering. This results in diplopia on upward gaze and a positive forced duction test. The inferior rectus does not function to elevate the eye, but its entrapment prevents the antagonist (superior rectus) from lifting the eye, which clinically presents as a limitation in upward gaze.
subject: Anatomy

stem:
A 38-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with severe abdominal pain radiating to the back. A CT scan of the abdomen reveals a mass in the region of the uncinate process of the pancreas.

Which vessel is located posterior to the uncinate process of the pancreas?
explanation: The superior mesenteric vein (SMV) lies posterior to the uncinate process of the pancreas and runs vertically in the right midline of the abdomen. The uncinate process is a hook-like projection of the pancreatic head that curves behind the SMV and sometimes the superior mesenteric artery (SMA). This close anatomical relationship makes the SMV particularly vulnerable to compression, invasion, or encasement by pancreatic masses, especially tumours arising from the head or uncinate process. The SMV is essential in draining the small intestine, cecum, ascending colon, and part of the transverse colon.
subject: Anatomy

stem:
A 32-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with swelling and pain in the region of his left cheek. He reports that the symptoms began after he experienced trauma to the area while playing rugby. Examination reveals tenderness and swelling over the parotid gland with difficulty in facial movements.

Which branch of the facial nerve is most likely to be damaged when cutting the parotid duct?
explanation: The buccal branch of the facial nerve is most likely to be damaged when cutting the parotid duct because it runs close to the duct itself. The buccal branch innervates the muscles of facial expression in the midface, including the buccinator muscle, which is in proximity to the parotid duct. Damage to this branch can result in weakness of the muscles responsible for controlling facial expressions such as smiling or puffing out the cheeks. The proximity of the buccal branch to the parotid duct makes it particularly susceptible to injury during procedures involving the duct.
subject: Anatomy

stem:
A 62-year-old man presents to his General Practitioner with weight loss, haemoptysis and a persistent cough. Imaging reveals a left hilar lung mass encasing the pulmonary artery, and biopsy confirms non-small cell lung carcinoma. The tumour expresses a ligand that inhibits cytotoxic T-cell activity.

Which class of agent is most appropriate in this context?
explanation: PD-1 checkpoint inhibitors are immunotherapeutic agents that block the interaction between PD-1 receptors on T-cells and PD-L1 on tumour cells, thereby reactivating the immune response against the tumour. In non-small cell lung cancer, neoadjuvant immunotherapy with PD-1 inhibitors has shown improved pathological response rates and may facilitate resectability in locally advanced cases. This is particularly relevant in thoracic surgery, where surgical margins can be compromised by vascular invasion. Their integration into preoperative planning highlights the growing interface between oncology and surgical decision-making.
subject: Cardiothoracic surgery

stem:
A 52-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with shoulder pain and difficulty lifting her arm above her head. She reports that the pain started after lifting a heavy object at work. On examination, abduction of the arm is limited to 90°.

Which muscle is responsible for abduction of the shoulder past 90°?
explanation: The trapezius muscle is responsible for the upward rotation of the scapula, which is necessary for abduction of the arm beyond 90°. It stabilises and rotates the scapula to allow the glenoid cavity to face upwards, facilitating further abduction. Without the action of the trapezius, the scapula cannot rotate adequately, limiting the range of motion of the arm. This muscle works in conjunction with the serratus anterior to achieve full abduction of the shoulder.
subject: Anatomy

stem:
A 75-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with left leg pain. On examination, she is able to perform a straight leg raise up to 60°. There is no history of trauma or recent surgery.

What is the most likely anatomical cause of her symptoms?

options.text: Compression of the common peroneal nerve

explanation: Compression of the sciatic nerve is the most likely cause of the symptoms in this elderly lady. The sciatic nerve is responsible for innervating the posterior compartment of the thigh and the entire lower leg and foot, except for the medial aspect. Sciatic nerve compression can result in pain radiating down the leg, which is often exacerbated by movements such as straight leg raising. In this case, the ability to perform a straight leg raise up to 60° suggests involvement of the sciatic nerve, as this test is commonly used to assess sciatic nerve irritation or compression.
topic: Nerve Supply Of The Lower Limbs
topicRaw: Nerve Supply Of The Lower Limbs
subject: Anatomy

stem:
A 29-year-old woman presents to the General Practitioner with concerns about her inability to lose weight despite dieting. She reports feeling constantly hungry and struggles to control her appetite.

What hormone is most likely responsible for her persistent hunger?
explanation: Ghrelin is a hormone produced mainly by the stomach and is known as the hunger hormone because it stimulates appetite. It is secreted when the stomach is empty and signals the hypothalamus to increase hunger, promoting food intake. In individuals who are dieting or have lost weight, ghrelin levels can increase, making it challenging to maintain weight loss due to increased hunger and appetite. This hormone plays a significant role in energy balance and is a key factor in regulating appetite, making it the most likely hormone related to this patient's persistent hunger.
subject: Head and neck surgery

stem:
A 32-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department after sustaining a stab wound to the right fifth intercostal space at the midclavicular line. CT imaging shows that the tip of the knife lies just inferior to the hilum of the right lung, near the pulmonary ligament.

Which of the following structures is most likely to lie closest to the tip of the knife?
explanation: The pulmonary veins lie most inferiorly within the lung hilum and are closest to the pulmonary ligament, which is a fold of pleura extending from the lung hilum to the mediastinum. The inferior pulmonary vein passes through or near the pulmonary ligament, anchoring it and facilitating venous drainage from the lower lobe of the lung. In a penetrating injury at the fifth intercostal space, just below the hilum, the inferior pulmonary vein would likely be the structure nearest the knife tip. Injury to this vein can result in significant haemorrhage and impaired pulmonary venous return.
subject: Critical care

stem:
A 47-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with severe pain in both his legs for 2 days. On examination, bilateral lower limbs are oedematous, tender and erythema is present. He is diagnosed with DVT and is started on heparin therapy.

Which of the following is the target of heparin's action?
explanation: Heparin acts by binding to antithrombin 3, a serine protease inhibitor, and enhances its activity. This interaction leads to the inactivation of several coagulation factors, primarily thrombin (factor IIa) and factor Xa. The binding of heparin to antithrombin 3 induces a conformational change that accelerates the inactivation of these factors, resulting in anticoagulation. This mechanism is crucial for the prevention and treatment of thromboembolic disorders.
subject: Perioperative care

stem:
A 35-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with severe flank pain radiating to the groin. He has no significant past medical history and is otherwise fit and well. A non-contrast CTKUB confirms the presence of a kidney stone.

What is the most likely composition of his kidney stone?
explanation: Calcium oxalate stones are the most common type of kidney stones, accounting for approximately 70-80% of cases. They typically form in individuals who are otherwise healthy and have no underlying metabolic disorders. The formation of calcium oxalate stones is often related to dietary factors and can be influenced by high oxalate intake from foods such as spinach, nuts and tea. These stones are radio-opaque and can be detected on a plain X-ray or CT scan without contrast.
subject: Head and neck surgery

stem:
A 65-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with muscle weakness and confusion. His blood tests show hypomagnesaemia.

Where is the majority of magnesium stored under normal physiological conditions?
explanation: Approximately 50–60% of total body magnesium is stored in bone, making it the largest reservoir of magnesium in the body. Within bone, magnesium is incorporated into the hydroxyapatite crystals and can be mobilised when serum levels fall. Bone magnesium serves both structural and metabolic functions, providing a buffer during periods of magnesium deficiency. Although some magnesium is found in extracellular fluid and soft tissues, these compartments account for a much smaller proportion of total body magnesium.
topic: Calcium Homeostasis, Vitamin D And Hypercalcaemia

subject: Breast and endocrine surgery

stem:
A 42-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with tremor and gum hypertrophy. He is two weeks post-renal transplant and is taking ciclosporin.

What is the mechanism of action of ciclosporin?
explanation: Ciclosporin is a calcineurin inhibitor that suppresses the immune response by preventing T-cell activation. It binds to the cytoplasmic protein cyclophilin, and the resulting complex inhibits the phosphatase activity of calcineurin. Calcineurin is required to activate the nuclear factor of activated T cells (NFAT), which promotes interleukin-2 transcription. Inhibiting this pathway reduces interleukin-2 production, thereby limiting T-cell proliferation and preventing transplant rejection. Tacrolimus is another example of a calcineurin inhibitor.
subject: Organ transplantation

stem:
A 38-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with confusion and lethargy. He has a history of chronic back pain, for which he takes long-term nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and epilepsy managed with anticonvulsants. He is also on antihypertensive medication and recent blood tests reveal hyponatraemia.

What is the most likely cause of his hyponatraemia?
explanation: Carbamazepine is known to cause hyponatraemia through the mechanism of the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH). This anticonvulsant can lead to excessive water retention and dilutional hyponatraemia due to increased ADH activity. Patients on carbamazepine should be monitored for electrolyte imbalances, especially if they present with symptoms such as confusion or lethargy. The drug's propensity to cause hyponatraemia is well-documented and should be considered in patients with unexplained low sodium levels.
subject: Pharmacology

stem:
A 76-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with progressive lower back and right hip pain. He denies recent trauma. On examination, there is localised tenderness over the lumbar spine and right pelvis. Imaging shows multiple bony lesions in the right pelvis, right femur, right ribs, and spine. These lesions appear osteoblastic on radiographic evaluation.

Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Prostate cancer is the most common malignancy in elderly men and frequently metastasises to bone, particularly the spine, pelvis, ribs, and proximal femur. Unlike most other cancers, it classically produces osteoblastic (sclerotic) lesions, which appear as dense areas on imaging. Patients may present with progressive bone pain, particularly in the back or hips. The Batson venous plexus allows direct spread of tumour cells to the vertebral column. The age, sex, distribution of lesions, and osteoblastic nature all point strongly toward metastatic prostate cancer, making this the most likely diagnosis.
subject: Urology

stem:
A 42-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department following a road traffic collision. He is haemodynamically stable but has sustained multiple lacerations and is actively bleeding from a deep thigh wound. He is administered IV tranexamic acid (TXA).

What is the primary mechanism by which TXA reduces bleeding?

options.text: Binding to plasminogen to prevent fibrinolysis
Promotion of platelet aggregation via glycoprotein IIb/IIIa
Stimulation of tissue factor pathway inhibitor

explanation: TXA is a synthetic derivative of lysine that exerts its antifibrinolytic effect by reversibly binding to plasminogen. This binding blocks the interaction between plasminogen and fibrin, thereby preventing the conversion of plasminogen to plasmin, which is responsible for fibrin degradation. By preserving the integrity of formed fibrin clots, TXA reduces excessive bleeding in both surgical and trauma settings. Its use has been shown to reduce mortality when administered early after major trauma, particularly within the first three hours.
subject: Perioperative care

stem:
A 35-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department following a minor laceration on his right forearm after a bar fight. On examination, there is redness and swelling around the site of injury. There is also tenderness at the site of injury.

What is the first step that occurs when a neutrophil binds to the site of inflammation?
explanation: When a neutrophil binds to the site of inflammation, the first step is rolling adhesion. This process involves the neutrophils loosely attaching to the endothelial cells of blood vessels via selectins, which are adhesion molecules. Rolling adhesion allows neutrophils to slow down and roll along the vessel wall, enabling them to detect chemical signals from the site of inflammation. This step is crucial for the subsequent firm adhesion and transmigration of neutrophils into the tissue, where they can perform their immune functions.
subject: Pathology

stem:
A 65-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with sudden-onset severe right-sided flank pain radiating to the groin. He has experienced nausea and vomiting over the past few hours. A non-contrast CT scan of the abdomen reveals a 6 mm obstructing calculus in the proximal right ureter.

What is the primary physiological trigger for the acute colicky pain in this scenario?

options.text: Activation of the parasympathetic nervous system

explanation: The pain associated with ureteric colic is primarily due to the stretching of the ureteral wall by the calculus. This stretching activates nociceptive fibres, which are pain receptors, leading to the severe colicky pain experienced by the patient. The ureter's muscular wall attempts to expel the stone through increased peristalsis, further contributing to the pain. The location of the pain, radiating from the flank to the groin, is characteristic of ureteric colic as the stone moves down the ureter.
subject: Physiology

stem:
A 36-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with dyspareunia. She has a non-tender hard lump in the inguinal region.

What is the most likely site of her cancer?
explanation: The presence of a non-tender hard lump in the inguinal region, along with dyspareunia, suggests possible lymphatic spread of cancer. Anal cancer can metastasise to the inguinal lymph nodes due to its drainage pattern. Inguinal lymphadenopathy is a common presentation in anal cancer because the lower part of the anal canal drains into the inguinal nodes. The combination of these symptoms and findings makes anal cancer the most likely primary site.
subject: Upper gastrointestinal surgery

stem:
A 46-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with dizziness, fatigue, and vomiting. On examination, she is hypotensive and has hyperpigmentation of the oral mucosa. Laboratory investigations reveal hyponatremia and hyperkalaemia.

What is the most appropriate immediate definitive treatment for this patient’s presentation?
explanation: IV hydrocortisone is the first-line treatment in acute adrenal crisis (also known as Addisonian crisis). Hydrocortisone is a glucocorticoid with both glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid activity, making it ideal in this setting. It helps rapidly restore vascular tone, correct hypotension, and reverse electrolyte abnormalities. The standard regimen includes an initial bolus (eg 100 mg IV), followed by continuous infusion or intermittent doses every 6-8 hours. It not only treats the crisis but also addresses the underlying hormone deficiency. This option is lifesaving and most appropriate in the immediate situation.
subject: Physiology

stem:
A 65-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with difficulty walking following a recent hip operation using the antero-lateral approach. On examination, she exhibits a Trendelenburg gait.

What is the most likely nerve that has been damaged during the procedure?
explanation: The superior gluteal nerve is most likely to be damaged during a hip operation using the antero-lateral approach. This nerve innervates the gluteus medius and minimus muscles, which are crucial for stabilising the pelvis during the stance phase of walking. Damage to this nerve results in weakness of these muscles, leading to the characteristic Trendelenburg gait, where the pelvis tilts downwards on the side opposite to the affected limb. The antero-lateral approach to the hip joint places the superior gluteal nerve at risk due to its proximity to the surgical field.
topic: Nerve Supply Of The Lower Limbs
topicRaw: Nerve Supply Of The Lower Limbs
subject: Anatomy

stem:
A 49-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with sudden onset of hearing loss and facial weakness. On examination, he is unable to close his right eye and has decreased taste sensation on the anterior two-thirds of his tongue.

Which of the following does NOT pass through the internal acoustic meatus?
explanation: The nerve to stapedius does not pass through the internal acoustic meatus. It is a branch of the facial nerve which exits the skull through the stylomastoid foramen before giving off the nerve to stapedius. The internal acoustic meatus is a canal in the temporal bone through which the facial nerve and vestibulocochlear nerve travel together. The facial nerve then continues through the facial canal to give rise to the nerve to stapedius within the middle ear cavity.
subject: Anatomy

stem:
A study is being conducted to compare postoperative heights between men and women following spinal surgery. An appropriate statistical test is required to compare preoperative height data between the sexes.

What is the most appropriate statistical test to apply to the women’s preoperative height data?
explanation: An unpaired t-test (also known as an independent t-test) is appropriate when comparing the means of a continuous variable between two independent groups, such as men and women. Since height is a continuous variable and the groups (men vs women) are unrelated, this test evaluates whether there is a statistically significant difference in mean height between the two sexes. It assumes that the data are normally distributed and that the variances between groups are equal. If these assumptions are met, the unpaired t-test is both valid and efficient for comparing preoperative height measurements in this context.
subject: Statistics and research

stem:
A 49-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with a painful, gradually enlarging swelling in his right groin. Examination reveals a reducible mass consistent with an inguinal hernia. He is scheduled for an inguinal hernia repair.

Which dermatome is most appropriate to numb for this procedure?
explanation: The T12 dermatome, supplied by the subcostal nerve, innervates the skin just above the inguinal ligament and the lower part of the anterior abdominal wall, including the upper inguinal region. This is typically the site of the incision in open inguinal hernia repair. T12 is the primary dermatome involved in this surgical field, and its blockade is essential for effective cutaneous anaesthesia of the hernia site. The subcostal nerve also contributes branches to the internal and external oblique muscles, making it relevant for both somatic and muscular innervation in the surgical region.
subject: Anatomy

stem:
A 65-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with progressive fatigue and unintentional weight loss over the past several months. Laboratory investigations reveal normocytic anaemia, hypercalcaemia and impaired renal function. A serum protein electrophoresis shows a monoclonal spike and a bone marrow biopsy reveals increased plasma cells. Congo red staining of a tissue biopsy reveals apple-green birefringence under polarised light, consistent with amyloid deposits.

What is the most likely type of amyloid associated with this patient's presentation?
explanation: AL Amyloid is the most appropriate type of amyloid associated with multiple myeloma. In multiple myeloma, there is a proliferation of plasma cells that produce an excess of light chains. These light chains can misfold and deposit as amyloid fibrils, known as AL (amyloid light-chain) amyloid. This deposition can lead to organ dysfunction such as renal impairment, which is commonly seen in multiple myeloma. The presence of a monoclonal spike on serum protein electrophoresis further supports the diagnosis of multiple myeloma and its association with AL amyloid.
subject: Pathology

stem:
A 33-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with severe abdominal pain radiating to the back and vomiting. He has a history of chronic alcohol abuse and his serum amylase and lipase levels are significantly elevated.

Which enzyme is responsible for the autodigestion process in acute pancreatitis?
explanation: Trypsin is an enzyme that plays a crucial role in the autodigestion of the pancreas during acute pancreatitis. It is normally produced in an inactive form called trypsinogen, which is activated in the small intestine. However, in acute pancreatitis, trypsinogen is prematurely activated within the pancreas, leading to trypsin-mediated digestion of pancreatic tissue. This autodigestion results in inflammation and damage to the pancreatic tissue, contributing to the clinical manifestations of the disease.
subject: Upper gastrointestinal surgery

stem:
A 40-year-old man undergoes a computed tomography scan, which confirms a spinal tumour at the level of the bifurcation of the trachea. An image-guided biopsy is to be performed.

Which spinal level corresponds to the bifurcation of the trachea?
explanation:
The trachea bifurcation is at the level of the lower border of the T4 vertebrae.
