A 72-year-old man who is a lifelong smoker presents to his GP with a history of hoarse voice and some difficulty swallowing. Further questioning reveals otalgia and he is referred for urgent Ear, Nose and Throat (ENT) review. This leads to a diagnosis of carcinoma of the larynx.

Which one of the following head and neck cancers can also cause otalgia?

options.text: Basal cell carcinoma of nasolabial fold
Melanoma of the lower posterior neck

explanation: Referred otalgia is an important symptom in head and neck cancer. Vagus and glossopharyngeal nerves contribute to the sensory supply of the ear and so any malignant process in the regions supplied by these nerves may give rise to referred otalgia. The epiglottis is supplied by the vagus nerve.
subject: Head and neck surgery

stem: Which one of the following cells is cytotoxic?
explanation: CD8 T cells are cytotoxic and recognise cell-bound antigens only in association with class I MHC.
subject: Pathology

stem:
Oncologists have an essential role in any cancer MDT. You are discussing a patient with a rectal adenocarcinoma and the oncologist decides to see them in clinic before surgery to discuss neoadjuvant chemotherapy.

Which of the following is an example of a growth factor receptor oncogene?
explanation: erb B-2 is a growth factor receptor oncogene.
subject: Pathology

stem:
During a posterior approach to the right hip joint, you are asked to identify the gluteal muscles. You correctly identify the most superficial gluteal muscle, which is innervated by the inferior gluteal nerve.

What movements does this muscle produce?
explanation: The gluteus maximus is the most superficial muscle and is supplied by the inferior gluteal nerve. It extends and laterally rotates the hip. The superior and inferior gluteal arteries supply the gluteus maximus and are branches of the internal iliac artery.
subject: Anatomy

stem:
A 20-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with a 12-day history of purulent nasal discharge. On examination, he appears fatigued and has a moderate tenderness on maxillary sinus palpation on both sides and clear rhinorrhoea. Vital signs show BP of 95/65 mmHg and a pulse of 116 beats/min. He denies postnasal drip, sore throat or cough. He has a type I diabetes and no known allergies.

Which of the following is the next best step in the management of this patient?
explanation: The signs and symptoms in this patient are suggestive of acute sinusitis. If a person presents at any time and is systemically very unwell, has symptoms and signs of a more serious illness or is at high risk of complications, or more than 10 days have passed since the onset of symptoms, then the first-line antibiotic of choice according to the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) is co-amoxiclav 500/125 mg three times a day for 5 days.
subject: Head and neck surgery

stem:
A 75-year-old man who is a smoker presents to his General Practitioner with amaurosis fugax. He describes a shutter coming down in front of his left eye on an intermittent basis. On examination, there is a left-sided carotid bruit.

The affected artery enters the orbit through which of the following foramina?
explanation: Amaurosis fugax is a term used to describe transient monocular visual loss due to atherosclerosis of the ipsilateral internal carotid artery. This is noted in the question by the presence of a carotid bruit. In the case of a patient with amaurosis fugax, the central retinal artery is occluded. This artery is a branch of the ophthalmic artery, which enters the orbit through the optic canal. The blood supply to the optic nerve and retina is via the central artery, which is an end artery.
subject: Anatomy

stem:
A 35-year-old man presents with severe rib fractures. Their pain is poorly controlled and their respiratory effort is deteriorating. An arterial blood gas (ABG) is performed to get a more accurate idea of what is happening. On ABG, the patient’s p(CO2) is 8 kPa (normal 4.6–6.0 kPa).

Carbon dioxide retention can cause which one of the following?

options.text: A decrease in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) pressure

explanation: CO2 retention causes a respiratory acidosis, which increases serum potassium, in addition to catecholamine release causing an increased risk of cardiac arrhythmias and sweating.
subject: Physiology

stem:
A 26-year-old man sustains a laceration to his left foot just anteriorly to the medial malleolus. He is haemodynamically unstable but improves with resuscitation.

Which clinical structure is likely to be damaged in this injury?

options.text: The extensor digitorum, which is medial to the tibialis anterior

explanation: The great saphenous vein is found anterior to the medial malleolus. This is in contrast to the small saphenous vein, which is posterior to the lateral malleolus.
subject: Anatomy

stem:
A 78-year-old man presents with a lesion over the skin by the left nasolabial fold, which began as a small lump last year but within the last 2–3 months has developed to a papule with a central crater, with a pearly appearance and a raised rolled border. There are telangiectasiae over the lesion and it is 9 mm in maximal diameter.

Given the likely diagnosis which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: The lesion described is almost always invasive
These lesions occur most commonly in the hands
Radiotherapy is the first line treatment in most cases
These lesions are the second most common skin cancers.

explanation:
This man presents with a slow-growing lesion on the nasolabial fold. Basal-cell carcinomas are the most common form of skin cancers. They typically present in sun-exposed skin and are slow-growing and rarely metastasise. These are epithelial tumours, arising from the basal cells in the epidermis.

It initially presents as a small lump. As it grows, it acquires a pearly, waxy appearance with a central depression (appears like a crater) with rolled (raised) edges. These lesions are translucent with telangiectasia over the surface. These can sometimes ulcerate or bleed. Diagnosis is via a shave biopsy. Small, superficial BCCs may be treated with topical 5-fluorouracil, although BCCs are generally surgically excised. Advanced or extended lesions may require post-operative radiation.
subject: Skin and wound management

stem: Which muscle initiates abduction of the shoulder?
explanation:
The supraspinatus muscle is responsible for the initiation of abduction of the shoulder, between 0° and 15°. After 15°, it acts to hold the head of the humerus in the glenoid fossa. In tears of the supraspinatus tendon, patients often initiate abduction by leaning over to the affected side, allowing the deltoid muscle to take over. The muscles of the rotator cuff are shown in the image below, with the supraspinatus in red.

Original
Henry Gray (1918) Anatomy of the Human Body
Public domain
subject: Anatomy

stem:
A 58-year-old woman presents with persistent upper abdominal pain and a low-grade fever, but no jaundice. On examination, there is an ill-defined fullness in the epigastrium. She is currently awaiting laparoscopic cholecystectomy following an episode of acute gallstone pancreatitis 2 months earlier.

What is the most appropriate investigation?
explanation: Pancreatic pseudocysts can develop the following attacks of acute pancreatitis. They take 3–6 weeks to mature and usually present with low-grade fever, leucocytosis, chronic abdominal pain and/or persistent rise in serum amylase. If very large they can cause gastric outlet obstruction. The investigation of choice is CT of the abdomen, which enables the size and location of the collection to be determined. Often they are managed conservatively, but if very symptomatic they can be treated initially with percutaneous (with imaging guidance), internal or external drainage. If recurrence occurs, formal surgical drainage via cystogastrostomy or cystenterostomy are options.
subject: Upper gastrointestinal surgery

stem:
A 47-year-old woman who was receiving chemotherapy for cancer develops a disseminated varicella-zoster infection. She is given oral and topical aciclovir with some improvement in her symptoms.

Which of the following is the most likely reason for this viral infection?

options.text: Deficiency in the third component of complement
Outgrowth of virus from varicella-zoster immunisation

explanation: An undesirable side-effect of chemotherapy used to treat malignancies is the destruction of T cells, which play a key role in the development of immunity against viral infections. This is especially true for viral diseases in which the causative agent remains dormant in the body. Varicella-zoster is an excellent example of such a virus and flare-ups of varicella-zoster infections are well known occurrences in cancer patients who receive chemotherapy. The varicella-zoster virus is a single entity. It is a medium-sized (100–200 nm), double-stranded DNA virus of the herpesvirus group, with only one serological type.
subject: Surgical oncology

stem:
A 29-year-old man presents to hospital with a hoarse voice. A flexible nasendoscopy is performed in the ENT clinic which reveals the vocal cords are moving asymmetrically.

Which of the following intrinsic muscles of the larynx tenses (stretches) the vocal folds?
explanation: The cricothyroid is the only tensor muscle of the larynx. It brings the thyroid forward to tense and elongate the vocal cords.
topic: Airways Regional Anatomy Inc. Larynx And Trachea Regional Anatomy
topicRaw: Airways Regional Anatomy Inc. Larynx And Trachea Regional Anatomy
subject: Anatomy

stem:
A patient has fallen through his greenhouse and lacerated his dominant wrist on the central palmar aspect. Several tendons are clearly visible.

Concerning the muscles of the forearm, which of the following tendons is most vulnerable to damage?
explanation: The FCR is one of the five superficial muscles of the flexor compartment of the forearm. It arises from the medial epicondyle and inserts radial to the carpal tunnel (not through it) onto the second metacarpal. It is radial to the palmaris longus tendon and, along with it, would be at risk from a palmar wrist laceration. The median nerve is reliably located between the FCR tendon and palmaris longus.
subject: Anatomy

stem: What are the contents of the femoral triangle?

options.text: The femoral canal, which lies lateral to the femoral vein
The femoral canal, which is the most lateral structure in the femoral sheath
The femoral sheath, which contains the femoral vessels
The pubic branch of the inferior epigastric artery

explanation:
The femoral sheath is a downward continuation of the abdominal fascia (transversalis and iliacus) about 2.5 cm below the inguinal ligament. The sheath lies medially to the femoral nerve. Within the sheath itself, the structures are lateral to medial – artery, vein, ‘empty space’, and lymphatics. The ‘empty space’ and lymphatics are better known as the femoral canal, and this space is for the femoral vein to expand into during periods of increased venous return, e.g. walking. The femoral canal is where femoral hernias can develop and commonly strangulate due to the sharp lacunar ligament on the medial aspect of the canal opening.

A 40-year-old man is reviewed after resection of a carcinoid tumour. They would like to know what the future treatment may be.

Which one of the following is correct regarding these tumours?

options.text: Carcinoid tumours are the most commonly found tumours of the appendix
Carcinoid tumours are always associated with hypertension
Cause flushing via production of adrenaline
Are most commonly found in the adrenal gland

explanation: Appendix tumours are most commonly of carcinoid histology, they rarely metastasise.

stem:
A 67-year-old man recently underwent a left femoral nailing procedure. Postoperatively, he suffered a myocardial infarction. He now presents to the Emergency Department with severe pain in his left femur.

What is the effect of severe pain on myocardial blood flow?
explanation: Pain, especially severe pain, can lead to increased sympathetic nervous system activity, which results in elevated heart rate and blood pressure. This elevation in myocardial oxygen demand, combined with vasoconstriction, can reduce myocardial blood flow. Additionally, stress hormones such as vasopressin (antidiuretic hormone) released during pain can further contribute to reduced myocardial blood flow. Therefore, severe pain is most likely to lead to decreased myocardial blood flow.
subject: Emergency medicine and trauma

stem:
A patient has been severely injured and lost a significant amount of blood. On the VBG, the lactate is noted to be raised, you hypothesise that this is due to increased anaerobic respiration at a cellular level.

At a given pO2, haemoglobin gives up oxygen more readily in the following situation:
explanation: Increased temperature promotes a shift of the oxygen-haemoglobin dissociation curve to the right, whereby for a given pO2, oxygen dissociates more readily from haemoglobin.
subject: Physiology

stem:
A 35-year-old man has undergone an emergency laparotomy and is on the intensive care unit. He is maintained on controlled mechanical ventilation via an endotracheal route.

What physiological changes would you expect in someone with this type of ventilation?

options.text: Decreased thoracic pressure, decreased venous return and decreased cardiac output
Decreased thoracic pressure, increased venous return and decreased cardiac output
Increased thoracic pressure, decreased venous return and decreased cardiac output
Increased thoracic pressure, increased venous return and decreased cardiac output
Increased thoracic pressure, increased venous return and increased cardiac output

explanation: Increased thoracic pressure secondary to mechanical ventilation and positive airway pressures causes decreased venous return and subsequently reduced cardiac output. Controlled mechanical ventilation requires intubation and hence necessitates intensive therapy unit (ITU) admission. The patient must be sedated to tolerate the endotracheal tube. Oxygen concentration can reach 100%, although this is avoided to prevent its toxic effects. Mechanical ventilation causes increased thoracic pressure due to the need for positive end-expiratory airway pressure. Positive end-expiratory pressure ventilation increases the risk of barotrauma, which can result in the rapid formation of a tension pneumothorax.
subject: Critical care

stem:
A 78-year-old man with pseudobulbar palsy, lying supine in bed, aspirates one of his tablets into his lungs while swallowing.

The tablet would most likely be found in which of the following bronchopulmonary segments?

options.text: Anterior segmental bronchus of the right superior lobe
Medial segmental bronchus of the right middle lobe
Superior segmental bronchus of the right inferior lobe
Medial basal segmental bronchus of the left inferior lobe
Inferior segmental bronchus of the lingular

explanation: The right main bronchus is more vertical than the left and is the usual site where aspirated foreign bodies end up. As this patient has aspirated the tablet while lying supine, it is likely to fall into the superior segmental bronchus of the right inferior lobe, which branches posteriorly.

topicRaw: Airways Regional Anatomy Inc. Larynx And Trachea Regional Anatomy

stem: Which one of the following is concerned with the chemoreceptor control of breathing?

options.text: The aortic body is located in the root of the aorta
When the CO2 concentration of plasma falls, the central chemoreceptors stimulate the inspiratory area of the brain
Central chemoreceptors are sensitive to the CO2 content of the CSF
The carotid bodies are located on the external carotid artery
Central chemoreceptors are sensitive to the O2 content of the CSF

explanation: Central chemoreceptors are sensitive to CO2 concentration of CSF. A rise in CO2 stimulates the respiratory centres in the medulla to increase rate and depth of breathing.

stem:
A 58-year-old man is undergoing open-heart surgery. A two-vessel bypass graft is performed, which starts bleeding during the closure. He is given two volumes of packed red blood cells rapidly to maintain volume. Diffuse bleeding into the incision and suture lines leads to hypotension and renal failure.

Which of the following is LEAST likely to be part of the management plan in this patient at this stage?
explanation: The trisodium salt of citric acid is sodium citrate. It acts as a flavouring agent as well as an anticoagulant, however, it is not used for anticoagulation in the cardiopulmonary bypass; instead, heparin is used for anticoagulation purposes.
subject: Vascular surgery

stem:
A patient with Crohn's has had multiple resections for stricturing disease. They are developing further symptoms and attend the Emergency Department.

In a patient who has undergone an extensive ileocolic resection, which one of the following biochemical abnormalities would be most expected?
explanation: The terminal ileum is an important site of bile salt re-absorption as well as lipid soluble vitamins including Vitamin A, D, E and K. Extensive resection leads to short bowel syndrome. Vitamin D deficiency and the reduction of calcium absorption surface in the ileum can lead to hypocalcaemia and secondary hyperparathyroidism.
subject: Breast and endocrine surgery

stem:
A 6-year-old boy is having an elective umbilical hernia repair. Intraoperatively his temperature is noted to be 31°C.

Which of the following responses to hypothermia is most likely to occur in this patient?

options.text: Decreased duration of action of anaesthetic drugs

explanation: Temperatures below 35°C can cause mild platelet dysfunction and below 33°C can also affect the clotting cascade resulting in an increased bleeding risk.
subject: Emergency medicine and trauma

stem:
A 37-year-old woman presents to her General Practitioner with an irregular, erythematous, scaly plaque on her right forearm. The lesion has been slowly enlarging over the past few months. She reports a history of prolonged sun exposure. On histological examination of the biopsy, there is atypia of the keratinocytes across the full thickness of the epidermis.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Squamous cell carcinoma in situ (SCCIS), also known as Bowen's disease, is an early stage of squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) that primarily affects the skin. It is characterised by the presence of atypical or abnormal squamous cells in full thickness of epidermis. SCCIS typically appears as well-defined, reddish, scaly patches that may slowly enlarge. It is most commonly caused by prolonged sun exposure, making it more prevalent in sun-exposed areas. While SCCIS is non-invasive and confined to the epidermis, it has the potential to progress into invasive SCC if left untreated.
subject: Skin and wound management

stem:
An 87-year-old man with perforated diverticular disease undergoes a lengthy laparotomy. The anaesthetists are concerned about maintaining the patient’s temperature during the operation.

Which of the following would be most effective in maintaining the patient’s core body temperature during the procedure?

options.text: Use of a heated blanket set at 35 °C
Use of warm saline soaked packs to cover the bowel

explanation: A heated blanket is highly effective in maintaining the patient’s core body temperature. It provides consistent warmth and counters the effects of conductive, convective, and evaporative heat loss during the procedure.
topic: Fitness For Surgery And General Anaesthetic
topicRaw: Fitness For Surgery And General Anaesthetic
subject: Perioperative care

stem:
An 84-year-old woman who was initially admitted and treated for a neck of femur fracture remains an in-patient 3 weeks later as she cannot be safely discharged. The night Foundation Year 1 Doctor sees the patient and concludes that she has developed a deep vein thrombosis (DVT).

Which of the following features is not a component of Wells’ score for DVT?
explanation: Patients with a low Wells’ score should have a D-dimer test to further investigate for DVT, but the D-dimer value is not an initial component of the score.
subject: Vascular surgery

stem:
A 48-year-old man who was previously fit and well has an emergency splenectomy after a road traffic accident.

Which one of the following would be found on his blood film after surgery?
explanation: Pappenheimer bodies are basophilic granules composed of iron found in red blood cells typically removed by the spleen and would therefore be seen in patients post splenectomy.
subject: Upper gastrointestinal surgery

stem:
A 55-year-old man is admitted to the Emergency Department with a very high international normalised ratio due to warfarin. He is likely to need surgery on this admission and warfarin with intravenous vitamin K should be reserved.

In which of the following clotting factors is Vitamin K NOT involved in the carboxylation of glutamic acid residues?
explanation: Factor XI is not dependant on vitamin K. Vitamin K is essential for activation of clotting factors II (prothrombin), VII, IX and X.
subject: Physiology

stem:
A 54-year-old woman presents with a neck lump which raises when she swallows. On examination there is no lymphadenopathy, but a chest X-ray shows a pulmonary nodule. Cytology is not conclusive and a hemithyroidectomy is performed.

Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Follicular carcinomas are the second most common thyroid cancer and account for around 20% of all thyroid cancers. They metastasise by haematogenous spread to lungs and bone. Fine-needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) is capable of diagnosing benign colloid, involutional or cellular nodules and papillary, medullary and anaplastic carcinoma. It cannot however distinguish between follicular adenoma and follicular carcinoma as this requires histological confirmation of the presence of capsular or vascular invasion in the latter.
subject: Breast and endocrine surgery

stem:
You are performing a zone 2 repair of a flexor tendon on a patient's right middle finger.

Which of the following is most likely to be used?
explanation: When repairing a tendon it is important not to cut through the tissues as they may be damaged leading to fraying of the edges and rupture. A round bodied needle does not cut the tissue as it passes through, and so is the most likely here.
subject: Perioperative care

stem:
A 22-year-old man is brought into the Emergency Department with severe jaw pain while yawning. On examination, his mouth is wide open and he cannot close it. A dislocated temporomandibular joint is diagnosed.

Which of the following muscles carries out protrusion and depression of the mandible?
explanation: Being a masticatory muscle, the lateral pterygoid aids in chewing and biting actions by controlling the movements of the mandible. The sphenoid attachment of the muscle is always fixed, meaning that the direction of pull is oriented towards it. Bilateral contraction of the left and right pterygoid muscles results in translation and rotation within both temporomandibular joints. The inferior heads pull the mandibular condyle anteriorly, which results in rotation of the condyle against the inferior surface of the articular disc. At the same time, the superior heads pull the articular capsule and the disc in the same direction (anteriorly) to cushion the movements of the condyle. The end result is anterior translation of the disc and condyle, occurring concurrently with rotation of the condyle – this is seen as protrusion and depression of the mandible.
topic: Mandible And Temporomandibular Joint Regional Anatomy
topicRaw: Mandible And Temporomandibular Joint Regional Anatomy

stem: Which of the following would be most consistent with femoral nerve damage in a patient with pelvic trauma?

options.text: Loss of sensation over the anterior thigh
Loss of power in the biceps femoris muscle
Loss of sensation over the posterior thigh

explanation: The femoral nerve may be damaged from fractures of the pelvis or femur, or dislocations of the hip, and hip or hernia surgery. It can also be involved in psoas abscesses, thigh wounds and frequently in large psoas haematomas in patients with haemophilia and diabetic amyotrophy. It leads to a loss of power in the knee extension. In addition there is quadriceps wasting, loss of knee jerk and impaired sensation over the front of the thigh as it gives off the anterior cutaneous branches of the femoral nerve. Partial lesions are common from thigh wounds with the nerve to the quadriceps most frequently involved causing great problems with walking especially when descending stairs as the knee gives way.
subject: Anatomy

stem:
A 3-year-old presents with a history of 3–4 days of sore throat and temperature, but today his parents noticed excessive salivation, excessive halitosis, and they were concerned that he was refusing to drink or eat. Examination is difficult as the patient finds it extremely distressing to open their mouth, however, the uvula appears to be displaced to one side.

What are the most likely bacteria to be cultured?
explanation: This patient presents with typical signs and symptoms of quinsy, a peritonsillar abscess, of which Streptococcus pyogenes is the most common causative organism. History may reveal a severe sore throat, possibly unilaterally sore, with fevers. Swallowing may be especially painful with the patient drooling their saliva as a result, with difficulty opening their mouth (trismus), and a ‘hot potato voice’. Additionally neck stiffness and headache are common, sometimes the patient will complain of torticollis. Examination reveals a unilateral bulging, often above the tonsils, resulting in uvula displacement and the patient may also have halitosis. Examination may be difficult due to the trismus, as is likely the case in this patient. Definitive management requires surgical intervention – either needle aspiration, incision and drainage or tonsillectomy. Additionally, the patient will require IV antibiotics and usually IV fluids (either due to signs of sepsis, or because of dehydration due to difficulty in swallowing).
subject: Clinical microbiology

stem:
A 60-year-old previously fit and well man dies suddenly after two separate syncopal episodes. The family are very distressed as no cause of death is obvious.

At post mortem examination, which one of the following congenital cardiac defects that could be associated with his sudden death would you expect to find?
explanation: Aortic stenosis is associated with ‘drop attacks’ such as described here, as the stenosed valve causes a fixed limitation on maximal cardiac output which is then unable to maintain cerebral perfusion with peripheral vasodilation. This is also why anaesthesia in patients with severe aortic stenosis is more risky. The classic triad for aortic stenosis is heart failure, angina, and syncope. Bicuspid aortic valves are prone to early calcification, causing aortic stenosis that presents in middle-age rather than in the elderly. They are also associated with sudden death. Bear in mind that the commonest congenital causes of sudden cardiac death are arrhythmogenic conditions such as a long QT interval, Brugada or catecholaminergic polymorphic VT (CPVT).
subject: Critical care

stem:
A 40-year-old woman suffers from recurrent urinary tract infections caused by Proteus spp. isolated from her mid-stream urine samples. Cystoscopic bladder examination confirms the presence of a bladder calculus.

What is the most likely composition of the bladder calculus?
explanation: Magnesium ammonium phosphate calculi account for approximately one-sixth of all bladder stones and are particularly associated with Proteus spp. infections (eg Proteus mirabilis and Proteus vulgaris).
subject: Urology

stem:
A 46-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with pain over the right flank. She has obesity, a buffalo hump and diabetes. She also has a weakness of the proximal limb muscles. Imaging reveals a 10 cm right adrenal mass and a 2 cm metastatic deposit over the base of the left lung. The 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test is abnormal.

What is the best approach in the management of this patient?

options.text: Right open radical adrenalectomy and left-lung lower-lobe wedge resection
Left adrenalectomy and right lung lower lobe lobectomy

explanation:
Patients with stage IV adrenocortical carcinoma are usually not offered curative surgery. If there are limited metastatic lesions restricted to a small region, as in this patient, an attempt to perform an R0 resection (complete resection with negative microscopic margins) can be made. Right open radical adrenalectomy and left-lung lower-lobe wedge resection is the ideal approach. Up to 74% of functional adrenocortical tumours produce excess cortisol.

Since this patient has obesity, diabetes and weakness of proximal limb muscles, indicating the presence of a hormone-secreting tumour, cytoreductive surgery is preferred. This results in a better quality of life and better overall outcome. The 5-year survival rate in adrenal cortical carcinoma is 20–47% in adults.
subject: Urology

stem:
You are called to the delivery room with your registrar to see a baby who the midwife says has ‘no abdominal wall’. When you get there you find a baby with an abdominal defect with loops of bowel outside the abdomen, and no covering layers.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: In gastroschisis there is no peritoneal covering, and it is rarely associated with congenital defects seen in patients with omphalocoele. However, sometimes it may be associated with intestinal atresia. Management initially consists of covering the defect with cling film to prevent heat and moisture loss, while establishing intravenous (IV) access for IV fluids.
subject: Breast and endocrine surgery

stem:
A 22-year-old woman student presents with epistaxis. This fails to improve with pressure.

Which one of the following methods would be attempted next?
explanation: Application of sustained pressure for epistaxis is the primary first aid measure. If unsuccessful, silver nitrate or chemical cautery can be utilised and can be very effective in stemming epistaxis. However, in higher risk patients (particularly the elderly on anticoagulation), nasal packing, both anterior and posterior, may be required. Progression to surgery and artery ligation would then be the next management method.
subject: Anatomy

stem:
A 78-year-old life-long smoker presents with a painful ulcerated lesion on the side of his tongue. This has grown considerably in size.

Which one of the following statements regarding carcinoma of the tongue is correct?

options.text: It causes death through local complications or aspiration pneumonia
The floor of mouth is the most common site for oral squamous cell carcinoma
Surgical excision is contraindicated for oral cavity cancers

explanation: Aspiration pneumonia secondary to carcinoma-induced dysphagia is a common cause of death for patients with carcinoma of the tongue.
subject: Anatomy

stem:
A patient with significant clotting derangement is under your care. After arranging a blood film you seek advice from the haematologist on call as the patient may be higher risk for their surgical procedure.

Testing for factor V Leiden is warranted in patients with which one of the following options?
explanation: Factor V Leiden tests are indicated for venous thrombo-embolism presenting at a relatively young age, or in an unusual part of the body. They are also indicated when a patient has a strong personal or family history of recurrent deep vein thromboses (DVTs), or when they are experiencing unexplained miscarriages. In Britain, 5% of the population carry one or more genes for factor V Leiden. These patients are at an increased risk of venous thrombosis. This risk is five times greater than that of the general population.
subject: Vascular surgery

stem:
A 35-year-old woman with a body mass index (BMI) of 33 presents to the pregnancy assessment unit at 26 weeks gestation with numbness and burning to her thigh, which developed gradually in the last 2 weeks. Neurological examination reveals only a sensory deficit in the right lateral thigh.

Which of the following nerves of the lower limb is most likely to be affected?
explanation:
Entrapment syndrome of the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve is also called meralgia paraesthetica. The lateral cutaneous nerve originates from the femoral nerve, L2 and L3 roots, and is sensory only.

The nerve travels lateral to the psoas muscle, crossing the iliacus and under the lateral inguinal ligament. From there, it becomes superficial and innervates the lateral thigh. The most common site of impingement is under the inguinal ligament. It is more common in men. Risk factors include tense ascites, obesity, surgery, tight clothing and pregnancy.

It presents with paraesthesia & numbness in the upper lateral thigh on the affected side. Symptoms are worsened by standing and relieved by sitting.

Examination reproduces the pain by compression below the anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS) and hip extension. The motor examination is intact.

Management is with NSAIDs, TENS and ultrasound-guided injections. In severe cases, operative decompression may be performed.
topic: Nerve Supply Of The Lower Limbs
topicRaw: Nerve Supply Of The Lower Limbs
subject: Anatomy

stem:
A 42-year-old man presents with chronic swelling of his jaw. An orthopantomogram (OPG) shows a small jaw cyst in the body of his left mandible.

What would be the preferred treatment option?
explanation: Jaw cysts are the most common cause of chronic swelling of the jaw. They grow slowly, displacing rather than absorbing teeth. They are usually asymptomatic unless infected, and are rarely large enough to cause pathological fractures. Pseudocysts do not contain epithelial linings, but are still classified as cysts. The cysts are benign and therefore wide local excision or removal of significant amounts of surrounding bone are not required. Both enucleation and marsupialisation are valid treatment options and can be combined, with marsupialisation being more commonly used if infection is present to allow this to drain, whereas enucleation removes the cyst itself.
subject: Breast and endocrine surgery

stem:
A 60-year-old man is 2 weeks post-renal transplant, complaining of polyuria and polydypsia.

His blood tests show the following:

Investigation	Result	Normal value
Haemoglobin	10.1 g/l	13.5–17.5 g/l
Mean Corpuscular Volume	80 fl	76–98 fl
Ca2+	2.95 mmol/l	2.20–2.60 mmol/l
Phosphate	1.8 mmol/l	0.7–1.4 mmol/l
Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)	150 iu/l	30–130 iu/l

What is the most likely underlying problem?
explanation: The patient presents with symptoms relating to hypercalcaemia that is caused by tertiary hyperparathyroidism. Following a long-standing period of secondary hyperparathyroidism, such as that occurring during renal failure, tertiary hyperparathyroidism can arise. This is commonly seen following renal transplantation to treat renal failure. Due to the prolonged stimulation that has occurred in the parathyroid glands, in response to the relative serum hypocalcaemia caused by renal failure, the glands continue to secrete PTH autonomously and inappropriately, even after the correction of hypocalcaemia. As in the above scenario, this results in: raised PTH levels, hypercalcaemia and hyperphosphataemia. Alkaline phosphatase level is mildly raised in all forms of hyperparathyroidism but can also be normal.
subject: Breast and endocrine surgery

stem:
A patient becomes hypoxic on the Ward. As the first doctor to review them, you support their respiratory system with 15 L high-flow oxygen through a non-rebreathe mask while you gain more information.

Pulmonary gas exchange occurs under which one of the following physiological principles?

options.text: Only about 0.15% of oxygen is carried in solution in the plasma
Gas exchange can occur in the final seven branches of the bronchoalveolar tree
Oxygen delivery to tissues is independent of cardiac output
Haemoglobin concentration does not affect oxygen carrying capacity
Dissolved oxygen in plasma provides the majority of oxygen delivery at rest

explanation: The final seven branches of the bronchoalveolar tree are the respiratory zone and gas exchange can occur here.
subject: Physiology

stem:
A 30-year-old man has been stabbed in the abdomen. On arrival at the Emergency Department, he is haemodynamically unstable and transferred straight to theatre for an exploratory laparotomy. On exploration of his abdomen, there is blood in the left upper quadrant. Examination of the spleen demonstrates that it is intact but actively bleeding and it appears that the splenic artery has been damaged.

What degree of splenic injury has this patient most likely suffered?
explanation: Trauma to the spleen is graded on a 1–5 scale based on the degree of severity (with 5 being the most severe injury). A grade 4 splenic injury is defined by the presence of a splenic vascular injury or active bleeding within the splenic capsule. It is also described by a laceration to the spleen, which results in ≥ 25% of the spleen losing its blood supply. As the splenic artery has been damaged, it is a grade 4 splenic injury. Treatment for this injury usually requires splenectomy to prevent further blood loss.
subject: Upper gastrointestinal surgery

stem:
A 78-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with obstructive jaundice and weight loss. A computed tomography scan of the abdomen reveals a mass in the head of the pancreas involving the common bile duct.

The fluids produced by the pancreas drain into which part of the gastrointestinal tract?

options.text: Second part of the duodenum medially
Second part of the duodenum laterally
Second part of the duodenum posteriorly
First part of the duodenum medially
Third part of the duodenum medially

explanation: The joining of the pancreatic duct and the bile duct forms the ampulla of Vater, which enters the second part of the duodenum at the major duodenal papilla. The hepatopancreatic ampulla enters the second part of the duodenum at the major duodenal papilla. Through this papilla, endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography can enable the relief of obstructive jaundice via placement of a biliary stent.
subject: Breast and endocrine surgery

stem:
A 24-year-old rugby player was injured during a match and sustained a significant eye injury. Subsequently, he presented to the Emergency Department and was diagnosed with an orbital floor fracture

Which of the following complications results from fractures of the orbital floor (‘blowout fractures’)?
explanation: Blowout fractures occur along the orbital floor, as this is the thinnest part of the bone. Structures may herniate through into the ethmoidal or maxillary sinuses, causing the ‘trapdoor’ appearance on plain X-ray. Ocular injury occurs in 24% of cases, with enophthalmos and diplopia the commonest signs. Computed tomography scan helps to delineate the fracture and aids in planning surgery if required.
subject: Head and neck surgery

stem:
A 75-year-old man is admitted to the Emergency Department following a road traffic collision. A head computed tomography scan reveals a base-of-skull fracture with possible extension towards the foramen magnum.

What does NOT pass through the foramen magnum?
explanation: The hypoglossal nerve exits the skull through its own foramen (the hypoglossal foramen).
subject: Anatomy

stem:
You are reviewing a follow-up patient in the cardiothoracic clinic with an ‘EGFR’ mutation in their lung cancer, according to the pathology report in the notes. This is an example of an oncogene.

Which one of the following statements is correct regarding oncogenes?

options.text: Exhibit a high degree of evolutionary variability
Code for proteins involved in cellular regulatory processes
Are only found in viral genomes
Code for structural proteins of the cell membrane only

explanation: Oncogenes tend to code for proteins (oncoproteins) involved in key cellular regulatory processes.
subject: Pathology

stem:
Following emergency surgery for an open femoral fracture, the anaesthetist notices petechial haemorrhages. The patient was intubated on arrival at the Emergency Department and taken straight to theatre. His medical history is unknown.

What is the most likely cause of these petechial haemorrhages?
explanation: Fat embolism can occur following long bone fracture and its treatment. Clinical features often include fever, shortness of breath, cyanosis, tachypnoea and petechial haemorrhages. Given the history, fat embolism is the most likely cause in this case.
subject: Perioperative care

stem:
A 30-year-old man with ulcerative colitis (UC) attends the coloproctology clinic following a Gastroenterology referral for restorative proctocolectomy.

Which one of the following is most accurate regarding restorative proctocolectomy?

options.text: Restorative proctocolectomy is absolutely contra-indicated in patients who have an internal anal sphincter defect
Patients with both ulcerative colitis and primary sclerosing cholangitis are at higher risk of requiring proctocolectomy than patients with ulcerative colitis alone
Panproctocolectomy with permanent ileostomy is the only surgical option for UC
Pouch surgery has no risk of pouchitis
Total colectomy cures all extraintestinal manifestations of UC

explanation:
Indications for proctocolectomy in UC include (non-exhaustive list):

elective – chronic steroid dependency or systemic side-effects from treatment, dysplasia or adenocarcinoma on biopsy, refractory disease despite medical management
PSC, in particular, is associated with an increased risk of developing colorectal cancer so, in line with the above indications, is more likely to require restorative proctocolectomy. (A 1999 study found that 25% of 132 UC patients with PSC developed colorectal cancer, compared to 11% of the control group).
subject: Colorectal surgery

stem:
You notice that the rate of surgical site infection has risen in the last 6 months. You would like to commence a project on this, but you are not sure whether your project is classified as an audit or as research.

Which statement is true of clinical audit only, and not research?

options.text: May be short term or long term

explanation: Clinical audit is concerned with current practice, and how it can be improved; and should not be comparing novel treatments. Audit is comparing practice to accepted standards, eg guidelines. Research is the generation of new data/practice.
subject: Statistics and research

stem:
You undertake a local anaesthetic list but when a basic plastics set is opened, your scrub nurse notes the blade handle has residual material on it. She is not happy with the sterility of her instruments

Consider the process of sterilisation, which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: Sterilisation may be confirmed by the Elson test
Sterilisation using saturated steam is the method of choice for surgical instruments
Sterilisation by ethylene oxide requires no aeration period afterwards
Autoclaving is performed at 100 degrees Celsius for 15 minutes
Chemical sterilisation with glutaraldehyde is the first choice for all instruments

explanation: Sterilisation by steam can be used for all instruments that can withstand moist heat and is the most commonly used method. Moisture sensitive instruments such as non-stainless metals, instruments with fine cutting edges for example (that cannot tolerate corrosion) require dry-heat sterilisation in hot-air ovens.
subject: Perioperative care

stem:
A 27-year-old woman reports pain in the front of her neck, which radiates to her jaw and ears. She has been feeling lethargic for a few days and recently experienced symptoms resembling a viral infection (e.g., fever, malaise). Examination reveals a slight swelling in the anterior neck, which elevates on swallowing and exacerbates her pain. Blood tests show slightly elevated T4 and T3 levels.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: De Quervain’s thyroiditis is a rare condition thought to be associated with a viral infection. It causes an influenza-like illness and there is painful diffuse swelling of the thyroid gland. Pain is worsened by swallowing and coughing. Initially the inflammation causes release of hormones causing T3 and T4 to be elevated for 4–6 weeks after which a period of hypothyroidism may occur due to depletion. Monitoring of thyroid function is important to identify if thyroxine is required to be prescribed temporarily if hypothyroidism occurs.
subject: Breast and endocrine surgery

stem:
A 42-year-old man with a history of a road traffic accident and injury to his back and neck presents with global muscle wasting of the left hand.

Which is the nerve or nerve root most likely to be involved?
explanation:
Isolated damage to the C7 nerve root would be expected to cause elbow extension weakness, which is not described in the question. Although it may cause some mild weakness in the median nerve, it would not affect the ulnar nerve and would not cause global wasting in the hand.

Close

subject: Anatomy

stem:
A 56-year-old accountant is diagnosed with a liver abscess. He has no recent history of foreign travel, or significant past medical history. He has always lived in the United Kingdom, with his wife and two children.

Which of the following micro-organisms is most likely to be the causative agent?
explanation: Pyogenic abscesses account for 75% of liver abscesses in developed countries. Most pyogenic liver abscesses are secondary to coliforms such as E. coli and Klebsiella. The most common cause is cholangitis associated with biliary stones followed by diverticulitis. Most are polymicrobial with Gram-negative aerobic and anaerobic organisms predominating.
subject: Hepatobiliary and pancreatic surgery

stem:
A 78-year-old man presents with difficulty of micturition. Prostate-specific antigen levels are significantly raised and, on digital rectal examination, he is noted to have a hard, craggy prostate gland.

In which histological portion of the prostate gland is adenocarcinoma most likely to develop?
explanation: The peripheral zone of the prostate contains around 75% of all the glandular tissue. Accordingly, 70–80% of all prostate cancers originate here.

stem:
Carotid sinus baroreceptors are located in the carotid sinus at the bifurcation of the external and internal carotids. Direct pressure in the area increases vagal tone and has use in managing supraventricular tachycardias.

These baroreceptors are stimulated by which one of the following?
explanation: Baroreceptors are pressure receptors, they respond to alterations in the stretch of the carotid sinus. They are found in the adventitia of the blood vessels and wall of the heart. The arterial baroreceptors are located in the carotid sinus and aortic arch. When the arterial blood pressure drops, the arterial wall is subjected to less stretch, and the sensory nerves coming from the carotid sinus (sinus nerve) and from the aortic arch (depressor nerve) become less active and send fewer impulses. Upon receiving fewer impulses from the baroreceptors, the cardiovascular centres respond by exciting the sympathetic and inhibiting the parasympathetic nervous systems. This leads to an increase in heart rate and stroke volume, and generalised constriction of arterioles (not brain or heart) and veins. On the venous side, receptors are found in the wall of the left and right atria, at the entrances of the inferior vena cava and superior vena cava and in the pulmonary circulation.

stem: Which one of the following is true regarding carbon dioxide (CO2)?

It is less soluble than oxygen in blood
The majority of CO2 is transported dissolved in plasma
Carbonic anhydrase is found only in the lungs
CO2 does not combine with haemoglobin

explanation:
Carbon dioxide (CO2) produces H+ when dissolved in blood. This is buffered mainly by Hb.

CO2 decreases the oxygen binding power of Hb and it is 25 times more soluble in blood than is oxygen. CO2 is dissolved in the blood and via carbonic anhydrase forms hydrogen and bicarbonate ions. The bicarbonate diffuses out of the cell in exchange for chloride ions, the so-called chloride shift.

The thoracodorsal nerve innervates latissimus dorsi, T, which extends and internally rotates the humerus and is a powerful adductor of the shoulder. The thoracodorsal nerve, a branch of the posterior cord of the brachial plexus, arises between the upper and lower subscapular nerves. It derives its fibres from C6, C7 and C8. It follows the course of the subscapular artery, along the posterior wall of the axilla to the apex of the latissimus dorsi. The latissimus dorsi is responsible for adduction, extension and internal rotation of the humerus. In the scenario described, it is the affected muscle due to injury to the thoracodorsal nerve. The latissimus dorsi is a key muscle for climbing, as it powerfully adducts and depresses the humerus, enabling the trunk to be brought up to the arm, for example, in pull-ups.

You are performing an open reduction and plate fixation of a distal radius fracture.

Which of the following maximum tourniquet pressure and tourniquet time would you consider to be the safest and most effective for a tourniquet placed on the proximal part of the arm?

options.text: Pressure: 50 mmHg above systolic blood pressure/time: 60 min
Pressure: 100 mmHg above systolic blood pressure/time: 120 min

explanation:
Pressure: 150 mmHg/time: 90 min

Pressure: 50 mmHg above diastolic blood pressure/time: 60 min

Pressure: 100 mmHg above diastolic blood pressure/time: 90 min

A pressure of 50 mmHg above systolic blood pressure would be just above arterial pressure and therefore be suitable to prevent blood from obscuring the surgical field while also minimising the risk of vascular damage, thrombosis, soft-tissue and nerve injury. A tourniquet time of 60 min would be safe, beyond 2 h there is a higher risk of injury. It is also good practice to release the tourniquet before suturing the wound to identify the bleeding vessels and so prevent post-operative haemorrhage.

Lymphoma

explanation: The clinical picture is of intussusception which occurs in 0.4% of children. It is more common in boys, usually younger than 1 year old. Intussusception occurs when one section of the bowel invaginates into another, the most common form is ileocolic. Blood and mucus or ‘redcurrant jelly’ stool may be passed after the first 24 h as a late manifestation. Sausage-shaped mass may be felt in upper abdomen. Rectal examination is very important as occasionally the apex of intussusception is palpable. The majority of cases are successfully treated conservatively with an air enema.

stem:
A 60-year-old woman is treated after a partial gastrectomy with duodenal exclusion (Polya gastrectomy). She is seen in the clinic post-operatively and is advised of ongoing risks to her health.

What bone complication of this surgery might you commonly expect?
explanation: Post-partial gastrectomy with duodenal exclusion (Polya gastrectomy) results in a reduction of calcium absorption causing osteomalacia 10–20 years after surgery. Under normal circumstances, calcium absorption, which occurs in the duodenum and proximal small bowel, is modest at best. Following gastric surgery, calcium absorption is even less efficient as a result of rapid emptying of the stomach and bypassing of the duodenum in the case of a Billroth II. Which of the following statements concerning frostbite (freezing cold injury) is correct?

The outcome of Freezing cold injury (frostbite) cannot be predicted based on the degree or grade of the injury.
The muscle and bone are never affected
Aspirin or ibuprofen should be administered to the patient suffering frostbite

explanation: Use of aspirin (or ibuprofen) is now recommended to improve circulation to affected extremities. The pathophysiology behind frostbite is complex, but is a combination of intracellular ice crystal formation with cell membrane dysfunction/rupture alongside loss of microvascular haemostasis. The release of prostaglandin and thromboxane promotes platelet aggregation and thrombosis, so aspirin (or ibuprofen) can be utilised to reduce these effects. Of note, no studies have directly demonstrated that any particular anti-inflammatory agent or dosing is clearly beneficial to outcome.

The early phase of increased intracranial pressure (ICP) causes which one of the following?
explanation:
Bradycardia is associated with the late stages of rising intracranial pressure.

At standard cervical mediastinoscopy, what is the least likely lymph node station to be sampled?

The pretracheal space is entered as part of the mediastinoscopy procedure, and these nodes are therefore available for sampling.

Anterior Mediastinum Regional Anatomy

stem:
The radial artery crosses the floor of the anatomical snuffbox.

What are the palmar and dorsal boundaries of the anatomical snuffbox?

options.text: Palmar: flexor pollicis longus - dorsal: extensor pollicis longus
Palmar: abductor pollicis brevis and extensor pollicis longus - dorsal: abductor pollicis longus
Palmar: abductor pollicis brevis and extensor pollicis brevis – dorsal: abductor pollicis longus
Palmar: extensor pollicis brevis and abductor pollicis longus – dorsal: extensor pollicis longus
Palmar: extensor pollicis longus and abductor pollicis longus – dorsal: extensor pollicis brevis

explanation: The dorsal border of the anatomical snuffbox is the extensor pollicis longus tendon. The palmar border is formed by both the abductor pollicis longus and the extensor pollicis brevis tendons. Proximally, the border is formed by the radial styloid process. The trapezium and scaphoid form the floor. As it leaves the cubital region, the radial artery passes medial to the biceps tendon and superficial to the insertion of the pronator teres muscle. At the wrist, the artery passes across the floor of the anatomical snuffbox over the trapezium. It enters the hand between the two heads of the first dorsal interosseous and the oblique and transverse heads of the adductor pollicis muscles, continuing as the deep palmar arch. The arch is completed medially by a branch of the ulnar artery and allows for anastomosis between these two arteries.
subject: Anatomy

stem:
A 25-year-old man presents to the Burn Outpatient Clinic with excess hypertrophic scarring over his chest following a severe burn.

Which of the following is a characteristic of hypertrophic scarring?

options.text: It tends to grow for years
It characteristically extends beyond the margins of the original scar
It has a strong genetic predisposition
It is characteristically seen in deep dermal burns

explanation:
A hypertrophic scar is a form of excessive healing resulting from overproduction of all components of the healing process, including fibroblasts, collagen, elastin and proteoglycans. The incidence of hypertrophic scars is highest in:

wounds crossing flexor surfaces
wounds crossing tension lines
areas of excessive skin (wound) tension and movement
deep dermal burns
wounds left to heal by secondary intention (more than 3 weeks).
subject: Emergency medicine and trauma

stem:
You are reviewing a patient in the plastic surgical clinic referred by their General Practitioner with a query of squamous cell carcinoma (SCC). They are listed for surgical excision biopsy of the lesion.

Which of the following is correct in respect of these tumours?

options.text: Are most commonly found on the trunk
Are not associated with UV exposure

explanation:
Bowen’s disease is also called SCC in situ. The cancer cells are restricted to the epidermis. It predominantly occurs on the legs as a result of sun exposure.

Are not caused by sun exposure

Squamous Cell Carcinoma
subject: Skin and wound management

stem:
You are treating a patient who underwent a heart transplant 7 days ago. The patient has had a routine recovery, with no complications.

When assessing their pulse, at rest, what would you normally expect to find?
explanation: In a denervated or transplanted heart the vagus nerves have been severed and therefore do not exert a ‘braking’ effect on the cardiac rate. This leads to an elevated resting heart rate, with a sinus tachycardia.
subject: Cardiothoracic surgery

stem:
A 74-year-old woman on rivaroxaban for atrial fibrillation falls down eight steps and sustains a head injury. A computed tomography (CT) scan of the head is performed and demonstrates a white, crescenteric lesion concave to the skull.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Subarachnoid haemorrhage is suspected when there is hyperattenuation of the subarachnoid space, most commonly around the circle of Willis.

Subdural Haematoma

stem:
Your friends have persuaded you to participate in a 10 km run for charity. As your legs begin to tire at the 7 km mark, you consider what influences increased blood flow through muscle.

Which one of the following increases blood flow through the muscle?
explanation: Bradykinin is a vasodilator metabolite and will increase muscle blood flow.
subject: Physiology

stem:
The cell cycle is a series of programmed events which take place to ensure the duplication and division of genetic material to produce two daughter cells. During one phase of mitosis, the paired chromosomes separate and are dragged to the opposite sides of the cell by the microtubules.

What is the best description of this phase of the cell cycle?
explanation:
In telophase, the chromatids arrive at the opposite poles of the cell and disperse after new nuclear membranes are formed.

Cell Cycle
subject: Pathology

stem:
A young man sustains a skull-base fracture at the middle cranial fossa that injures his right abducens (VI) nerve.

Which signs are most likely to be present on clinical examination?

options.text: There is ptosis on the right side
The pupil on the right side is constricted and fails to respond to light
The patient is unable to deviate his right eye medially
The patient is unable to deviate his right eye laterally

explanation: The abducens nerve innervates the lateral rectus muscle of the eye exclusively; the sole effect of damage to this nerve is that the patient is unable to abduct (laterally deviate) the eye.
subject: Anatomy

stem:
The serum electrolyte analysis of a patient shows hypokalaemia, with a serum potassium of 2.8 mmol/l. (normal range 3.5–5.0 mmol/l). The patient is sent for an electrocardiogram (ECG) to ensure there is no impact on the myocardium.

What is the most likely cause of this abnormality?
explanation:
Serum potassium levels are intimately linked with serum H+ levels via the sodium-potassium ATPase. This cell membrane pump principally exchanges intracellular sodium ions with extracellular potassium ions to maintain the cell membrane potential. Potassium ions compete with hydrogen ions in the exchange pump and, therefore, in the presence of metabolic acidosis more hydrogen ions will move into the intracellular compartment via this pump, maintaining the serum potassium levels.

Potassium Imbalance
subject: Perioperative care

stem:
A 68-year-old woman complains of easy fatigability and shortness of breath after abdominal aortic aneurysm repair. She is subsequently diagnosed with iron-deficiency anaemia and prescribed an oral iron preparation.

Which one of the following statements about iron metabolism is correct?

options.text: Ferritin is a plasma protein that transports iron in the blood
Haemosiderin is composed of ferritin and biliverdin
Iron is more efficiently absorbed in the ferrous state (Fe2+) than in the ferric state (Fe3+)
Most iron in the body is stored as haemosiderin
The gastrointestinal rate of iron absorption is extremely high

explanation: The iron in the ferrous state (Fe 2+) is more efficiently absorbed than in the ferric state (Fe3+). In the physiological pH the iron is oxidised to the ferric state (Fe3+) which is insoluble. Gastric acid secretions however, lower the pH and assist the absorption of iron in the ferrous state in the duodenum and first part of the jejunum.
subject: Physiology

stem:
A 65-year-old man is brought to the Emergency Department with a sudden, onset chest pain radiating to the jaw and left arm. An electrocardiogram shows ST elevation in leads II, III and AVF. Emergency cardiac catheterisation is planned.

Which of the following is the initial step in the pathogenesis of the patient’s condition?
explanation:
Depending upon the degree of obstruction, there can be the development of acute coronary syndrome in the form of unstable angina, non-ST-elevation MI (NSTEMI) or STEMI. Ischaemia is the diminished volume of perfusion to the heart, while infarction is the cellular response to lack of perfusion which causes injury.

Coronary Heart Disease
subject: Cardiothoracic surgery

stem:
A 20-year-old male was hit on the side of the head by a cricket ball. He initially lost consciousness for a few seconds but then carried on with the game. Later that afternoon he collapsed.


What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: An extradural haematoma caused by damage to the anterior branch of the middle meningeal artery
A subdural haematoma caused by damage to the bridging veins on the surface of the brain
A subdural haematoma caused by damage to the parenchymal surface of the brain
An extra-dural haematoma caused by damage to the posterior branch of the middle meningeal artery

explanation:
Subdural haematomas do not present in this manner. In a young patient, blood usually arises from the damaged brain surface. In these cases, there is an underlying brain injury, and so no ‘lucid’ interval.

Subdural haematomas more commonly present in the elderly and alcoholics. The history is often of an innocuous head injury, and due to fragility of the bridging veins and a higher prevalence of anticoagulant use, subdural haematomas occur; however, they often do not require surgical intervention.

Blood Supply Of The Head And Neck
topic: Blood Supply Of The Head And Neck
