stem:
A 60-year-old man is seen in a Speech and Language Clinic for speech therapy for residual dysphasia stemming from a previous stroke.

Which of the following statements is the most accurate regarding the neuroanatomy of language processing?

options.text: Wernicke’s area is responsible for comprehension of language and is located in the temporal lobe of the dominant cerebral hemisphere
Wernicke’s area is responsible for language production and is always found in the frontal lobe of the left hemisphere
Broca's area is responsible for language comprehension and is located in the parietal lobe
The angular gyrus is not involved in language processing
Wernicke's area is located in the frontal lobe and controls motor speech

explanation:
Wernicke’s area is responsible for language comprehension. Damage to this area causes receptive dysphasia, in which speech will be fluent but lack meaning. Patients with this condition are generally unaware that their words lack meaning. Wernicke’s aphasia is mostly caused by stroke.

Wernicke’s area is responsible for language production and is located in the temporal lobe of the dominant cerebral hemisphere

Cerebrum Neuroanatomy
subject: Anatomy

stem:
During an elective Vascular Surgery list, the Specialty Registrar and the Consultant are discussing the physiology underlying vasoconstriction and vasodilatation of arterial beds. The Consultant mentions reading an in vitro experiment, during which a drug blocked the transmembrane proteins mainly responsible for the resting membrane potential of vascular smooth muscle cells.

Which of the following transmembrane proteins was most likely to have been blocked by the drug?
explanation:
The resting membrane potential of excitable cells is largely due to the selective permeability of the cell membrane to potassium ions. Voltage-gated Na+ channels play a major role in regulating cell excitability, particularly as it pertains to the generation of action potentials in neurons, skeletal muscle and cardiac myositis. However, as regards vascular smooth muscle, action potentials are not dependent on Na+ channels since tetrodotoxin (TTX – a known sodium channel blocker) has little effect on these tissues during in vitro experiments.

Metabolic Pathways And Abnormalities
subject: Physiology

stem:
A 7-year-old boy is seen by his General Practitioner for otitis media of his left ear. He has had recurrent upper respiratory tract infections and has erythematous swollen tonsils.

Which part of the skull does the Eustachian tube penetrate?
explanation: The Eustachian tube, also known as the pharyngotympanic tube or auditory tube connects the middle ear to the nasopharynx. The posterolateral third of the tube is bony and the remainder cartilaginous. The bony part of the Eustachian tube perforates the petrous temporal bone. The Eustachian tube in a child is shorter and more horizontal. The opening of the auditory tube lies above the soft palate adjacent to the tubal tonsil.
subject: Anatomy

stem:
A 75-year-old man attends the clinic with predominantly voiding lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS) including hesitancy, poor flow, terminal dribbling and nocturia. He is counselled about further tests and investigations to further assess the cause of his symptoms.

Which one of the following is NOT one of the next steps/first-line investigations in the evaluation of a male patient with LUTS?

options.text: Post-void residual (PVR) urine volume and flow rate

explanation:
This is not one of the first-line investigations that should be performed. The patient may subsequently go on to have a biopsy of the prostate gland, however it is an invasive procedure and should not be done without other vital information obtained through less invasive methods. The following investigations/tests are considered as first line in investigation of LUTS:

DRE
prostate specific antigen (PSA)
serum creatinine
post-void residual volume (PVR)
flow rate measurement
pressure flow studies
renal ultrasonography.
subject: Urology

stem:
An 18-year-old man presents to Accident and Emergency with acute pain passing urine, haematuria and a dull ache over his flank. He is known to have cystinuria.

Which one of the following statements about cystinuria is correct?

options.text: Can be prevented with allopurinol therapy
Renal stones may be demonstrated by ultrasonography
Occur more commonly than uric acid stones
Tend to precipitate in alkaline urine

explanation:
Cystine stones tend to precipitate in acidic urine. Alkalinisation with potassium citrate is a treatment for cystinuria.

Urinary Tract Calculi
subject: Urology

stem: Which one of the following statements concerning the parasympathetic nervous system is most accurate?

options.text: Parasympathetic nerve fibres carried by the vagus nerve (cranial nerve X) innervate only the larynx
Efferent nerve fibres leave from the central nervous system through cranial nerves IV, VII, IX and X
Efferent nerve fibres leave from the second, third and fourth sacral segments of the spinal cord
Preganglionic nerve fibres synapse in para-vertebral ganglia before passing to the target organ
Some efferent nerve fibres are distributed to skin and muscle fibres

explanation:
Preganglionic parasympathetic nerve fibres tend to be long as most synapse in terminal ganglia which are within or immediately adjacent to the target organ. Postganglionic fibres are therefore short. This is in contrast to the sympathetic nervous system where preganglionic fibres are short and postganglionic fibres are long.

Parasympathetic System Physiology
subject: Physiology

stem:
A 75-year-old man presents to his General Practitioner with a simple inguinal hernia. He has extensive co-morbidities and elects to have his operation under spinal anaesthesia.

Which of the following is correct regarding this technique?

options.text: It involves injecting local anaesthetic into the sub-dural space
It results in hypotension which can be due to splanchnic vasodilatation
It is associated with a symptomatic dural tap in 15-20% of cases
It is unsuitable for operations of duration greater than one hour
It can be used to provide anaesthesia for patients undergoing mastectomy operations

explanation: Hypotension is a common complication of spinal anaesthesia. This is due to a reduction in sympathetic tone causing splanchnic vasodilatation and venous pooling. It can be managed with intravenous fluids or inotropic support if refractory to fluid replacement.
subject: Perioperative care

stem:
A middle-aged patient is admitted to the Emergency Department resus and the acute stroke team are asked to assess them urgently. He develops dysarthria, nystagmus and a tremor that worsens with directed movement.

Which of the following does this patient most likely have?

options.text: Damage to pontine and caudate nuclei

explanation:
The tremor associated with parkinsonism is a resting tremor that ceases on voluntary movement, this is contrary to the tremor described in the case history that worsens on voluntary movement.

Cerebellar Ataxia
subject: Anatomy

stem:
You are watching your ENT consultant perform functional endoscope sinus surgery (FESS) for a patient with persistent and recurrent sinusitis. The Consultant guides you through the anatomy and highlights essential landmarks.

The nasolacrimal duct empties into which of the following?
explanation: The nasolacrimal duct is a membranous canal, about 18 mm in length, extending from the lower part of the lacrimal sac to the inferior meatus of the nose. It ends as the plica lacrimalis (Hasner’s fold), formed by a fold of the mucous membrane. It is contained in an osseous canal, formed by the maxilla, the lacrimal bone and the inferior nasal concha. It is narrower in the middle than at either end and is directed downward, backward, and slightly lateral. The mucous lining of the lacrimal sac and nasolacrimal duct is covered with columnar epithelium, which in places is ciliated.
topic: Nose And Paranasal Sinuses Regional Anatomy
topicRaw: Nose And Paranasal Sinuses Regional Anatomy
subject: Anatomy

stem:
You are performing the approach for a thyroidectomy.

Which of the following options is correct regarding this approach?

options.text: The ansa cervicalis is seen readily
The anterior jugular veins should be divided
The flaps raised should be deep to platysma
The incision is made vertically at the level of the cricoid
The strap muscles are commonly divided

explanation:
The incision in thyroidectomy is made following the skin creases at about 4 cm above the sternoclavicular joints.

Goitre And Thyroid Surgery
subject: Breast and endocrine surgery

stem:
A 3-year-old boy is brought to the Paediatric Clinic for evaluation of an undescended testis. Previously, the child was weak and developmental milestones were delayed. He has gained excessive weight recently due to overeating. The paediatrician assesses for childhood obesity and genetic testing is ordered.

Which hormone is most likely associated with hyperphagia and obesity in this child?
explanation:
Leptin is a hormone produced by adipocytes and the small intestine epithelium. It acts on the hypothalamus and tegmentum to inhibit hunger and regulate feeding. It helps in the reduction of fat storage in adipocytes. Obesity is associated with a decreased sensitivity to leptin and its blood levels are directly proportional to the amount of body fat.

Gastrointestinal Absorption
subject: Physiology

stem:
A neonate is born with an abnormal mass. The parents and midwife are concerned and request an emergency review by the paediatric surgical team.

Which of the following sites in this patient would most commonly give rise to tumours derived from all three germ-cell layers?
explanation: Tumours derived from all three cell layers are called ‘teratomas’. In a newborn infant, the most common location is the sacrococcygeal area. Overall, however, a haemangioma is the most common tumour in infancy and most of these regress over time.
subject: Paediatric surgery

stem:
A 40-year-old fit and well Polish woman presents to the Ear, Nose and Throat (ENT) clinic with a solitary thyroid nodule. She has no symptoms of thyroid dysfunction or compression.

What is the most useful first line investigation?
explanation:
Thyroid nodules are common, and the majority are within multinodular goitres. The most useful initial investigations are ultrasound and fine-needle aspiration cytology of any dominant nodules.

Thyroid function tests in patients with multinodular goitre or a solitary thyroid nodule are usually normal. These are therefore usually only necessary if you suspect a hot nodule in a symptomatic patient. Only around 10–20% of cold nodules in adults and 50% in children are malignant.
subject: Breast and endocrine surgery

stem:
A patient undergoes a successful kidney transplant with a compatible donor. They can look forward to many years of better health however they will require lifelong immunosuppression. They are commenced on ciclosporin.

This drug acts via which immune mechanism of action?

options.text: Inhibiting release of interleukin (IL)-2 from T cells
Decreasing expression of the T cell receptor

explanation:
IL-10 is a natural anti-inflammatory cytokine but no successful analogues are available in clinical practice.

Renal Transplantation
subject: Organ transplantation

stem:
A 25-year-old man is being nursed on a surgical ward after being admitted with an acute abdomen. While taking a blood sugar sample a student nurse sustains a needle stick injury and is advised to attend the Emergency Department.

Which of the following routes has the highest rate of transmission of HIV for healthcare workers?
explanation:
The most likely route of transmission of HIV for a healthcare worker is bloodborne via a needle stick injury. The risk of transmission of HIV is related to the depth of injury and the amount of blood and viral concentration load. Hollow needles potentially contain more blood, and hence virus, so the risk of transmission is higher. Grossly, the risk of seroconversion following a needlestick injury is as follows:

HIV 0.3%
hepatitis C 3%
hepatitis B 30%.
subject: Breast and endocrine surgery

stem: What are the contents of the popliteal fossa?

options.text: The deepest structure is the popliteal vein
The popliteal artery and vein and the tibial nerve

explanation:
The sciatic nerve divides at the apex of the popliteal fossa into common peroneal and tibial branches.

External Learning Resources
TeachMe Anatomy - The Popliteal Fossa

The Knee Regional Anatomy
subject: Anatomy

stem:
A patient undergoes excision of the left submandibular salivary gland for sialectasia. Unfortunately, his hypoglossal (CN XII) nerve on that side is damaged.

What is the most likely clinical consequence?

options.text: There is numbness of the posterior one-third of the tongue
On protruding the tongue, it deviates towards the right
The uvula deviates towards the left
All the extrinsic muscles of the left side of the tongue, except the palatoglossus, are paralysed

explanation: The hypoglossal nerve supplies the extrinsic muscles of the tongue. The palatoglossus muscle, however, is supplied by the vagus nerve.
subject: Anatomy

stem:
Your team is on call for gastrointestinal bleeds, you take a call regarding a young woman who has taken an overdose of over the counter medications, one being ibuprofen. You cast your mind back to medical school and try to remember its mechanism of action.

What does it inhibit?
explanation: Ibuprofen inhibits cyclooxygenase enzymes, therefore, inhibiting the conversion of arachidonic acid to prostaglandin H2.
subject: Perioperative care

stem:
A 32-year-old man is found to have a phaeochromocytoma of the right adrenal gland. You are excising the right suprarenal (adrenal) gland and your Consultant asks you about its anatomy.

Which of the following descriptions is most correct?

options.text: It has a longer vein than the left suprarenal gland
It lies anterior to the inferior vena cava
It receives an arterial supply from the subcostal artery
It forms a boundary with the bare area of the liver

explanation:
The right lobe of the liver is an anterior relation of the right (pyramidal) suprarenal gland. The suprarenal glands lie in the posterior abdomen, lying between the upper pole of the kidneys and the diaphragm. The suprarenal glands have a rich blood supply, which is supplied via three arteries:

superior adrenal artery – arises from the inferior phrenic artery
middle adrenal artery – arises from the abdominal aorta
inferior adrenal artery – arises from the renal arteries.

The right and left adrenal veins drain the glands. The right adrenal vein drains into the inferior vena cava, whereas the left adrenal vein drains into the left renal vein.
subject: Breast and endocrine surgery

stem:
A 36-year-old man is admitted to the Emergency Department with a mycotic aneurysm. He is being considered for an operation.

Which of the following conditions is most commonly associated with a mycotic aneurysm?
explanation: Mycotic aneurysms arise from bacterial infection of the arterial wall, most commonly following endocarditis. Bacteria invade the vessel wall and as the wall becomes digested and hence weakened, leading to the formation of a false aneurysm, which has a high risk of rupture. They most commonly occur in the intracranial and lower limb arteries, but can affect any artery. A mycotic aneurysm is usually painful, rapidly growing and occurs in the background of infection (leucocytosis, fever, positive blood cultures). The most common causative agent is Staphylococcus aureus. Other organisms include: Pneumococcus, Group A streptococci and Salmonella species. Diagnosis is via computed tomography (CT) scan.
subject: Anatomy

stem:
A 29-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with thirst and polyuria. She does not smoke and had a rash that resolved three months previously. Her history is otherwise unremarkable. A lung X-ray shows hilar shadowing, for which she is treated with normal saline and started on a course of hydrocortisone. A week later, her corrected calcium is within normal range, but her parathyroid hormone (PTH) is 0.4 pmol/l (normal 1.0–6.5 pmol/l).

Which of the following is the most likely cause?
explanation: Secondary hyperparathyroidism typically occurs as a compensatory response to chronic hypocalcaemia or vitamin D deficiency, leading to overactivity of the parathyroid glands. It is commonly seen in conditions such as chronic kidney disease. While secondary hyperparathyroidism can cause hypercalcaemia, thirst and polyuria, it is usually associated with low levels of vitamin D and elevated levels of PTH, contrary to the low PTH levels described in the patient. Additionally, lung involvement is not a characteristic feature of secondary hyperparathyroidism.
subject: Head and neck surgery

stem:
A 56-year-old woman presents with a rapidly growing raised solitary lesion on her face. Over the course of 4 weeks it has reached 2 cm in diameter. The lesion has now developed a necrotic, crusted centre.

Which of the following skin lesions is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Pyogenic granulomas also grow rapidly, however they usually occur on the fingers after trivial trauma and appear as raised, wet, pedunculated lesions.

Head And Neck Cancers
subject: Head and neck surgery

stem:
A newborn baby girl with gastroschisis is being closely monitored on the neonatal intensive care unit.

Which one of these mechanisms is important with regards to conserving body temperature in this patient?
explanation: Noradrenergic sympathetic stimulation will cause vasoconstriction to the extremities and vasodilation to the trunk to reduce heat loss.
subject: Emergency medicine and trauma

stem:
You are about to see a young man in the post-operative clinic following a recent diagnosis of a cancer. The Multidisciplinary Team (MDT) meeting outcome had been for discussion with the patient about adjuvant treatment.

Chemotherapy can achieve long-term survival in which tumour types?
explanation: Normal lifespans have been achieved using chemotherapy in the following: acute leukaemia in children, Hodgkin’s disease, histiocytic lymphoma, testicular carcinoma, embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma, Ewing’s sarcoma, Wilms’ tumour, Burkitt’s lymphoma, retinoblastoma and choriocarcinoma.
subject: Urology

stem:
A 28-year-old woman presents with pain, erythema and swelling of the labia. She was initially referred to General Surgery as a perianal abscess but the surgical registrar diagnoses an infected Bartholin’s cyst and refers her to Gynaecology.

Which one of the following is true regarding the development of Bartholin’s glands?

options.text: Bartholin’s glands are the embryological equivalent to the seminal vesicles in men
Bartholin’s glands are the embryological equivalent to the bulbourethral glands in men
Bartholin's glands are located in the anterior labial fold
Bartholin's glands drain into the vaginal vault
Bartholin's gland cysts are most common in postmenopausal women

explanation:
The Bartholin’s glands lie on either side of the urethral opening

The Bartholin’s glands are located on the anterior wall of the vagina and are the embryological equivalent to the prostate gland

The Bartholin glands are also known as the greater vestibular glands. They are homologous to the bulbourethral glands in men.

Bartholin’s glands are embryological outgrowths of the paramesonephric ducts

The Urogenital Region And Perineal Pouches Regional Anatomy
topic: The Urogenital Region And Perineal Pouches Regional Anatomy
topicRaw: The Urogenital Region And Perineal Pouches Regional Anatomy

stem:
A 50-year-old man presents with pain in his right shoulder. The pain started 2 days ago, after he had painted a ceiling. The pain is present on forward flexion and abduction between 70–120°. Hawkins’ test is positive, Jobe’s test, internal and external rotation lag signs, and Gerber’s lift-off tests are negative.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Subacromial impingement is tested by Hawkins–Kennedy impingement sign. During this test, the patient’s shoulder is placed into 90° of forward flexion; the elbow is placed in 90° flexion and then passively internally rotated. Presence of pain suggests that space between the humeral head and acromion process has been reduced. Internal rotation causes the supraspinatus tendon or the subacromial bursa to become compressed and elicit a painful response.
subject: Anatomy

stem:
A 36-year-old woman presents with primary breast cancer of her left breast and undergoes mastectomy and axillary node sampling in which two out of the four nodes were positive for cancer cells. Following discussion at the multidisciplinary team (MDT) meeting, she is put forward for chemotherapy.

Which of the following is the most likely side-effect of adjuvant chemotherapy for breast cancer?
explanation:
Incidence among cancer patients is about 10%. It would follow that the incidence of Chemotherapy related cardiomyopathy is lower. Pulmonary fibrosis may result from bleomycin containing chemotherapy regimens.

External Learning Resources
NICE - Adjuvant Chemotherapy For Invasive Breast Cancer

Malignant Breast Disease

stem: With regards to the lumbar spine anatomy, which part of the vertebra is responsible for causing spondylolysis?
explanation:
The transverse process is not involved in spondylolysis; instead, it is caused by a defect in the pars interarticularis.

Lumbar Spine Regional Anatomy
subject: Critical care

stem:
A 10-year-old girl requires assessment following an open appendicectomy. The nurse is concerned about her observations: respiratory rate 22/min, saturations 99% on air, heart rate 110/min, blood pressure 90/47 mmHg and temperature 37°C. The patient is comfortable, and is mildly tender around the operative site.

What is the best next step in management of this patient?

options.text: Prepare to take the patient back to theatre

explanation:
At present there is no indication this patient needs to return to theatre. The observations are within normal range for a child of 10 years and clinically there does not appear to be any concerning features.

Metabolic Response To Trauma
subject: Emergency medicine and trauma

stem:
A 35-year-old man is seen in clinic complaining of a tender right forearm lump. He was involved in a road traffic accident 6 months previously, when several windscreen fragments entered his forearm, which were removed at the time in the Emergency Department. At elective surgery another glass fragment is recovered from his right forearm.

Which of the following cell types would be most characteristic of the inflammatory response in this situation?
explanation:
A few neutrophils might be present, but giant cells are more specific for a foreign body inflammatory response.

Immune Recognition
subject: Critical care

stem:
A 19-year-old man attends an Occupational Health appointment and is found to have an abnormally prominent mid-sternum. His face is thinner vertically, he has long limbs and his arm span is longer than his height. Chest auscultation reveals a pan-systolic murmur of the mitral valve. He wears glasses because of myopia due to ectopia lentis. A connective tissue disorder is suspected.

Which connective-tissue component is most likely affected?
explanation:
Type IV collagen is mainly found in the basement membrane. A mutation in the gene responsible for the production of type IV collagen is associated with progressive inherited glomerulonephritis or Alport syndrome. This usually presents with microhaematuria and may rarely progress to end-stage renal disease. Other associated conditions include hearing loss and eye abnormalities.

Marfan Syndrome

You are in the paediatric surgery outpatient clinic. In between cases your consultant discusses relevant embryology with you about the next case.

Which one of the following is derived from the mesonephric ducts?
explanation: In men the mesonephric ducts give rise to the tubular system of the genito-urinary system, ie epididymis, vas deferens, ureter, renal pelvis, calyces, collecting tubules, seminal vesicle and ejaculatory duct. In women they only contribute to the tubular system of the urinary system leading to the formation of the ureter, renal pelvis, calyces and collecting tubules.

A 65-year-old woman who was previously fit and well suffers a hip fracture. Subsequent investigations a few months after her accident reveal that her bone mineral density T-score is -1.8

Which of the following serum biochemical changes will most likely be seen?
explanation: This woman has osteopenia, her low bone mineral density T-score being the chief sign – osteopenia is essentially low bone mineral density, with a T-score of between -1 and -2.5. Osteoporosis is defined as a T-score less than -2.5. The T-score is comparing the bone mineral density to a healthy 30-year-old. The Z-score assesses age-matched patients. There are no changes in serum biochemistry in osteopenia.

A 74-year-old man presents to his GP with a neck lump that has increased in size over the last 6 weeks. Further questioning reveals his family have noted his voice has become hoarse and on examination he has a diffuse hard swelling over the anterior aspect of his neck and lymphadenopathy.

Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Medullary cell carcinoma is a malignancy of the parafollicular cells which produce calcitonin. It represents less than 5% of all thyroid cancers. The rapidly growing neck mass in a patient of this age makes anaplastic carcinoma more likely.

Thyroid Cancer

Recurrent branch of the median nerve
Superficial branch of the Ulnar nerve

A 71-year-old man underwent a planned robotic cystoprostatectomy for muscle invasive bladder cancer. One week post-operatively, he developed shortness of breath and had a computed tomography pulmonary angiogram, which confirmed a pulmonary embolus. He is started on treatment dose low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH).

What is the mechanism of action of LMWH?
explanation: LMWH such as enoxaparin and dalteparin bind to anti-thrombin and accelerates its inhibition of factor Xa, which converts prothrombin to thrombin. Thrombin therefore is unable convert fibrinogen to fibrin, which is required in clot formation.

A 48-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with symptoms of fulminant hepatic failure secondary to alcohol abuse. He is noted to have hepatosplenomegaly, anorectal varices and caput medusa.

Which anatomical structure is just anterior to the origin of the hepatic portal vein?
explanation: The pancreatic neck is anterior to the origin of the portal vein. The hepatic portal vein is formed of the confluence of the splenic and superior mesenteric veins, just posterior to the pancreatic neck. It supplies 75% of all blood flow to the liver. The inferior vena cava lies posterior to its origin.

A 58-year-old woman undergoes an abdominal ultrasound for suspected cholecystitis. This incidentally reveals a 4.5 cm abdominal aortic aneurysm that appears to be infrarenal. Her abdomen is soft and non-tender, and the aneurysm itself is asymptomatic. Hypertension is her only co-morbidity.

What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Discharge to primary care for blood pressure control

explanation: NICE recommends that patients with aneurysms of 3–4.4 cm in diameter should have repeat surveillance scans with ultrasonography every year. Patients with an aneurysm of 4.5–5.4 cm diameter should have 3-monthly surveillance with ultrasonography. If an aneurysm is found and is 5.5 cm or larger, then the patient should be referred to a surgeon in the vascular network.

An 86-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with confusion and lethargy. He has a history of chronic pain for which he takes NSAIDs, epilepsy managed with antiepileptic drugs, and hypertension treated with antihypertensives. Blood tests reveal significant hyponatraemia.

Which of the following medications is the most likely cause of his hyponatraemia?
explanation: Phenytoin is another antiepileptic drug, but it is less commonly associated with hyponatraemia compared to carbamazepine. Phenytoin's side effects more frequently include gingival hyperplasia, hirsutism, and ataxia. While it can affect sodium channels, it does not typically lead to the SIADH.

A 26-year-old man presents to the General Practitioner with multiple GI polyps. A biopsy reveals hamartomatous polyps.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer

Peutz-Jeghers syndrome (PJS) is an autosomal dominant condition caused by mutations in the STK11 (LKB1) gene on chromosome 19. It is characterised by the presence of multiple hamartomatous polyps throughout the gastrointestinal tract, most commonly in the small intestine, stomach, and colon. These polyps can lead to complications such as intussusception, GI bleeding, and obstruction. A distinguishing feature of PJS is mucocutaneous hyperpigmentation, which manifests as dark pigmented spots on the lips, oral mucosa, fingers, and toes.. The biopsy findings of hamartomas are highly indicative of PJS, making it the most likely diagnosis for this patient.

Sarcoidosis

Turcot syndrome

He has a history of a heart transplant six months ago and is currently on immunosuppressive therapy. His chest X-ray shows diffuse interstitial infiltrates.

What is the most likely causative agent?
explanation:
S. aureus, including MRSA, is a common bacterial cause of pneumonia, especially in hospitalised or immunocompromised patients. However, it typically presents with lobar consolidation rather than diffuse interstitial infiltrates. The patient's lack of improvement with broad-spectrum antibiotics also makes a bacterial cause less likely. Therefore, while S. aureus can cause pneumonia, it is not the most likely agent in this context.

On examination, there is weakness in shoulder elevation and difficulty shrugging his shoulders. Sensory function in the affected region remains intact and there is no significant bleeding from the wound.

Which of the following nerves is the most likely to be damaged?
explanation:
Axillary nerve

Brachial plexus

Dorsal scapular nerve

The suprascapular nerve travels with the suprascapular artery through the suprascapular notch and supplies the supraspinatus and infraspinatus muscles. Injury to this nerve would primarily affect shoulder abduction and external rotation, rather than shoulder elevation or shrugging, making it an unlikely cause for the patient's symptoms.

What is the most likely site of nerve injury relative to the sternocleidomastoid muscle (SCM)?
explanation:
The lateral aspect of the sternocleidomastoid muscle is not typically associated with the path of the spinal accessory nerve. Injury to the lateral part would not likely affect the nerve as it runs more medially and posteriorly. Therefore, weakness in neck flexion and head rotation would not be explained by a lateral injury.

A 35-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with severe anal pain accompanied by bright red blood on the toilet paper. On examination, a small tear is noted in the anal canal. There is no history of inflammatory bowel disease or previous anorectal surgeries.

What is the most likely location for an anal fissure in this patient?
explanation:
Lateral fissures are uncommon and often suggest underlying pathology such as Crohn's disease, syphilis, tuberculosis, or malignancy. Unlike the midline locations, the lateral anal canal has a richer blood supply, making it less prone to ischemic tears. When lateral fissures are present, they often indicate an underlying pathology rather than simple mechanical trauma from defecation.

A 56-year-old woman with a 10-year history of rheumatoid arthritis presents to the Emergency Department with progressive dysphagia to both solids and liquids over the past few months. She also reports frequent heartburn and regurgitation, especially at night. She denies weight loss or choking episodes. She has no neurological deficits, and a cardiovascular and respiratory examination is unremarkable.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Scleroderma is a connective tissue disease that often affects the gastrointestinal tract, particularly the oesophagus. In patients with scleroderma, fibrosis and atrophy of the smooth muscle lead to decreased peristalsis and lower oesophageal sphincter incompetence, causing dysphagia to both solids and liquids, as well as heartburn due to gastroesophageal reflux. The association with rheumatoid arthritis is also relevant, as both are autoimmune conditions. The clinical presentation of dysphagia to both solids and liquids, along with heartburn, aligns with scleroderma-induced oesophageal dysfunction.

Zenker's diverticulum

Where is the site of magnesium storage in the body?
explanation:
Muscles contain a portion of the body's magnesium, approximately 20%, but it is not the primary storage site. Magnesium in muscles is essential for muscle contraction, energy production, and the maintenance of cellular function. However, the amount stored in muscle tissue is significantly less than that in the bones, making it a secondary site.

A 62-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with haematuria and flank pain. Imaging and biopsy confirm transitional cell carcinoma (TCC) of her distal ureter. She has a solitary kidney.

What is the most appropriate management option?
explanation:
Complete ureterectomy

Distal ureterectomy involves the surgical removal of the affected portion of the distal ureter while preserving the rest of the urinary tract. This is the most appropriate management option for a patient with a solitary kidney and TCC of the distal ureter, as it allows for the removal of the tumour while preserving renal function. Given the patient's solitary kidney, preserving maximal renal function is crucial. This approach balances oncologic control with renal function preservation.

A 76-year-old man with dementia is brought to the Emergency Department by his carer. He has a small, ulcerating lesion on his scalp which has been growing. He has a history of GI surgery for colon cancer.

What is the most appropriate next step in management?
explanation: CT scan of the head might be useful in cases where there is suspicion of intracranial involvement, but it is not the next most appropriate step in the management of an ulcerating scalp lesion. Imaging is generally used to assess internal structures, and in the case of an external lesion, tissue histology from a biopsy or excision is more definitive for diagnosing possible skin malignancies. Moreover, the clinical presentation of a growing ulcerating lesion suggests that prompt surgical intervention rather than further imaging would be warranted.

A 49-year-old man is brought to the Emergency Department with neck pain following a road traffic accident. On examination, there is tenderness over the cervical spine and limited range of motion. Imaging is performed to assess for potential cervical spine injury.

Which of the following vertebrae does not have a bifid spine?
explanation:
C3

C4

C6

C7
The seventh cervical vertebra (C7) is also known as the vertebra prominens due to its prominent spinous process, which is not bifid. This vertebra is easily palpable at the base of the neck and serves as an important anatomical landmark. Unlike the other cervical vertebrae, C7 has a long, non-bifid spinous process that is more similar to the thoracic vertebrae. This distinctive feature helps in identifying C7 on physical examination and imaging.

Which of the following muscles is attached to this region of the scapula?
explanation: The teres major muscle originates from the dorsal aspect of the inferior angle of the scapula and inserts into the medial lip of the intertubercular groove of the humerus. It is involved in the medial rotation and adduction of the arm. Given its origin at the inferior part of the lateral border of the scapula, this is the most appropriate answer.

Which lymph nodes are most commonly involved in the pelvic spread of cervical cancer?

Para-aortic nodes are generally affected after involvement of pelvic nodes, such as the iliac groups. Sacral nodes are indeed part of the pelvic spread, but they are more often involved in combination with iliac nodes rather than jumping directly to the para-aortic spread. For this reason, this combination does not represent the most typical spread pattern.

Which lymph nodes are most likely to be affected?
explanation:
These lymph nodes are located in the superficial fascia of the upper thigh and are responsible for draining the skin and superficial tissues of the lower abdomen, including the area around the umbilicus. A 56-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with severe dysphagia and weight loss. He is scheduled to undergo an oesophageal/gastric conduit procedure.

What will predominate the blood supply to the conduit?
explanation: The right gastroepiploic artery is the most appropriate choice for the predominant blood supply to a gastric conduit. It supplies the greater curvature of the stomach, which is typically used in the creation of the conduit. The artery arises from the gastroduodenal artery, a branch of the common hepatic artery, and provides a robust blood supply to the greater curvature, making it ideal for the conduit.

Which of the following is the target of heparin?
explanation:
Xa
This is incorrect because, although heparin does inhibit factor Xa, it does so indirectly. Heparin binds to antithrombin 3, which then inactivates factor Xa. Therefore, the primary action of heparin is on antithrombin 3, which then exerts its effect on factor Xa and thrombin.

A 49-year-old man is brought to the Emergency Department with severe bleeding following a road traffic accident. Tranexamic acid (TXA) is administered to help control the bleeding.

What is the compound that TXA binds to?
explanation:
Glucine

TXA works by binding to lysine binding sites on plasminogen, which prevents plasminogen from binding to fibrin. This inhibits the conversion of plasminogen to plasmin, a molecule responsible for breaking down fibrin clots. By preventing fibrinolysis, TXA helps in stabilising blood clots and reducing bleeding. This mechanism is particularly useful in trauma and surgical patients where excessive bleeding is a concern.

He has a temperature of 38.7 °C and will not let anyone examine the area. On examination, there is a discrete tender swelling corresponding to a submandibular lymph node. The dentition appears normal.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Suppurative lymphadenitis is the most likely diagnosis in this case. It is characterised by the infection and inflammation of lymph nodes, leading to swelling, redness, and tenderness in the affected area. The high fever and the boy’s refusal to allow examination due to pain are consistent with this diagnosis. Suppurative lymphadenitis typically requires antibiotic treatment and sometimes drainage if an abscess has formed.

Which branch of the facial nerve is most likely to be damaged when cutting the parotid duct?
explanation:
The zygomatic branch of the facial nerve travels towards the lateral aspect of the orbit and innervates the muscles around the eye. Although it is closer to the parotid duct compared to the temporal branch, it is still not the most likely to be damaged when the parotid duct is cut. Damage to the zygomatic branch would primarily affect the muscles responsible for closing the eyelid.

What is the primary site of insulin production in the pancreas?
explanation: The tail of the pancreas contains a high density of islets of Langerhans, which are responsible for the production of insulin. These islets contain beta cells that secrete insulin in response to elevated blood glucose levels. The tail is anatomically situated near the spleen and is known for its endocrine function.

What is the most likely cause of his symptoms?

explanation:
Infection

Nerve injury

Post-traumatic osteoarthritis can develop after fractures involving the joint surfaces, leading to chronic pain and stiffness. However, the presentation typically includes a more gradual onset of symptoms over several years rather than acute pain one year post-surgery. The patient's acute presentation of hip pain makes post-traumatic osteoarthritis less likely.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Slipped upper femoral epiphysis (SUFE) generally occurs in older children and adolescents, typically between the ages of 10 and 16 years. It is associated with obesity and presents with hip, thigh, or knee pain and a limp. The age of the child and the absence of typical risk factors make SUFE an unlikely diagnosis in this case.

Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Osteoarthritis

Papillary thyroid carcinoma usually presents as a painless thyroid nodule and may occasionally cause cervical lymphadenopathy. It does not typically cause systemic symptoms like fatigue or weight loss, and it is not associated with proteinuria or hepatomegaly. Therefore, this diagnosis is not consistent with the patient’s presentation.

stem:
A 37-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with severe episodic headaches, palpitations and sweating. She is found to have paroxysmal hypertension and there is clinical suspicion of phaeochromocytoma.

Which is the most appropriate first-line diagnostic investigation?

options.text: CT scan of the adrenal glands

explanation:
Clonidine suppression test

Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan

Metaiodobenzylguanidine (MIBG) scintigraphy

Plasma free metanephrines are the most appropriate first-line investigation for suspected phaeochromocytoma. They have the highest sensitivity of all available tests, meaning a normal result effectively excludes the disease. Although false positives can occur, especially with certain medications or stress, abnormal results can be confirmed with urinary fractionated metanephrines or imaging. This combination of accuracy and safety makes plasma free metanephrines the best initial diagnostic test in current clinical practice.

A 60-year-old man presents to his General Practitioner following an incidental finding of an anterior mediastinal mass on a computed tomography (CT) scan. Further imaging shows that the lesion is confined to the thymus with no definite invasion of adjacent structures. He is otherwise well and has no significant past medical history.

What is the most appropriate next step in his management?
explanation:
Midline sternotomy and thymectomy

Up to 50% of patients with thymoma also have myasthenia gravis, and identifying it is crucial prior to surgery. Screening typically involves testing for acetylcholine receptor antibodies and a clinical evaluation for muscle weakness. Pre-operative diagnosis allows optimisation with medical therapy, intravenous immunoglobulin or plasmapheresis to reduce peri-operative morbidity. Recognising MG also influences anaesthetic choices and postoperative monitoring, making this the most appropriate next step before considering surgery.

stem: Which one of the following is the strongest indication for splenectomy?

options.text: Splenic trauma with a haemodynamically stable patient
Idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura refractory to medical therapy

explanation:
Splenic infarction

Splenic vein thrombosis can cause left-sided portal hypertension, which may lead to gastric or oesophageal varices and potentially life-threatening gastrointestinal bleeding. In such cases, splenectomy is regarded as definitive treatment because it removes the source of venous congestion and abolishes the variceal pressure. Although endoscopic measures or splenic artery embolisation may offer temporary control, surgery provides a curative option. This makes splenic vein thrombosis with bleeding or symptomatic portal hypertension one of the clearest and strongest elective indications for splenectomy.

A 45-year-old woman who is breastfeeding her 3-month-old daughter presents to her General Practitioner with a new breast lump. She is worried it could be cancer. On examination, the lump is firm, but there are no skin changes or palpable lymph nodes.

Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Clinical examination, mammogram, ultrasound and tissue biopsy
Ultrasound alone is sufficient for evaluation
Fine needle aspiration cytology should be avoided during lactation
Mammography is not possible during breastfeeding

explanation:
Clinical examination, mammogram and tissue biopsy

Triple assessment consists of clinical examination, appropriate imaging, and core biopsy. In a lactating 45-year-old, ultrasound is the first-line, and mammography is commonly added due to age to detect microcalcifications and additional lesions. Combining both imaging modalities provides complementary information and guides sampling. This approach gives the safest, most accurate assessment.

Which of the following is a commonly recognised feature?

Shingles

Infectious mononucleosis classically presents with fever, sore throat, and marked lymphadenopathy, particularly of the posterior cervical nodes. This is one of the most common and reliable clinical features. Splenomegaly and fatigue are also typical. For this reason, lymphadenopathy is the .

What is the most likely cause of his symptoms?

options.text: Intracranial haemorrhage leading to brain herniation
Diffuse axonal injury without space-occupying lesion

explanation:
This is the most likely cause of the patient’s condition. Intracranial haemorrhage results in a rapid rise in ICP, and when compensatory mechanisms fail, the brain herniates, compressing the brainstem. This produces the Cushing reflex, classically defined as hypertension, bradycardia and irregular respirations, which is a pre-terminal sign. The combination of drowsiness, GCS 6 and the described vital signs is highly consistent with this process, making this the .

A 35-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department after a motorcycle accident. He has altered consciousness and defective vision. A CT brain scan reveals a fracture of the floor of the orbit with entrapment of the inferior rectus muscle.

Which eye movement is most likely to be clinically impaired in this patient?
explanation:
The inferior rectus normally acts to depress the eye. When entrapped in an orbital floor fracture, it cannot relax and lengthen, so the patient cannot elevate the eye. This produces diplopia when the patient attempts to look upwards, and this clinical finding is characteristic of orbital floor fractures. For this reason, impaired upward gaze is the .

A 75-year-old man is investigated in the Urology Clinic with lower urinary tract symptoms. On examination, he has a bilaterally enlarged smooth prostate. After further investigation, a diagnosis of benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) is made.

Which part of the prostate gland does this condition affect?
explanation:
Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) is usually caused by hyperplasia of the glands from the transitional zone of the prostate. This part of the prostate is located centrally and surrounds the urethra. Hyperplasia of the glands in the transitional zone leads to a frequent urge to urinate, a weak stream, dribbling at the end of a stream and difficulty in fully emptying the bladder.

A 3-year-old boy is brought to his General Practitioner with complaints of high-grade fever, irritability and pulling on the left ear for the last 5 days. He currently goes to nursery and is up to date with the immunisations. Physical examination reveals bulging tympanic membranes on the left side with frank pus in the middle ear. Which of the following is the most appropriate management for this patient?

options.text: Advise analgesia and observation for 48 hours with safety-netting advice
Refer to ENT for urgent myringotomy

explanation:
Prescribe a 5-day course of co-amoxiclav

Immediate antibiotics should be prescribed in all systemically unwell patients, those who have a high risk of complications, where 4 days have passed since the start of the symptoms and where there is either bilateral acute otitis media or perforation and/or discharge in the ear canal. A 5-day course of erythromycin or clarithromycin should be prescribed to all children who are allergic to penicillin.

Provide a delayed antibiotic prescription

stem:
A 65-year-old man is admitted with epigastric pain, muscle spasms and thirst. An electrocardiogram (ECG) reveals lengthened QT intervals and short QRS duration.

Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Hypocalcaemia results from a variety of causes such as acute pancreatitis, hypoparathyroidism, vitamin D deficiency and diuretics. Symptoms include neuromuscular excitability, carpopedal spasm, tetany and seizures. Its main effect on an ECG is prolongation of the QT interval.

Hypokalaemia

stem:
A 76-year-old man presents with progressive dysphagia, weight loss and iron deficiency anaemia. He has a past medical history of Barrett’s oesophagus, however, he did not attend for follow-up OGD after the initial diagnosis. Endoscopy reveals a tumour extending from 35–38 cm from the incisors and 2 cm above the gastrooesophageal junction.

Which one of the following statements is correct?

options.text: Endoscopic ultrasound should not be exclusively used in distinguishing between T2 and T3 tumours
Response to chemotherapy should be measured with plain computed tomography (CT)
CT staging is superior to endoscopic ultrasound for determining tumour depth (T-stage)
Oesophageal cancer most commonly presents with weight gain
PET-CT has no role in the staging of oesophageal carcinoma

explanation:
Response to chemotherapy is measured with PET CT. In addition to assessing tumour size, PET CT allows calculation of a standardised uptake value (SUV) which provides a measure of tumour activity.

The patient should undergo staging laparoscopy

It passes through the second part of the duodenum
It passes through the body of the pancreas
It passes through the hilum of the kidneys
It corresponds to the level of L2 vertebra

explanation:
It passes through the duodenojejunal junction rather than the second part of the duodenum.

stem:
A patient admitted under your care with appendicitis underwent successful surgery and is ready for discharge. You notice their blood glucose has been high throughout their admission.

The 2011 WHO criterion for diagnosis of diabetes mellitus is which of the following?

options.text: 2-hour plasma glucose > 11.1 mmol/l during an OGTT

explanation:
Random plasma glucose > 10.0 mmol/l

Plasma glucose < 7.8 mmol/l at 2 h after glucose-tolerance test

The 2011 WHO recommendations for the diagnosis of type II diabetes mellitus suggest that HbA1c can be used as a diagnostic test for diabetes, provided that stringent quality assurance measures are in place, assays are standardised to criteria aligned with international reference values, and no conditions are present that preclude its accurate measurement. An HbA1c of 48 mmol/mol (6.5%) is recommended as the cut-off for diagnosing diabetes. A value of less than 48 mmol/mol (6.5%) does not exclude diabetes diagnosed using glucose tests. Situations when HbA1c is not appropriate for the diagnosis of diabetes include:

children and young people
patients suspected of having type I diabetes
pregnancy
patients with symptoms of diabetes for less than 2 months
patients at high diabetes risk who are acutely ill
patients taking medication that may cause rapid glucose rise, eg steroids, antipsychotics
patients with acute pancreatic damage, including pancreatic surgery
presence of other factors that influence HbA1c and its measurement (such as haemoglobinopathies, haemolytic disorders, alcohol excess or chronic kidney disease).
Glucose-tolerance test is required for confirmation of diagnosis

stem:
A 75-year-old man has gangrene of the left hallux. There are no palpable pulses present inferior to a weak femoral pulse on the ipsilateral side. A duplex scan reveals an obstruction of flow within the superficial femoral artery.

Which of the following statements pertaining to the arterial system of the lower limb best accords with usual clinical findings?

options.text: The femoral vein lies on the lateral side of the common femoral artery at the groin
The popliteal artery lies against the popliteal surface of the femur deep to the popliteal vein, which itself lies deep to the tibial nerve
The anterior tibial artery passes through the interosseous membrane in the upper leg
The posterior tibial artery is palpable behind the medial malleolus
The dorsalis pedis artery is a continuation of the anterior tibial artery

explanation:
The femoral artery passes into the popliteal fossa, as the popliteal artery, by passing through a gap in adductor longus known as the adductor hiatus.

The popliteal artery is a continuation of the superficial femoral artery (also known as the femoral artery) as it passes through the adductor hiatus. It is the deepest structure found in the popliteal fossa. The fossa also contains the popliteal vein, tibial nerve, the common peroneal nerve, and lymph nodes. The popliteal fossa can be seen below, with the popliteal artery lying deepest.

The pulse of the posterior tibial artery is felt behind the lateral malleolus

stem:
A 55-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department after falling off a ladder. An X-ray is performed, which reveals a fracture of the shaft of the femur. The Orthopaedic Team take him to theatre the next day and perform intramedullary nailing of the femur. Two days’ post-op, he is complaining of shortness of breath and confusion. A petechial rash is noted on his trunk and arms.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Pneumonia is characterised by acute inflammation with an intense infiltration of neutrophils in and around the alveoli and the terminal bronchioles. The affected bronchopulmonary segment or the entire lobe may be consolidated by the resulting inflammation and oedema. Symptoms include cough, purulent sputum which may be bloodstained or rust-coloured breathlessness, fever and malaise.

Pneumothorax

Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura

Fat Embolism
subject: Head and neck surgery

stem: Which one of the following is a function of atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP)?

options.text: Increases sodium reabsorption in the collecting duct
Stimulates renin release from juxtaglomerular cells

explanation:
ANP is an endogenous antagonist of the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system. Hence the secretion of renin, angiotensin and aldosterone is reduced.

Causes renal vasoconstriction

Promotes the feeling of thirst

Close
Renin–Angiotensin–Aldosterone System
subject: Physiology

stem: The pressure within the pleural space is negative with respect to atmospheric pressure, except for which of the following?

options.text: If the patient has a tracheostomy

explanation: During a Valsalva maneuver, forced expiration against a closed glottis raises intrathoracic pressure above atmospheric pressure, making it the exception. At all other times (including with a tracheostomy), intrapleural pressure remains sub-atmospheric.
subject: Physiology

stem: A 30-year-old alcoholic man presents with acute severe upper abdominal pain and vomiting. He is admitted to the intensive therapy unit with a diagnosis of severe acute pancreatitis. Forty-eight hours later he develops peripheral paraesthesiae and carpopedal spasms. The most likely underlying metabolic abnormality is:
explanation: Severe acute pancreatitis causes hypocalcaemia through saponification — free fatty acids released by pancreatic lipase bind calcium ions, forming insoluble calcium soaps in areas of fat necrosis. Hypocalcaemia presents with paraesthesiae, carpopedal spasm (Trousseau's sign), and a positive Chvostek's sign.
subject: Upper gastrointestinal surgery

stem: A 50-year-old woman attends her General Practitioner due to a change in appearance. She finds difficulty removing her rings, reports an increase in shoe size and photographs reveal a change in her facial appearance. Visual field tests are performed to direct confrontation. Which of the following defects is most likely to be associated with her presentation?
explanation: The clinical features (ring tightness, increased shoe size, facial change) are classic acromegaly caused by a growth-hormone-secreting pituitary adenoma. As the tumour expands it compresses the optic chiasm from below, damaging the crossing nasal fibres and producing a bitemporal hemianopia.
subject: Critical care

stem: A 24-year-old man falls off his motorbike, fracturing one arm, both femurs, and rupturing his spleen. He required surgery and 20 units of blood. Twenty-four hours after admission he has passed 350 ml of urine. His blood pressure is 90/50 mmHg and he has low skin turgor. Which of the following best describes the changes in the renin-angiotensin system initiated at the juxtaglomerular apparatus in the patient? (Renin / Angiotensin II / Aldosterone)
explanation: The patient is hypovolaemic (low BP, low urine output, low skin turgor). Reduced renal perfusion stimulates the juxtaglomerular cells to release renin, which converts angiotensinogen to angiotensin I, then ACE converts it to angiotensin II. Angiotensin II stimulates aldosterone release from the adrenal cortex. All three are elevated in hypovolaemia.
subject: Physiology

stem: A 35-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with a second attack of painful frank haematuria. What is the most likely pathology underlying this presentation?
explanation: Recurrent painful frank haematuria in a young adult is most likely transitional cell carcinoma (urothelial carcinoma) of the bladder. Renal cell carcinoma typically causes painless haematuria and is more common in older males. UTIs cause dysuria but rarely frank haematuria. Interstitial cystitis causes frequency and pain but not frank bleeding.
subject: Urology

stem: A 60-year-old man presents with a short history of pain in the right cheek and right upper teeth. Maxillary sinus infection is diagnosed. This sinus is particularly prone to infection because of?

options.text: Absence of cilia on the epithelium lining the sinus
Closeness of the sinus to the nasal cavity
Position of the sinus ostium high on the medial wall
Relationship of the front teeth to the floor of the sinus

explanation: The maxillary sinus ostium is located high on the medial wall, which means drainage depends on ciliary action against gravity. This poor gravitational drainage makes the sinus particularly susceptible to fluid accumulation and infection.
subject: Critical care

stem: A 75-year-old insulin-dependent diabetic man has undergone a hemicolectomy. On the first postoperative day he is nil-by-mouth, on subcutaneous insulin, maintenance IV infusion with saline and intravenous morphine via patient controlled analgesia. He is confused after a brief convulsion, has slurred speech and weakness of his right side. His pulse is 110 beats/minute, respiratory rate 25 breaths/minute, blood pressure 160/95 mmHg and SpO2 95% on room air. The most likely cause of this convulsion and confusion is:
explanation: This insulin-dependent diabetic is nil-by-mouth but receiving subcutaneous insulin — the classic setup for hypoglycaemia. Hypoglycaemia causes seizures, confusion, focal neurological deficits (hemiparesis mimicking stroke), and sympathetic activation (tachycardia, hypertension). Always check blood glucose in a confused post-operative diabetic patient.
subject: Perioperative care

stem: A 30-year-old woman presents to the general surgical clinic with a 1.5 cm cervical lymph node along the anterior border of sternocleidomastoid muscle. Clinical examination and routine blood tests are unremarkable. She undergoes an excisional biopsy of the lump as a day case. The histology report reveals encapsulated infiltrative carcinoma with marked fibrosis and cystic changes within the lymph node. What is the most likely primary pathology?
explanation: Papillary thyroid carcinoma characteristically metastasises to cervical lymph nodes and can present as a lymph node mass before the primary is detected. The histological description of encapsulated carcinoma with fibrosis and cystic changes within a lymph node is classic for metastatic papillary thyroid cancer. It spreads via lymphatics (unlike follicular which spreads haematogenously).
subject: Anatomy

stem: A 37-year-old man presents with severe headache, photophobia and neck stiffness. Kernig's sign is positive and a midline lumbar puncture is performed immediately to determine if a cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) pathogen is involved. In performing this procedure, which is the first of the following structures to be pierced by the lumbar puncture needle?
explanation: In a midline lumbar puncture the needle passes through (in order): skin → subcutaneous fat → supraspinous ligament → interspinous ligament → ligamentum flavum → epidural space → dura mater → arachnoid mater → subarachnoid space. Of the listed structures, the interspinous ligament is encountered first. The anterior and posterior longitudinal ligaments are not pierced.
subject: Neurosurgery

stem: A 26-year-old woman presents with severe headache, photophobia and neck stiffness. Among other investigations, a lumbar puncture is carried out and cerebrospinal fluid is sent for microscopy and culture. Culture shows a growth of Neisseria meningitidis. What is likely to be the predominant cell type in the cerebrospinal fluid?
explanation: Bacterial meningitis (including Neisseria meningitidis) produces a predominantly neutrophilic (polymorphonuclear) CSF pleocytosis, with elevated protein and low glucose. Viral meningitis, by contrast, produces a lymphocytic predominance. Neutrophils are the hallmark of acute bacterial infection.
subject: Neurosurgery

stem: A 70-year-old woman from a nursing home presents to the Emergency Department with abdominal pain and vomiting. On examination, she is dehydrated and her abdomen is distended. There is a 3 cm × 4 cm swelling in her right groin which is non-tender, and there is no cough impulse. At operation, a femoral hernia is found. Which of the following lies medial to the neck of the hernia?
explanation: The femoral ring (neck of a femoral hernia) has the following boundaries: anteriorly the inguinal ligament, posteriorly the pectineal ligament (Cooper's ligament), laterally the femoral vein, and medially the lacunar ligament (Gimbernat's ligament). The sharp edge of the lacunar ligament medially is what often causes strangulation.
subject: Anatomy

stem: A 26-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with extensive bleeding from his arm after sustaining a glass injury. On examination there is a 7 cm transverse laceration across the anterior aspect of his elbow. On exploring the cubital fossa you would expect the brachial artery to be:
explanation: In the cubital fossa, from lateral to medial the key structures are: biceps tendon → brachial artery → median nerve. Therefore the brachial artery lies medial to the biceps tendon and lateral to the median nerve. The brachial artery lies deep to the bicipital aponeurosis.
subject: Anatomy

stem: A 52-year-old man is found to have multiple myeloma. What skull X-ray appearances would be characteristic?
explanation: Multiple myeloma produces multiple well-defined 'punched-out' osteolytic lesions on skull X-ray (pepper-pot skull). These are caused by osteoclast-activating factors secreted by myeloma cells. Hair-on-end appearance is seen in thalassaemia and sickle cell disease. Osteosclerotic lesions are seen in prostate cancer metastases.
subject: Pathology

stem: A 50-year-old woman presents with a history of right upper quadrant pain and jaundice. She reports that her urine was dark in colour and that her stools are offensive and difficult to flush. Which of the following explains the dark urine?
explanation: This is obstructive jaundice (pale stools, dark urine, RUQ pain). In biliary obstruction, conjugated bilirubin cannot enter the bowel and instead backs up into the blood. Being water-soluble, conjugated bilirubin is filtered by the kidneys, producing dark urine (conjugated bilirubinuria). Unconjugated bilirubin is protein-bound and NOT filtered.
subject: Hepatobiliary and pancreatic surgery

stem: A 45-year-old man presents with backache and leg pain due to a prolapsed lumbar intervertebral disc. The pain, which is aggravated by coughing and sneezing, radiates to the lateral aspect of the foot. On examination, there is weakness of the plantar flexors of the foot. Which nerve root is most likely to be involved?
explanation: S1 nerve root compression produces: pain radiating to the lateral foot and sole, weakness of plantarflexion (gastrocnemius/soleus) and eversion, diminished ankle jerk reflex, and sensory loss over the lateral foot. L5 affects dorsiflexion (foot drop) and the dorsum of the foot. L4 affects knee extension and the medial leg.
subject: Anatomy

stem: A 62-year-old woman presents to her General Practitioner with a two-week history of backpain. She has lost 8 cm in height over the last five years. Investigations reveal: Adjusted (corrected) Calcium 2.78 mmol/L (normal 2.15-2.55), Phosphate 0.84 mmol/L (normal 0.8-1.4), Estimated GFR >90 ml/minute, PTH 8.9 pmol/L (normal 0.95-5.7). Which of the following is the most likely cause?
explanation: High calcium (2.78), normal phosphate, normal renal function, and elevated PTH (8.9) = primary hyperparathyroidism. The parathyroid gland is autonomously overproducing PTH despite high calcium. Height loss suggests osteoporosis from chronic bone resorption. In secondary hyperparathyroidism (renal failure), calcium would be low. In tertiary, there would be a history of longstanding renal disease.
subject: Breast and endocrine surgery

stem: A 21-year-old man fractures his ulna and radius. He is treated by means of a plaster cast, which is removed after four weeks. What pathological process is most likely to have affected the immobilized muscles?
explanation: Disuse atrophy occurs when muscles are immobilised — reduced mechanical stimulation leads to decreased protein synthesis and increased proteolysis, causing muscle fibres to shrink. Aplasia is failure of tissue to develop. Hypertrophy and hyperplasia are growth responses. Neoplasia is uncontrolled cell proliferation.
subject: Pathology

stem: A 22-year-old man has been stabbed in the left fifth intercostal space at the edge of the sternum. Which structure is most likely to have been penetrated?
explanation: The right ventricle is the most anterior cardiac chamber and lies directly behind the sternum. A stab wound at the left sternal edge in the 5th intercostal space is most likely to penetrate the right ventricle. The left ventricle is more posterior and lateral. This is the most common chamber injured in penetrating cardiac trauma.
subject: Anatomy

stem: An 80-year-old man dislocates his shoulder. It is reduced in the Emergency Department. At review three weeks later, he is unable to actively initiate abduction of his arm. Which muscle is most likely damaged?
explanation: Initiation of abduction (first 0-15°) is the function of supraspinatus. In elderly patients, shoulder dislocation frequently causes a rotator cuff tear, particularly of the supraspinatus tendon. While axillary nerve injury (affecting deltoid) is also common after dislocation, the specific inability to INITIATE abduction points to supraspinatus.
subject: Anatomy

stem: An 8-year-old boy is admitted for assessment of rectal blood loss. His mother describes this as bright red blood in the toilet pan. He has no pain on defecation. There is no family history. What is the most likely cause?
explanation: Juvenile (retention) polyps are the commonest cause of painless rectal bleeding in children. They are hamartomatous polyps, typically solitary, found in the rectum. They are benign with no malignant potential (unlike adenomatous polyps). FAP is excluded by the lack of family history.
subject: Paediatric surgery

stem: A 48-year-old woman presents with abdominal pain and five to six episodes of bloody diarrhoea each day. She also complains of pain in the knees and elbows and recent visual problems. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Bloody diarrhoea with extraintestinal manifestations (arthralgia in large joints and eye problems — likely iritis/uveitis) is classic ulcerative colitis. UC has well-recognised extraintestinal features: arthritis, uveitis/iritis/episcleritis, erythema nodosum, pyoderma gangrenosum, and primary sclerosing cholangitis.
subject: Colorectal surgery

stem: A 56-year-old man presents with acute epigastric pain and vomiting. On examination he has guarding in the upper abdomen. Investigations reveal: Serum amylase 900 IU/L (≤100), Serum ALT 61 IU/l (≤50), Alkaline Phosphatase 98 IU/l (20-120), Albumin 38 g/L (35-50), Gamma GT 76 IU/L (≤60), Bilirubin 15 umol/L (0-20), Triglyceride 1.6 mmol/L (≤1.7), Corrected Calcium 3.30 mmol/L (2.20-2.70). Which of the following is the most likely etiology of this condition?
explanation: The markedly elevated corrected calcium (3.30 mmol/L) with acute pancreatitis points to hyperparathyroidism as the cause. Hypercalcaemia causes pancreatitis by activating trypsinogen to trypsin within the pancreatic duct. Triglycerides are normal (1.6). ALT and GGT are only mildly raised, making gallstones less likely. Remember 'GET SMASHed' — Gallstones, Ethanol, Trauma, Steroids, Mumps, Autoimmune, Scorpion sting, Hypercalcaemia/Hypertriglyceridaemia, ERCP, Drugs.
subject: Breast and endocrine surgery

stem: A 30-year-old man is admitted to the intensive care unit with an isolated severe head injury. A CT scan shows multiple intracerebral bleeds but no midline shift. He is intubated and ventilated. His pupils are dilated and react sluggishly to light. His heart rate is 50 beats/minute, blood pressure 170/110 mmHg and his respiratory rate is set at 10 breaths/minute. The rising blood pressure is likely to be caused by:

options.text: Sympathetic stimulation related to blood loss
Sympathetic stimulation related to intracranial pressure

explanation: This is the Cushing response (Cushing's reflex): rising intracranial pressure causes brainstem compression, triggering massive sympathetic discharge → hypertension. The baroreceptors detect the hypertension and cause reflex bradycardia. The triad of hypertension, bradycardia, and irregular respirations (Cushing's triad) indicates critically raised ICP and impending herniation.
subject: Neurosurgery

stem: A 42-year-old multiparous woman is admitted to the Emergency Department due to pelvic discomfort. The duty gynecologist diagnoses uterine prolapse. Which anatomical structure gives significant direct support to the uterus?

options.text: Mesometrial part of the broad ligament
Mesosalpingial part of the broad ligament

explanation: The cardinal ligaments (also called transverse cervical or Mackenrodt's ligaments) are the PRIMARY direct supports of the uterus, extending from the cervix to the lateral pelvic wall. They prevent uterine descent. The round ligaments maintain anteversion but provide little support. The broad ligament is a peritoneal fold with minimal supporting role. The pelvic floor provides indirect support.
subject: Anatomy

stem: An 80-year-old man is admitted to the surgical admission unit with central abdominal pain. His blood pressure is 100/60 mmHg and his pulse is 110 beats/minute with a respiratory rate of 25 breaths/minute. He is known to have severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and has been a heavy smoker all his life. On examination he has a rigid abdomen. Arterial blood gases show: pH 7.24, pO2 9 kPa, pCO2 5.3 kPa, Bicarbonate 17 mmol/L, Base Excess -3. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: pH is low (acidosis), bicarbonate is low (17, metabolic acidosis), and base excess is negative (-3). The pCO2 is within normal range (5.3 kPa, normal 4.7-6.0), so this is NOT a respiratory acidosis. The rigid abdomen indicates peritonitis. Peritonitis causes sepsis → tissue hypoperfusion → lactic acidosis → metabolic acidosis. The pCO2 being normal-ish in a COPD patient suggests some respiratory compensation.
subject: Perioperative care

stem: In describing the sino-atrial node, which one of the following statements is correct?

options.text: It is part of the somatic nervous system
It is usually supplied by the left coronary artery
It lies in the wall of the left atrium
It lies in the wall of the right ventricle
It receives fibers derived from the vagus nerves

explanation: The SA node lies in the wall of the RIGHT atrium (at the junction of the SVC and right atrium). It is usually supplied by the right coronary artery (in ~60% of people). It is part of the autonomic (not somatic) nervous system. It receives parasympathetic innervation from the vagus nerve, which slows the heart rate.
subject: Cardiothoracic surgery

stem: A fit 21-year-old man is admitted with an acute abdomen, subsequently diagnosed as gastroenteritis. As part of the host immune response, which of the following immunoglobulins and cells are correctly paired?
explanation: All immunoglobulins are produced by plasma cells (differentiated B lymphocytes). IgG is the most abundant serum immunoglobulin and is produced by plasma cells — this is the correctly paired option. IgA is associated with mucosal surfaces (not macrophages), IgD is found on B-cell surfaces, IgE with mast cells, and IgM with primary immune responses.
subject: Pathology

stem: A 45-year-old man presents with fever and pain in his right loin and groin. A soft swelling was noted in his femoral triangle. Diagnosis of a psoas abscess was made. Which of the following statements is most accurate regarding psoas major?

options.text: It arises from the lateral borders of the bodies of T12 to L5
It inserts into the greater trochanter of the femur
It is innervated from T12 and L1
It passes posterior to the capsule of the hip joint

explanation: Psoas major arises from the transverse processes and lateral borders of the vertebral bodies and intervertebral discs from T12 to L5. It inserts into the LESSER trochanter (not greater). It FLEXES the hip (not extends). It is innervated by ventral rami of L1-L3. It passes ANTERIOR to (not posterior to) the hip joint capsule.
subject: Anatomy

stem: Which one of the following muscles is an extensor of the hip?
explanation: Semitendinosus is one of the three hamstring muscles (along with semimembranosus and biceps femoris). The hamstrings are the primary extensors of the hip and flexors of the knee. Iliopsoas, pectineus, and adductor longus are all hip flexors. Gracilis is primarily an adductor.
subject: Anatomy

stem: A tall, thin, 25-year-old woman presents to the surgical clinic with a complaint of swelling in the front of her neck for the last four months. On clinical examination she has a swelling in the left lobe of the thyroid and multiple neuromatous lesions within the oral cavity. Her blood pressure is 220/120 mmHg. Laboratory investigations show that her calcium and electrolytes are normal and serum calcitonin and urinary VMA levels are elevated. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the hypertension?
explanation: This is MEN 2B (Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia type 2B): medullary thyroid carcinoma (elevated calcitonin) + phaeochromocytoma (elevated urinary VMA, causing severe hypertension) + mucosal/oral neuromas + Marfanoid habitus (tall, thin). The hypertension is caused by catecholamine excess from the phaeochromocytoma.
subject: Breast and endocrine surgery

stem: A 65-year-old man presents with haematuria and left loin pain. Computerised tomography demonstrates a left renal tumour. He undergoes a left radical nephrectomy. Where does the left renal artery lie?

options.text: Anterior to the left gonadal vein
Anterior to the left renal vein
Posterior to the left renal vein
Superior to the superior mesenteric artery

explanation: The left renal vein is ANTERIOR to the left renal artery. The renal vein crosses anterior to the aorta (between the aorta and SMA) to reach the IVC. Therefore, the left renal artery lies POSTERIOR to the left renal vein. This is a critical surgical relationship during nephrectomy — the vein is encountered first.
subject: Urology

stem: Within the posterior triangle, which nerve is at particular risk of damage during surgery?
explanation: The spinal accessory nerve (CN XI) crosses the posterior triangle superficially, running from the posterior border of sternocleidomastoid to the anterior border of trapezius. Its superficial course makes it vulnerable to iatrogenic injury during lymph node biopsy or other surgery in the posterior triangle. Damage causes shoulder drop and inability to shrug.
subject: Anatomy

stem: The right and left pulmonary arteries are derived from which of the following embryological aortic arches?
explanation: The sixth (pulmonary) aortic arch gives rise to the right and left pulmonary arteries. The left sixth arch also forms the ductus arteriosus. The third arch forms the common and internal carotid arteries. The fourth arch forms the aortic arch (left) and proximal right subclavian (right). The fifth arch regresses.
subject: Anatomy

stem: A 47-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department six hours after a climbing accident. Initial assessment suggests that he had lost 1 L of blood. His blood pressure is 105/70 mmHg and his pulse rate is 88 beats/minute. He is catheterised and his bladder contains 120 ml of urine. Activation of which of the following transport systems best describes how aldosterone leads to maintenance of the intravascular volume and oliguria in this man?

options.text: Na/H+ in the descending loop of Henle
Na+/K in the ascending loop of Henle

explanation: Aldosterone acts on the principal cells of the collecting ducts, upregulating ENaC (epithelial sodium channels) on the luminal membrane and Na+/K+-ATPase on the basolateral membrane. This promotes sodium reabsorption in exchange for potassium secretion (Na/K exchange). Water follows sodium, maintaining intravascular volume and reducing urine output.
subject: Physiology

stem: During arch aortography, the vertebral artery would be seen to arise directly from which of the following?
explanation: The vertebral artery is the first branch of the subclavian artery. It ascends through the transverse foramina of C6-C1 to enter the skull. On the left side, the subclavian artery arises directly from the aortic arch; on the right, from the brachiocephalic trunk.
subject: Anatomy

stem: A 65-year-old man remains on the high dependency unit following a gastrectomy, three days previously. His urine output has averaged 80 ml/hour for the last 24 hours. He has one dry abdominal drain and no nasogastric losses. His urea and electrolytes are normal. He is to stay nil by mouth for a further 24 hours. Which of the following fluid regimes is most appropriate to his electrolyte and water requirements over the next 24 hours?

options.text: 1 L of 0.9% saline plus 1.5 L of 4% dextrose/0.18% saline
1 L of 0.9% saline plus 1.5 L of 5% dextrose
1 L of 0.9% saline plus 1.5 L of Hartmann's solution

explanation: Standard maintenance fluid requirements are approximately 25-30 ml/kg/day (roughly 2-2.5L).
