The regime should provide sodium (~1 mmol/kg/day) and water. 1L of 0.9% saline provides sodium, and 1.5L of 5% dextrose provides free water and some calories. This is a standard post-operative maintenance regime. Too much saline alone risks hyperchloraemic acidosis; dextrose/saline alone provides insufficient sodium.
subject: Upper gastrointestinal surgery

stem: A 3-year-old boy is admitted to hospital with severe vomiting. Radiographic examination reveals that he is suffering from annular pancreas. Which of these structures is constricted?
explanation: Annular pancreas is a congenital anomaly where a ring of pancreatic tissue encircles the second part (descending part) of the duodenum, causing obstruction. It results from failure of the ventral pancreatic bud to rotate properly during embryological development. It presents with vomiting and proximal duodenal obstruction.
subject: Anatomy

stem: A 20-year-old man with a severe head injury is being ventilated using intermittent positive pressure. Which of the following is a physiological consequence of this?
explanation: Intermittent positive pressure ventilation (IPPV) increases intrathoracic pressure, which compresses the great veins and reduces venous return to the heart. This decreases cardiac preload (right ventricular filling), which in turn reduces stroke volume and cardiac output. This is an important consideration in managing ventilated patients with haemodynamic instability.
subject: Physiology

stem: A 36-year-old man presents with a two-month history of low back pain radiating to his left leg. After clinical examination he is referred for an MRI scan. This shows a prolapsed intervertebral disc. The clinical signs are consistent with pressure on S1 roots. Which combination of clinical signs is most likely?

options.text: Weak ankle plantarflexion; altered sensation on the dorsum of the foot; normal ankle jerk reflex
Weak ankle plantarflexion; altered sensation on the sole of the foot; loss of ankle jerk reflex
Weak hallux dorsiflexion; altered sensation on the anterior surface of the leg; loss of ankle jerk reflex
Weak hallux dorsiflexion; altered sensation on the dorsum of the foot; normal ankle jerk reflex
Weak hallux dorsiflexion; altered sensation on the sole of the foot; loss of knee jerk reflex

explanation: S1 nerve root compression produces: weakness of ankle plantarflexion (gastrocnemius), altered sensation on the sole/lateral aspect of the foot, and loss of the ankle jerk reflex. L5 compression produces weak hallux dorsiflexion (extensor hallucis longus), altered sensation on the dorsum of the foot, and a normal ankle jerk.
subject: Anatomy

stem: A 55-year-old woman undergoes a cholecystectomy. The gallbladder contains multiple dark irregular small stones. The most likely cause of this type of gallstone is an increased blood level of:
explanation: Multiple dark irregular small stones are pigment stones, composed of calcium bilirubinate. They form from excess unconjugated bilirubin (as in chronic haemolysis, cirrhosis, or biliary infection). Cholesterol stones are typically solitary, large, and pale/yellow. Conjugated bilirubin is water-soluble and excreted in bile — it does not precipitate to form stones.
subject: Hepatobiliary and pancreatic surgery

stem: A 55-year-old man presents with a deep venous thrombosis. His full blood count shows a haemoglobin of 18.3 g/dL (normal 13.5-17.5), a white cell count of 8 × 10⁹/L (normal 3.9-10.0 × 10⁹) and a platelet count of 200 × 10⁹/L (normal 150-400 × 10⁹). This hematological picture is most likely to be associated with:

options.text: Transitional cell carcinoma of the kidney

explanation: The raised haemoglobin (18.3 g/dL = polycythaemia) with DVT points to renal cell carcinoma. RCC produces erythropoietin (EPO) ectopically, causing secondary polycythaemia, which increases blood viscosity and predisposes to thrombosis. This is a classic paraneoplastic syndrome of RCC (along with hypercalcaemia from PTHrP production).
subject: Urology

stem: A 27-year-old has had pancolitis for the last five years. Which one of these complications is he least likely to develop?
explanation: Ulcerative colitis is associated with many extraintestinal manifestations: arthritis, primary sclerosing cholangitis, iritis/uveitis, erythema nodosum, pyoderma gangrenosum, and toxic megacolon. Polyarteritis nodosa is a vasculitis that is NOT an established association of UC — it is associated with hepatitis B infection.
subject: Colorectal surgery

stem: A surgeon makes a Pfannenstiel incision for access to the pelvic organs. He incises the abdominal wall down to and through the rectus sheath. He retracts the rectus abdominis muscles laterally from the midline to expose the:
explanation: A Pfannenstiel incision is made below the arcuate line (below the umbilicus). Below the arcuate line, the posterior rectus sheath is absent — all three muscle aponeuroses pass anterior to the rectus. After retracting the rectus muscles laterally, the structure exposed is the transversalis fascia (with peritoneum deep to it).
subject: Anatomy

stem: A 25-year-old man undergoes splenectomy following blunt abdominal trauma. Three days postoperatively venous blood testing is likely to reveal:
explanation: Post-splenectomy thrombocytosis (elevated platelet count) occurs because the spleen normally sequesters up to one-third of the platelet pool. After removal, these platelets remain in circulation. The platelet count typically peaks at 1-3 weeks post-splenectomy. Howell-Jolly bodies and target cells also appear on blood film. Leucocytosis (not leucopenia) is also common.
subject: Upper gastrointestinal surgery

stem: A 46-year-old woman is seen in the pre-admission clinic. She had a myocardial infarction two years ago. On examination she is in atrial fibrillation and a recent echocardiogram shows that she has a dilated left ventricle. She is on warfarin and her INR is 6.1. Warfarin inhibits which of the following?
explanation: Warfarin inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase, which is required for the gamma-carboxylation of vitamin K-dependent clotting factors: II (prothrombin), VII, IX, and X, as well as proteins C and S. Without carboxylation, these factors (especially prothrombin) are non-functional. Heparin works via antithrombin. Plasminogen is involved in fibrinolysis.
subject: Perioperative care

stem: A 75-year-old man is admitted for elective repair of an abdominal aortic aneurysm. Following the operation his systolic blood pressure falls below 90 mmHg and during resuscitation he is given an infusion of fluids. There is a choice of colloid or crystalloid. Which of the following best describes why the intensive therapy unit registrar decides to administer a colloid?

options.text: Colloids are not freely filterable across semi-permeable membranes
Colloids can prevent pulmonary oedema by inducing fluid flow out of the interstitial space
Colloids decrease the transcapillary oncotic pressure gradient
Colloids expand the plasma volume by 200 ml for each liter infused
Colloids migrate from the intravascular space

explanation: Colloid molecules (albumin, gelatin, starch) are too large to freely cross the semi-permeable capillary membrane. This means they remain in the intravascular compartment, maintaining oncotic pressure and expanding plasma volume more effectively than crystalloids (which distribute across the entire extracellular space). Approximately 100% of colloid stays intravascular initially, vs ~25% of crystalloid.
subject: Perioperative care

stem: A 35-year-old man develops septicaemia following surgery for perforated acute appendicitis. He is hypotensive. Arterial blood gas analysis reveals: pH 7.25, pO2 7.2 kPa, pCO2 7.5 kPa, Bicarbonate 17 mmol/L. What is the most likely explanation for these readings?
explanation: pH 7.25 (acidosis). Bicarbonate 17 (low = metabolic acidosis from sepsis/lactic acid). pCO2 7.5 kPa (high = respiratory acidosis — failure to compensate by hyperventilating, likely exhaustion or septic encephalopathy). Since BOTH pCO2 is elevated AND bicarbonate is low, this is a mixed metabolic and respiratory acidosis. In compensated metabolic acidosis, pCO2 would be LOW (hyperventilation).
subject: Perioperative care

stem: A 20-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with a stab injury to the thenar eminence. On examination he is found to have a 2 cm long laceration with loss of sensation in the thumb and index finger and weakness of the thenar muscles. Which of the following structures is most likely to have been injured?

options.text: Sensory and motor branches of median nerve
Sensory and motor branches of radial nerve
Sensory and motor branches of ulnar nerve

explanation: The median nerve supplies motor innervation to the thenar muscles (via the recurrent branch) and sensory innervation to the thumb, index, middle, and lateral half of the ring finger. Loss of BOTH sensation (thumb and index) AND thenar muscle weakness indicates injury to sensory AND motor branches of the median nerve. The recurrent branch alone would only cause motor loss.
subject: Anatomy

stem: A 65-year-old man presents with vomiting and weight loss. On examination he has a palpable epigastric mass. The transpyloric plane lies at which vertebral level?
explanation: The transpyloric plane of Addison lies at the level of L1, midway between the jugular notch and the pubic symphysis. Important structures at this level include: pylorus of the stomach, fundus of the gallbladder, hilum of the kidneys, neck of the pancreas, origin of the SMA, and the termination of the spinal cord (conus medullaris).
subject: Anatomy

stem: A 30-year-old motorcyclist is brought to the Emergency Department after a road traffic accident. He has an open fracture of the right femur. On arrival he is tachypnoeic and confused, with cold and clammy skin. Which of the following physiological changes is most likely to occur?

options.text: Decreased reabsorption of water from the collecting tubules
Increased secretion of sodium in the urine
Increased synthesis of glycogen in the liver

explanation: Haemorrhagic shock from an open femur fracture causes tissue hypoperfusion → anaerobic metabolism → lactic acid production → metabolic acidosis → decreased serum bicarbonate (consumed buffering the acid). ADH increases water reabsorption (not decrease). pH falls (not increases). Sodium is retained (not secreted). Glycogenolysis occurs (not synthesis).
subject: Emergency medicine and trauma

stem: In an emergency situation what is the most appropriate surgical method of obtaining an airway?

options.text: Cutting and retracting the cricothyroid muscle
Entering the trachea at the C7 level

explanation: Emergency cricothyroidotomy (piercing the cricothyroid membrane) is the fastest and safest surgical airway in an emergency. The cricothyroid membrane is superficial, avascular, and easily palpable between the thyroid and cricoid cartilages. Formal tracheostomy requires more time and has more complications, making it unsuitable as an emergency procedure.
subject: Critical care

stem: A 75-year-old man presents with hepatomegaly and ascites. Computerised tomography shows evidence of post-hepatic portal hypertension. The inferior vena cava passes through the diaphragm at which vertebral level?
explanation: The three major diaphragmatic openings and their vertebral levels are: IVC hiatus at T8 (in the central tendon), oesophageal hiatus at T10 (in the right crus), and aortic hiatus at T12 (behind the median arcuate ligament). Remember: 'I 8 10 Eggs At 12' — IVC=8, oEsophagus=10, Aorta=12.
subject: Anatomy

stem: A 20-year-old woman presents acutely with abdominal pain. Imaging reveals a right ovarian cystic lesion which is excised. Histological examination shows a cyst lined by keratinizing stratified squamous epithelium. Areas of fat, muscle, thyroid and neural tissue are seen in the wall. What is the appropriate pathological designation for this lesion?
explanation: A mature cystic teratoma (dermoid cyst) contains tissues derived from all three germ layers: ectoderm (skin, hair, neural tissue), mesoderm (muscle, fat, bone), and endoderm (thyroid, GI epithelium). The keratinizing squamous epithelium lining, plus fat, muscle, thyroid and neural tissue is pathognomonic. This is the commonest ovarian germ cell tumour in young women.
subject: Head and neck surgery

stem: A 25-year-old woman who is two months post-partum presents with a tender mass in the left breast. She is pyrexial with a raised white cell count and a raised C-reactive protein level. A diagnosis of lactational mastitis with abscess is made. Which of the following is the most likely causative organism?
explanation: Staphylococcus aureus is the causative organism in >90% of cases of lactational breast abscess. It enters through cracked or damaged nipples during breastfeeding and colonises the lactiferous ducts. Treatment is with flucloxacillin (anti-staphylococcal penicillin) and drainage if an abscess has formed.
subject: Head and neck surgery

stem: A 62-year-old alcoholic man is admitted with severe acute pancreatitis. Three days after admission he becomes hypoxic (pOa is 7.5 kPa) and confused. Chest X-ray shows a uniform opacification of both lung fields. Which of the following is the most likely clinical diagnosis?
explanation: ARDS (Adult Respiratory Distress Syndrome) is a recognised severe complication of acute pancreatitis. It presents 2-5 days after the initial insult with progressive hypoxia, confusion, and bilateral diffuse pulmonary infiltrates on CXR ('white-out'). The mechanism involves systemic inflammatory mediators causing increased pulmonary capillary permeability. PE typically shows wedge-shaped opacities, not bilateral uniform opacification.
subject: Head and neck surgery

stem: A 58-year-old woman presented to the Emergency Department with a large fluctuant swelling the site of a recent insect bite. She is anxious, tachycardic, and pyrexial. An ECG shows atrial fibrillation. She is noted to have a goiter. The swelling at the site of the bite requires surgical drainage. Which of the following classes of drug would be most appropriate as part of her preoperative preparation for surgery?
explanation: This patient has thyrotoxicosis (goiter, AF, anxiety, tachycardia) likely precipitated by infection (the bite abscess). Before any surgery in a thyrotoxic patient, beta-blockers (e.g., propranolol) are essential to control heart rate and reduce the risk of thyroid storm. Beta-blockers also reduce peripheral conversion of T4 to T3.
subject: Breast and endocrine surgery

stem: A nulliparous 30-year-old woman presents with a recurrent painful red area in the areola. She gives a history of smoking cigarettes. The lesion is excised and the histology shows squamous metaplasia of lactiferous ducts. Microbiological culture does not grow any organism. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: This is periductal mastitis/Zuska's disease — a condition associated with smoking. Cigarette smoke damages the lactiferous duct epithelium causing squamous metaplasia, which blocks the ducts leading to recurrent subareolar abscess. Cultures are often sterile (anaerobes may be present). It characteristically affects young female smokers and is NOT related to lactation.
subject: Breast and endocrine surgery

stem: A 65-year-old man undergoes right hemicolectomy. On the second postoperative day he is afebrile, nauseous, has a distended abdomen but very little pain. He is on intravenous morphine via a patient-controlled analgesia pump. Plain X-ray confirms distended loops of small intestine. The physiologic basis of postoperative paralytic ileus involves:

options.text: Stimulation of reversed migrating motor complexes
Suppression of motilin due to starvation

explanation: This patient is on morphine PCA, and opioid μ (mu) receptor stimulation in the myenteric plexus is a major contributor to postoperative ileus. μ-receptor activation inhibits acetylcholine release from excitatory motor neurons, reducing peristalsis and increasing gut transit time. This is why opioid-sparing analgesia and peripherally-acting μ-opioid antagonists (alvimopan) are used to reduce post-op ileus.
subject: Perioperative care

stem: A 42-year-old woman has a cholecystectomy and develops a self-limiting postoperative wound infection. By what process would bacterial ingestion have been enhanced?
explanation: Opsonisation is the process of coating pathogens with opsonins (IgG antibodies, complement fragments like C3b) which enhances their recognition and ingestion by phagocytes. Opsonins act as molecular 'handles' that phagocyte Fc receptors and complement receptors can grip. Phagocytosis is the actual process of engulfment, but the question asks what ENHANCES bacterial ingestion.
subject: Pathology

stem: A 60-year-old non-smoker presents with three-month history of loss of weight, malaise and breathlessness. On examination he has left supraclavicular lymph node enlargement. Chest radiograph reveals multiple bilateral opacities. What abnormality would a biopsy of a left supra-clavicular lymph node most probably show?

options.text: Multiple abnormal mitotic figures in cells

explanation: Left supraclavicular lymphadenopathy (Virchow's node/Troisier's sign) with bilateral lung opacities in a patient with weight loss suggests metastatic carcinoma (likely GI or lung primary). The biopsy would show malignant cells with multiple abnormal mitotic figures — a hallmark of cancer. Reed-Sternberg cells indicate Hodgkin's lymphoma. Granulomas suggest TB or sarcoidosis.
subject: Surgical oncology

stem: A 78-year-old woman with emphysema receiving 28% oxygen by mask has the following blood gas results: pH 7.28, pO2 6.2 kPa, pCO2 8 kPa, Bicarbonate 36 mmol/L, Base Excess +5. The most likely interpretation is:
explanation: pH 7.28 (acidosis). pCO2 8 kPa (elevated = respiratory acidosis from COPD/emphysema). Bicarbonate 36 mmol/L (elevated = metabolic compensation via renal HCO3⁻ retention). Base excess +5 (metabolic compensation). The pH is still below normal, so compensation is partial (not full). This is a partially compensated respiratory acidosis — chronic CO2 retention with renal bicarbonate compensation.
subject: Perioperative care

stem: A 2-year-old child is referred because of an impalpable testis in the left scrotum. Which of the following positions describes an ectopic testis?

options.text: At the root of the penis
In the upper part of the scrotum

explanation: An ectopic testis has deviated from the normal path of descent and lies in an abnormal position: root of the penis, perineum, femoral triangle, superficial inguinal pouch, or contralateral scrotum. An undescended testis is found along the normal path of descent (abdomen, inguinal canal, deep ring, superficial ring, high scrotum). The root of the penis is an ectopic location.
subject: Critical care

stem: A 60-year-old man is found to have a 2 cm diameter mass in the upper lobe of his left lung. The lesion is excised and it is found that the lesion includes connective tissue, mature cartilage and ciliated epithelium. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: A pulmonary hamartoma is a benign tumour containing a disorganised mixture of tissues normally found in the lung — cartilage, connective tissue, fat, and ciliated epithelium. It is the most common benign lung tumour, typically appearing as a well-defined 'coin lesion' with popcorn calcification on CXR. It is NOT a true neoplasm but a developmental malformation.
subject: Cardiothoracic surgery

stem: A 23-year-old man presents three months following extraction of carious teeth with a plaque-like infiltration over the upper jaw with sinus formation. Yellow granules are present in the discharging pus. What is the most likely causative organism?
explanation: Actinomycosis classically presents with chronic sinus-discharging infection containing 'sulfur granules' (yellow granules of bacterial colonies). Cervicofacial actinomycosis (lumpy jaw) typically follows dental procedures or trauma. Actinomyces israelii is a Gram-positive filamentous anaerobic bacterium (NOT a fungus despite the name). Treatment is prolonged penicillin.
subject: Head and neck surgery

stem: An 82-year-old man has complete occlusion of his inferior mesenteric artery on angiography but no symptoms or signs of colonic ischaemia. Which of the following arteries is the most likely additional source of blood supply to the territory of the inferior mesenteric artery?
explanation: The middle colic artery (a branch of the SMA) provides collateral flow to IMA territory via the marginal artery of Drummond and the arc of Riolan. This anastomosis between SMA and IMA territories is the critical collateral pathway that prevents colonic ischaemia when the IMA is occluded. The left colic and superior rectal are IMA branches (already occluded).
subject: Anatomy

stem: An intravenous drug abuser is having an echocardiogram for suspected endocarditis. Closure of the tricuspid valve occurs at the onset of which phase of the cardiac cycle?
explanation: The tricuspid (and mitral) valves close at the onset of isovolumetric contraction, when ventricular pressure exceeds atrial pressure. This closure produces the first heart sound (S1). All four valves are closed during isovolumetric contraction and isovolumetric relaxation. The aortic and pulmonary valves close at the onset of isovolumetric relaxation (S2).
subject: Physiology

stem: After being stabbed in the left groin, a previously healthy 20-year-old man was admitted to the emergency Department. He developed hemorrhagic shock. During resuscitation, 10 units of type O negative red cells and 6 L of colloid were administered. Twenty-four hours later, he noted to have severe dyspnoea for which he required intubation and ventilation on the intensive care unit. Which of the following would be the most likely cause of his respiratory insufficiency?
explanation: ARDS is the most likely cause 24 hours after massive transfusion (16 units total) and haemorrhagic shock. Massive transfusion and the systemic inflammatory response to shock/tissue damage cause increased pulmonary capillary permeability → non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema → ARDS. TRALI (transfusion-related acute lung injury) is also possible but is a form of ARDS.
subject: Emergency medicine and trauma

stem: An 80-year-old man with a history of hypertension, controlled with thiazide diuretics, undergoes transurethral resection of prostate under general anaesthetic. The surgery is prolonged and in the recovery room he complains of nausea and a headache. He later becomes agitated and confused. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: This is TURP syndrome — absorption of hypotonic glycine irrigation fluid during prolonged TURP causes dilutional hyponatraemia. Symptoms include nausea, headache, confusion, agitation, visual disturbance, and seizures. Risk is increased with prolonged surgery (>1 hour). Thiazide diuretics also predispose to hyponatraemia, compounding the problem.
subject: Perioperative care

stem: A 35-year-old man is admitted to hospital with vomiting, nausea and severe headaches. An MRI scan reveals a tumour of the cerebellopontine angle. Which one of the following pairs of cranial nerves is most likely to be compressed by this tumour?
explanation: The cerebellopontine angle is where cranial nerves VII (facial) and VIII (vestibulocochlear) emerge from the brainstem. A vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma) is the most common CPA tumour and characteristically compresses these two nerves, causing sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus, facial weakness, and loss of corneal reflex.
subject: Upper gastrointestinal surgery

stem: After resection of a rectal tumour a patient experiences erectile dysfunction. Which of the following nerves is most likely to have been damaged in surgery?
explanation: The pelvic splanchnic nerves (nervi erigentes, S2-S4) carry parasympathetic fibres responsible for penile erection. They run close to the lateral walls of the rectum and are at risk during rectal surgery, particularly during total mesorectal excision. Nerve-sparing surgical techniques aim to preserve these nerves. The pudendal nerve carries somatic sensation but is not the primary mediator of erection.
subject: Physiology

stem: A 45-year-old woman presents with pain, swelling and stiffness affecting all her metacarpophalangeal joints. She has noticed weakness in her grip and her handwriting has changed. She is unable to extend her fingers fully. The index, middle and ring fingers in both hands show an ulnar deviation. The most likely diagnosis is:
explanation: Symmetrical MCP joint involvement with ulnar deviation of the fingers is the hallmark of rheumatoid arthritis. RA is a chronic autoimmune inflammatory polyarthritis that characteristically affects the MCP and PIP joints symmetrically. Dupuytren's causes flexion contracture of the ring and little fingers without MCP swelling. Osteoarthritis typically affects DIPs (Heberden's nodes).
subject: Orthopaedics

stem: A 22-year-old man arrives to the Emergency Department with sudden breathlessness due to a large pneumothorax. A chest drain is inserted into the fifth left intercostal space in 5th mid-axillary line. There is haemorrhage into the drainage bottle. Which of the following structures is the most likely cause of this acute haemorrhage?
explanation: Intercostal artery injury is the most common cause of haemorrhage during chest drain insertion. The intercostal vessels (artery, vein, nerve) run in the subcostal groove along the inferior border of each rib. Drains should be inserted just ABOVE the rib (not below) to avoid the neurovascular bundle. Damage to these vessels can cause significant bleeding into the drain.
subject: Cardiothoracic surgery

stem: A 65-year-old woman collapses after a total hip replacement. A pulmonary embolism is suspected. Which of the following electrocardiogram changes would support this diagnosis?
explanation: Right heart strain from PE produces: T-wave inversion in V1-V3 (anterior leads), the classic S1Q3T3 pattern, right axis deviation, right bundle branch block, sinus tachycardia, and P-pulmonale. ST elevation in V1-V3 suggests anterior MI. Left axis deviation and dominant R in V6 suggest left-sided pathology, not PE.
subject: Vascular surgery

stem: A 40-year-old woman had the anterior lobe of the pituitary removed because of a tumour. Without postoperative supplements, which of the following could occur?

options.text: Failure to produce adequate amounts of thyroxine
Fail to produce parathyroid hormone in response to hypocalcaemia
Failure to secrete catecholamine in response to stress
Failure to secrete insulin in hyperglycemia
Inability to concentrate urine in response to water deprivation

explanation: The anterior pituitary produces TSH, which stimulates the thyroid to produce thyroxine. Without TSH, thyroxine production fails → hypothyroidism. PTH is from the parathyroid glands (unrelated). Catecholamines are from the adrenal medulla. Insulin is from the pancreas. ADH (urine concentration) is from the posterior pituitary, which is anatomically and functionally distinct from the anterior lobe.
subject: Critical care

stem: A 38-year-old man in end-stage renal failure resulting from polycystic kidney disease receives a cadaveric renal transplant. Good renal function is established but four weeks later deteriorates, the serum creatinine rising by 25%. Which of the following processes is most likely to be responsible for this deterioration?
explanation: Acute cellular rejection at 4 weeks post-transplant is most commonly T-cell (cell-mediated) rejection. Host T-lymphocytes recognise donor MHC antigens and mount a cellular immune response against the graft. Treatment is with high-dose methylprednisolone or anti-thymocyte globulin (ATG). Hyperacute rejection (antibody-mediated) occurs within minutes to hours.
subject: Organ transplantation

stem: In order to expose the right axillary artery, a transverse skin incision is typically made below the clavicle from a point just lateral to the sternal end of the clavicle to the deltopectoral groove. Which of the following structures would be encountered in the dissection down to the vessel?
explanation: The thoraco-acromial artery is a branch of the second part of the axillary artery that pierces the clavipectoral fascia — it would be directly encountered during dissection through this fascia to reach the axillary artery. The phrenic nerve runs on scalenus anterior (more medial). The thoracic duct is on the LEFT side. The lateral thoracic artery runs more inferiorly.
subject: Anatomy

stem: A 4-year-old boy presents to the Emergency Department with a two-day history of headache, vomiting and drowsiness. A CT scan reveals dilatation of both his lateral ventricles and his third cerebral ventricle. His fourth ventricle was of normal size. It is suspected that he has an obstruction to his cerebrospinal fluid flow. At which of the following sites is the obstruction most likely to be?

options.text: Lateral foramen of fourth ventricle (foramen of Luschka)
Median foramen of fourth ventricle (foramen of Magendie)

explanation: Both lateral ventricles AND the third ventricle are dilated, but the fourth ventricle is normal. CSF flows: lateral ventricles → (foramen of Monro) → third ventricle → (cerebral aqueduct of Sylvius) → fourth ventricle. Since the fourth ventricle is normal but everything above is dilated, the obstruction must be at the cerebral aqueduct of Sylvius (between 3rd and 4th ventricles).
subject: Neurosurgery

stem: A 12-year-old boy presents to the Emergency Department two hours after helping his father cut the grass. He complains of rhinorrhoea, itchy eyes, sneezing and a blocked nose. He is apyrexial with a haemoglobin of 12.2 g/dl and white blood cell count of 6.8 × 10⁹/L with a raised eosinophil count. Chest X-ray is clear. Which immunoglobulin is most likely to cause this reaction?
explanation: This is a Type I (immediate) hypersensitivity reaction / allergic rhinitis triggered by grass pollen. IgE mediates Type I reactions: allergen cross-links IgE on mast cell surfaces → degranulation → histamine release → rhinorrhoea, sneezing, itching. Eosinophilia is characteristic. IgG mediates Type II and III reactions. IgA is the mucosal immunoglobulin.
subject: Pathology

stem: A 35-year-old woman undergoes gastric bypass surgery for morbid obesity. At a subsequent surgical clinic review she complains of dizziness, sweating, palpitation and collapsing episodes after big meals without any vomiting or pain. She is otherwise well and has no medical problems. What is the most likely explanation for her symptoms?
explanation: This is late dumping syndrome: after gastric bypass, rapid transit of carbohydrate-rich food into the jejunum causes rapid glucose absorption → exaggerated insulin release → reactive hypoglycaemia (1-3 hours after eating) → dizziness, sweating, palpitations, collapse. Early dumping (within 30 min) is caused by osmotic fluid shifts. Late dumping is caused by excessive insulin release.
subject: Upper gastrointestinal surgery

stem: A 56-year-old man with chronic emphysema is on the high dependency unit (HDU), ten days after anterior resection. He has developed acute shortness of breath and hypotension. Which of the following landmarks would be the most appropriate to use to obtain a femoral arterial blood gas sample?

options.text: A point midway between the anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic tubercle
A point midway between the anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic symphysis
A point midway between the greater trochanter and the pubic symphysis
A point 1 cm inferior and 4 cm lateral to the pubic tubercle
A point 2 cm lateral to the midway point between the anterior superior iliac spine and pubic symphysis

explanation: The femoral artery enters the thigh at the mid-inguinal point, which is midway between the anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS) and the pubic symphysis. This is where the femoral pulse is palpated and where arterial blood gas samples are taken. Note: the mid-inguinal point (ASIS to pubic symphysis) differs from the midpoint of the inguinal ligament (ASIS to pubic tubercle).
subject: Anatomy

stem: A 70-year-old man complains of persistent numbness since an inguinal hernia repair one year previously. The numbness affects the top of the scrotum, root of penis, and a small area below the medial part of the inguinal ligament. Which nerve is likely to have been damaged?

options.text: Femoral branch of the genitofemoral nerve
Genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve
Medial cutaneous branch of the femoral nerve

explanation: The ilioinguinal nerve (L1) runs through the inguinal canal and is at risk during hernia repair. It provides sensory innervation to the skin of the upper medial thigh, root of the penis/scrotum (or mons pubis/labium majus in females), and the medial inguinal region. The genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve supplies the cremaster muscle, not this sensory territory.
subject: Anatomy

stem: A 12-year-old girl has a diastolic murmur. It is maximally audible in the second left intercostal space. Pathology of which structure is the most likely cause?
explanation: The second left intercostal space (parasternal) is the pulmonary auscultation area. A diastolic murmur here indicates pulmonary regurgitation (Graham Steell murmur). In a 12-year-old, this could be due to pulmonary hypertension (e.g., from a congenital left-to-right shunt). The aortic area is the second RIGHT intercostal space. The mitral area is the apex (5th left ICS, MCL).
subject: Anatomy

stem: A 34-year-old pregnant woman develops a swollen leg. Her mother and maternal aunt also had similar problems during their pregnancies. Which of the following tests is likely to be positive?
explanation: Recurrent thrombosis during pregnancy with a positive family history suggests antiphospholipid syndrome (APS/Hughes syndrome). Antiphospholipid antibodies (anticardiolipin, lupus anticoagulant, anti-β2 glycoprotein I) cause a prothrombotic state, particularly during pregnancy. It is the most common acquired thrombophilia and causes recurrent pregnancy loss, DVT, and stroke.
subject: Head and neck surgery

stem: The "fight or flight" response produces a release of epinephrine (adrenaline). What is the primary metabolic effect of epinephrine?
explanation: The primary METABOLIC effect of epinephrine is to promote glycogenolysis and glycolysis — rapidly mobilising glucose for energy. Epinephrine activates adenylyl cyclase → cAMP → protein kinase A → glycogen phosphorylase, breaking down glycogen to glucose-1-phosphate which enters glycolysis. Tachycardia and vasoconstriction are cardiovascular (not metabolic) effects.
subject: Physiology

stem: A 58-year-old man underwent an emergency appendectomy. Which of the following physiological parameters are consistent with sepsis? (Heart Rate / Systemic Vascular Resistance / Cardiac Output)
explanation: Sepsis (warm/distributive shock) is characterised by: tachycardia (↑HR), vasodilation (↓SVR due to inflammatory mediators like NO), and a hyperdynamic circulation (↑CO — the heart compensates for the low SVR by increasing output). This is 'warm shock' — warm peripheries, bounding pulse, wide pulse pressure. In late/decompensated sepsis, cardiac output eventually falls.
subject: Critical care

stem: A 50-year-old man with a 30-year history of pancolitis undergoes surveillance colonoscopy which reveals a plaque-like lesion in the descending colon. Biopsy reveals a pre-malignant change. What is the name of this pre-malignant change?
explanation: Dysplasia is the pre-malignant change found in longstanding ulcerative colitis. It represents disordered cellular growth with architectural and cytological abnormalities, but has not yet breached the basement membrane (unlike neoplasia/carcinoma). Colonoscopic surveillance in UC aims to detect dysplasia before progression to carcinoma. Anaplasia implies loss of differentiation (already malignant).
subject: Colorectal surgery

stem: A 60-year-old man undergoes cystectomy for a bladder carcinoma. During surgery, the ureters are identified. On which region of the bladder do the ureters pierce the bladder wall?
explanation: The ureters enter the bladder at its posterolateral angles, piercing the posterior surface (base) at the superolateral corners of the trigone. They run obliquely through the bladder wall for ~2 cm, which creates a valve mechanism preventing vesicoureteric reflux. The trigone is on the internal posterior/inferior surface of the bladder.
subject: Head and neck surgery

stem: A patient in the intensive care unit has a tracheostomy performed via the second, third and fourth tracheal rings. Which intervening structure is most likely to require transection?
explanation: The thyroid isthmus lies across the 2nd to 4th tracheal rings and must be divided (transected) or retracted during tracheostomy at this level. It is the most important structure encountered during the approach. The inferior thyroid veins may be encountered but are more variable. The sternothyroid muscles are retracted laterally, not transected.
subject: Breast and endocrine surgery

stem: A 23-year old man is assaulted and sustains a stabbing injury to the left groin. The wound is cleaned and a simple dressing applied. Six months later the patient returns with pulsatile swelling at the site of the injury. The most probable lesion present is:

options.text: False aneurysm of the femoral artery
Mycotic aneurysm of the femoral artery

explanation: A pulsatile swelling developing months after a penetrating groin injury is a false (pseudo) aneurysm of the femoral artery. The initial injury damages the arterial wall; blood leaks and is contained by surrounding tissues forming a pulsatile haematoma that communicates with the arterial lumen. A mycotic aneurysm is caused by infection, not trauma.
subject: Head and neck surgery

stem: A 72-year-old man with a body mass index of 18.4 has not eaten for four days following the removal of an adenocarcinoma from his descending colon. His urea is found to be 12 mmol/L (normal 3.2-7.5) and creatinine 346 umol/L (normal 35-110). A blood gas profile is ordered. The most likely set of results would be:

options.text: pH 7.23, pO2 13.6 kPa, pCo2 3.8 kPa, Bicarbonate 13.5 mmol/L
pH 7.30, pO2 8.8 kPa, pCo2 8.3 kPa, Bicarbonate 30.5 mmol/L
pH 7.36, pO2 11.5 kPa, pCo2 5.3 kPa, Bicarbonate 30.5 mmol/L
pH 7.43, pO2 16.4 kPa, pCo2 3.7 kPa, Bicarbonate 21.0 mmol/L
pH 7.49, pO2 12.6 kPa, pCo2 3.9 kPa, Bicarbonate 24.0 mmol/L

explanation: This patient has acute renal failure (urea 12, creatinine 346). The kidneys cannot excrete hydrogen ions or regenerate bicarbonate, leading to metabolic acidosis. Option A shows: low pH (acidosis), low bicarbonate (metabolic), low pCO2 (respiratory compensation by hyperventilation), normal pO2. This is a compensated metabolic acidosis consistent with renal failure.
subject: Head and neck surgery

stem: A 16-year-old boy is hit on the left side of the face by a ball. There are no broken bones but the boy complains of numbness of the face below the eye. Which nerve has most likely been compromised?
explanation: The infra-orbital nerve (a branch of the maxillary division of the trigeminal nerve, V2) exits through the infra-orbital foramen below the orbit. A blow to the cheek can cause a neuropraxia of this nerve, producing numbness of the cheek, upper lip, and lower eyelid. This is also the nerve at risk in zygomatic/orbital floor fractures.
subject: Anatomy

stem: A 74-year-old man, who has undergone emergency major abdominal surgery two days previously, is noted to be confused. He has been on furosemide for mild heart failure. The plasma sodium is 122 mmol/L. Inspection of the fluid chart shows that he has been written up for 1L, four-hourly intravenous 5% glucose infusions. What is the most likely cause for the hyponatremia?

options.text: An ACTH (Adrenocorticotrophic hormone) response to surgery
Osmotic effect of hyperglycemia induced by glucose infusions
Use of loop diuretic in the long term

explanation: 6L of 5% dextrose per day is excessive free water. 5% dextrose is effectively free water once the glucose is metabolised. Giving 6L/day of free water causes dilutional hyponatraemia (Na 122). The furosemide also contributes to sodium loss, but the primary cause is the excessive hypotonic fluid. Post-operative ADH secretion exacerbates water retention.
subject: Perioperative care

stem: The Cori cycle is important in lactate metabolism in the septic surgical patient. It is used to describe a pathway in which glucose is metabolised anaerobically to lactate in one tissue and the lactate is converted back to glucose in another. Which one of the following relies on this cycle to meet all of its energy needs?
explanation: Erythrocytes (red blood cells) lack mitochondria and therefore rely entirely on anaerobic glycolysis for energy, producing lactate as the end product. This lactate is transported to the liver where it is converted back to glucose via gluconeogenesis (the Cori cycle). The glucose is then released back into the blood for use by erythrocytes and other tissues.
subject: Hepatobiliary and pancreatic surgery

stem: After receiving an intramuscular injection in the buttock, a 25-year-old man complains of inability to evert his foot. Which nerve is most likely to have been injured?
explanation: The common peroneal (fibular) nerve supplies the muscles of the lateral and anterior compartments of the leg responsible for eversion and dorsiflexion. A misplaced gluteal injection (too medial or inferior to the upper outer quadrant) can damage the sciatic nerve, and the common peroneal component is most vulnerable due to its lateral position and fewer fascicles.
subject: Anatomy

stem: A 73-year-old man with a history of irregular bowel movements presents with dysuria, pneumaturia and an Escherichia coli urinary tract infection. CT scans show a mass involving the sigmoid colon and the bladder. What is the commonest cause of this presentation?

options.text: Transitional cell carcinoma of the bladder

explanation: Pneumaturia (air in urine) with E. coli UTI and a mass involving sigmoid colon and bladder indicates a colovesical fistula. The commonest cause is complicated diverticular disease (65%), followed by colorectal carcinoma (20%) and Crohn's disease (10%). The elderly age and sigmoid location strongly favour diverticular disease.
subject: Urology

stem: A 7-year-old woman is in the recovery area and receives 28% oxygen by mask. Blood gas shows: pH 7.2, pO2 12 kPa, pCo2 10 kPa. Reduced sensitivity of which receptors is most likely to be responsible for this blood gas picture?
explanation: pH 7.2 with pCO2 10 kPa indicates respiratory acidosis with CO2 retention. Despite high CO2, ventilation is inadequate — this indicates failure of the central chemoreceptors (in the medulla) which normally detect rising CO2/H+ in CSF and stimulate increased ventilation. Reduced sensitivity (e.g., from anaesthesia, opioids) leads to hypoventilation and CO2 retention.
subject: Physiology

stem: A 76-year-old woman falls and sustains an inter-trochanteric fractured neck of femur. Following operative fixation her recovery is prolonged and she is discharged to a rehabilitation unit. Six weeks after her original operation she is readmitted. She is drowsy, hypotensive and bradycardic. An ECG shows low voltage complexes and a prolonged QT interval. Under-activity of which of the following glands gives the best explanation of the clinical picture?
explanation: Drowsiness, hypotension, bradycardia, low voltage ECG complexes, and prolonged QT interval are classic features of severe hypothyroidism (myxoedema). Thyroid under-activity causes reduced cardiac output, bradycardia, low voltage ECG, and prolonged QT. This may have been pre-existing but decompensated after the stress of surgery and prolonged recovery.
subject: Orthopaedics

stem: A 36-year-old man falls on his outstretched right hand. Examination reveals tenderness in the anatomical snuff box. Which one of the following tendons form a boundary of the anatomical snuff box?
explanation: The anatomical snuff box boundaries are: laterally (radial side) — abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis tendons; medially (ulnar side) — extensor pollicis longus tendon. Of the options listed, extensor pollicis longus forms the medial (ulnar) boundary. Tenderness here suggests a scaphoid fracture.
subject: Anatomy

stem: A 65-year-old woman with metastatic breast cancer is admitted to hospital confused and acutely unwell, with nausea and vomiting. Her vital signs are within normal limits. What abnormality is most likely to contribute to her clinical condition?
explanation: Hypercalcaemia is the commonest metabolic emergency in malignancy. Breast cancer metastases to bone cause osteolytic destruction releasing calcium, and some produce PTHrP. Symptoms include confusion, nausea, vomiting, constipation, polyuria, and dehydration. The normal vital signs with confusion and nausea point to a metabolic rather than infective cause.
subject: Breast and endocrine surgery

stem: A 4-year-old boy presents to the Emergency Department with a two-day history of fever, difficulty walking and is unable to weight bear on the right leg. He has been on oral Amoxycillin 250 mg three times a day for a chest infection over the last five days. He is irritable with a temperature of 39.4°C. He does not allow examination and keeps his right hip flexed and abducted. Blood tests are: white blood cell count (WBC) 12.3 x 10⁹/dL, C-Reactive protein (CRP) 146, haemoglobin 11.3 g/dL. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Fever, inability to weight bear, raised WBC and CRP (146), and a hip held in flexion and abduction (the position of maximum joint volume) in a young child is septic arthritis until proven otherwise. This is an orthopaedic emergency requiring urgent joint aspiration and washout. Perthes presents more insidiously without high inflammatory markers.
subject: Paediatric surgery

stem: A 35-year-old woman presents with recurrent peptic ulceration. She is on proton pump inhibitors and previously received Helicobacter pylori eradication therapy three months ago. Which of the following is likely to be raised on venous blood testing?
explanation: Recurrent peptic ulceration despite PPI and H. pylori eradication suggests Zollinger-Ellison syndrome (gastrinoma). The serum gastrin level will be markedly elevated. Gastrinomas are usually found in the gastrinoma triangle (pancreas/duodenum) and secrete gastrin autonomously, causing excess acid production and refractory ulceration. PPIs themselves also raise gastrin but not to ZE levels.
subject: Upper gastrointestinal surgery

stem: A 55-year-old man presents with back ache. Neurological examination reveals lack of extension of the left great toe. Which of the following spinal cord segments are likely to be involved?
explanation: Extension (dorsiflexion) of the great toe is performed by extensor hallucis longus, which is primarily innervated by the L5 nerve root (with contributions from L4 and S1). This is a key test for L5 radiculopathy. L4,L5,S1 is the correct segment grouping.
subject: Head and neck surgery

stem: A 34-year-old man is seen in the Emergency Department with a fibular fracture following a football match. On examination he is noted to have loss of foot eversion. Which area of skin should be examined to confirm loss of the cutaneous distribution of the affected nerve?

options.text: Along the lateral aspect of the foot
Along the medial aspect of the foot
Cross the dorsal surface of the foot
On the plantar surface of the foot

explanation: Loss of foot eversion indicates damage to the superficial peroneal (fibular) nerve. This nerve supplies the peroneus longus and brevis (evertors) and provides cutaneous innervation to the dorsum of the foot (except the first web space, which is deep peroneal). A fibular fracture at the neck commonly damages this nerve.
subject: Anatomy

stem: A 68-year-old man with insulin-dependent diabetes presents to the preadmission clinic prior to surgery for rectal carcinoma. His creatinine is found to be 590 pmol/L. He is referred to a renal unit where a measure of his glomerular filtration rate (GFR) is made. Which of the following best describes why inulin could be used to measure his GFR?

options.text: It is filtered and not reabsorbed
It is filtered, secreted and reabsorbed
It is filtered, secreted but not reabsorbed
It is not filtered but is secreted and not reabsorbed

explanation: Inulin is the gold standard for GFR measurement because it is freely filtered at the glomerulus, and is neither reabsorbed nor secreted by the tubules. Therefore, the amount of inulin filtered equals the amount excreted in urine, making its clearance equal to GFR. Creatinine clearance is a practical approximation but creatinine is slightly secreted by tubules.
subject: Physiology

stem: A 60-year-old man presents with a one-month history of headache, confusion and recent onset of right sided hemiparesis. A CT scan demonstrates a 4 cm × 4 cm lesion with central necrosis in the left frontal lobe. It is seen extending across the midline along the corpus callosum. There is extensive oedema around the lesion. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis of this lesion?
explanation: A large frontal lobe lesion with central necrosis, crossing the midline via the corpus callosum ('butterfly glioma'), and extensive surrounding oedema is the classic presentation of glioblastoma multiforme (GBM, WHO Grade IV). It is the most common and most aggressive primary brain tumour in adults. Crossing the corpus callosum is almost pathognomonic.
subject: Neurosurgery

stem: A 65-year-old woman presents with a 2.5 cm diameter mass in the upper outer quadrant of the left breast with associated axillary lymphadenopathy. A core biopsy is taken which confirms the presence of carcinoma. Which of the following types of carcinoma is this most likely to be?
explanation: Invasive ductal carcinoma (no special type, NST) is the most common type of breast cancer, accounting for 70-80% of all invasive breast cancers. When a breast mass is confirmed as carcinoma without specific features, invasive ductal carcinoma is statistically the most likely type.
subject: Breast and endocrine surgery

stem: A 26-year-old man is admitted to the Emergency Department with multiple peripheral fractures. He is clinically shocked. Which is the structure responsible for the first hemostatic response to a fall in systemic arterial blood pressure?
explanation: Baroreceptors (in the carotid sinus and aortic arch) detect the fall in arterial blood pressure within seconds and are the FIRST responders. They reduce their firing rate, which disinhibits the sympathetic nervous system → vasoconstriction, increased heart rate, and increased contractility. The kidney (RAAS) and neurohypophysis (ADH) respond more slowly.
subject: Emergency medicine and trauma

stem: Vitamin K is required for normal blood clotting. Which one of the following statements is true about the effects and availability of vitamin K?

options.text: Causes bleeding if taken in excess
Is provided only by fresh food
Is depleted by broad spectrum oral antibiotics
Vitamin K absorption is affected by resection of the terminal ileum

explanation: Vitamin K is a fat-soluble vitamin absorbed in the terminal ileum (along with bile salts and B12). Terminal ileum resection impairs its absorption. Vitamin K is also synthesised by gut bacteria, so broad-spectrum antibiotics CAN reduce production, but option E about terminal ileum resection is more definitively true. Vitamin K does not affect platelet function — it affects clotting factor carboxylation.
subject: Clinical microbiology

stem: In septic shock, norepinephrine (noradrenaline) is used to increase the systemic vascular resistance. This action is a result of the stimulation of which of the following receptors?
explanation: Noradrenaline acts primarily on α₁ adrenergic receptors on vascular smooth muscle, causing vasoconstriction and increasing systemic vascular resistance. This is why noradrenaline is the first-line vasopressor in septic shock (distributive shock with pathologically low SVR). It also has some β₁ activity (increasing cardiac contractility).
subject: Pharmacology

stem: A 10-year-old child presents with progressive facial weakness and a squint. On examination there is a lower motor neuron facial weakness and failure of abduction of one eye. An MRI scan shows a small, intrinsic mass lesion within the central nervous system. Where is this most likely to be located?
explanation: The pons contains the nuclei of CN VI (abducens — eye abduction) and CN VII (facial nerve — facial expression). An intrinsic pontine lesion affecting both these nuclei explains the combination of LMN facial weakness and failure of abduction. In children, diffuse intrinsic pontine glioma (DIPG) is a devastating tumour at this location.
subject: Head and neck surgery

stem: A 65-year-old man, with a history of ischaemic heart disease, has an abdomino-perineal excision of the rectum after which he is stable. Two days later he is clammy, has cool peripheries, a tachycardia and a blood pressure of 80/60 mmHg. His temperature is normal. What is the most likely cause?
explanation: History of ischaemic heart disease, cool clammy peripheries, tachycardia, hypotension, and normal temperature 2 days post-op points to cardiogenic shock (likely perioperative MI). In septic shock, peripheries would be warm. Hypovolaemic shock is possible but the IHD history and cool peripheries make a cardiac cause more likely. Neurogenic shock causes warm, dry peripheries with bradycardia.
subject: Emergency medicine and trauma

stem: A 55-year-old man presents to his General Practitioner with a four-month history of feeling tired. The General Practitioner notes breast enlargement. Investigations reveal: TSH 0.2 mIU/L (normal 0.4-4.3), Free T4 6 mmol/L (normal 9-23). Which of the following is the most likely cause?
explanation: Low TSH (0.2) AND low Free T4 (6) = secondary (central) hypothyroidism. The pituitary is failing to produce adequate TSH, so the thyroid is understimulated. In primary hypothyroidism, TSH would be HIGH (the pituitary compensates). Gynecomastia can occur in hypothyroidism due to altered sex hormone metabolism. Sick euthyroid typically shows low T3 with variable T4/TSH.
subject: Head and neck surgery

stem: A 40-year-old woman presents with a parotid tumour. A biopsy reveals extensive perineural invasion. Which is the most likely pathology?
explanation: Adenoid cystic carcinoma is notorious for perineural invasion — it is the hallmark feature. It tracks along nerves (particularly the facial nerve in the parotid) causing pain and facial nerve palsy. Despite being slow-growing, it has a high rate of local recurrence and late distant metastases due to this perineural spread pattern.
subject: Anatomy

stem: A 50-year-old man presents with malaise, abdominal pain, weight loss, fever and myalgia. Polyarteritis nodosa is associated with all of the following except:
explanation: Polyarteritis nodosa (PAN) is a medium-vessel vasculitis associated with livedo reticularis, mononeuritis multiplex, nailfold infarcts, and palpable purpura. Erythema nodosum is NOT a typical feature of PAN — it is associated with sarcoidosis, IBD, streptococcal infection, and drugs. PAN is associated with hepatitis B.
subject: Head and neck surgery

stem: A 30-year-old woman undergoes subtotal thyroidectomy. Five days later the wound appears red and inflamed. Which of the following is the most likely causative organism?
explanation: Staphylococcus aureus is the most common cause of surgical wound infection, typically presenting 5-7 days post-operatively with wound erythema, swelling, and purulent discharge. It colonises the skin and enters through the surgical incision. Clean wound infections (like thyroidectomy) are most commonly caused by S. aureus.
subject: Critical care

stem: A 50-year-old man complains of recent onset diplopia. On examination he is unable to look inwards and downwards with his right eye. The most likely diagnosis is a lesion of the:
explanation: The trochlear nerve (CN IV) innervates the superior oblique muscle, which depresses the eye when it is adducted (looks down and in). Inability to look downwards and inwards is the classic trochlear nerve palsy. Patients often tilt their head away from the affected side to compensate. The abducens (CN VI) abducts the eye; the oculomotor (CN III) does everything else.
subject: Anatomy

stem: A 57-year-old heart transplant recipient is keen to join the cardiac rehabilitation programme. Which of the following factors is most likely to increase cardiac output in this patient during moderate exercise?
explanation: A transplanted heart is denervated — it lacks sympathetic and parasympathetic innervation. It cannot increase rate via vagal withdrawal or sympathetic stimulation in the normal way. Instead, cardiac output increases through the Frank-Starling mechanism: increased venous return → increased atrial filling → increased preload → increased stroke volume. Circulating catecholamines also help but with a delayed response.
subject: Cardiothoracic surgery

stem: A 69-year man with rectal cancer undergoes low anterior resection. The liver is disease free. The pathology of his tumour was reported as a large tumour invading from the rectum into the mesorectum. Two nodes of 24 lymph nodes, close to the tumour were carcinoma on histology. The tumour was completely excised. What is the correct pathological staging of his tumour?
explanation: Dukes' staging: A = confined to bowel wall, B = through bowel wall but no lymph node involvement, C = lymph node metastases present, D = distant metastases. This tumour invades through the wall (into mesorectum) WITH positive lymph nodes (2/24) but no distant metastases — this is Dukes' C. It would be T3 N1 M0 in TNM staging.
subject: Colorectal surgery

stem: A 21-year-old man is admitted to the Emergency Department with a stab injury to his right chest. Pulse rate is 110 beats/minute and blood pressure is 85/40 mmHg. Chest X-ray shows a large right haemothorax and a very small light apical pneumothorax. Which is the first substance secreted in the process leading to increased renal reabsorption of sodium in response to the above injury?
explanation: Renin is the FIRST substance secreted in the RAAS cascade. Hypovolaemia from haemothorax → reduced renal perfusion → juxtaglomerular cells secrete renin → renin converts angiotensinogen to angiotensin I → ACE converts angiotensin I to angiotensin II → angiotensin II stimulates aldosterone → sodium reabsorption. Renin initiates the entire cascade.
subject: Physiology

stem: During the second (proliferative) phase of wound healing the predominant cells in the wound site are fibroblasts. This cell is of mesenchymal origin and produces the matrix and collagen needed to strengthen the scar. Cross linkage of collagen requires hydroxy-proline and hydroxy-lysine residues, which requires a specific vitamin to be available in sufficient quantities. Deficiency of which vitamin results in collagen that is unstable?
explanation: Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) is an essential cofactor for prolyl hydroxylase and lysyl hydroxylase enzymes that hydroxylate proline and lysine residues in procollagen. Without hydroxylation, collagen cannot form stable triple helices or proper cross-links, resulting in weak, unstable collagen. This is the basis of scurvy — impaired wound healing and collagen weakness.
subject: Pathology

stem: A 62-year-old woman presents with a firm irregular mass in the upper outer quadrant of the right breast. This appears malignant on mammography, and fine needle aspiration cytology is reported as C5. Which is the first lymph node to which the tumour is most likely to metastasise?
explanation: The sentinel lymph node is the first node to receive lymphatic drainage from the tumour — it is the first node to which cancer is likely to metastasise. Sentinel lymph node biopsy (using blue dye and/or technetium-99m) is standard practice in breast cancer staging. If the sentinel node is negative, axillary clearance can be avoided.
subject: Breast and endocrine surgery

stem: Which of the following statements is true with relation to cardiac muscle?

options.text: Contraction does not involve release of Ca by the sarcoplasmic reticulum
Contraction is triggered by an influx of Ca through the sarcolemma
Excitation is passed from one cardiac cell to another through desmosomes
Hypertrophy is brought about by division of existing cardiac cells

explanation: Cardiac muscle contraction is triggered by calcium-induced calcium release (CICR): an influx of extracellular Ca²⁺ through L-type calcium channels in the sarcolemma (triggered by depolarisation) causes a larger release of Ca²⁺ from the sarcoplasmic reticulum. Excitation passes through gap junctions (not desmosomes). Cardiac myocytes do not divide — they hypertrophy.
subject: Physiology

stem: A 70-year-old retired farm worker presents with a scaly lesion on the back of his left wrist. Biopsy shows enlarged pleomorphic squamous cells with mitoses that have breached the basement membrane. What is the name of this process?
explanation: Pleomorphic squamous cells with mitoses that have BREACHED the basement membrane = invasive squamous cell carcinoma = neoplasia. Dysplasia is pre-malignant change ABOVE the basement membrane. Once the basement membrane is breached, it becomes invasive neoplasia. Sun exposure in a farm worker is the risk factor for cutaneous SCC.
subject: Pathology

stem: A 45-year-old man has established cirrhosis. At a follow-up appointment a palpable spleen four fingers breadths below the costal margin is noticed. Full blood counts have shown a persistent thrombocytopaenia. Bone marrow examination shows megakaryocyte hyperplasia. What is the most likely cause of the thrombocytopaenia?

options.text: Ineffective production in the bone marrow
Platelet destruction in the bone marrow

explanation: Cirrhosis causes portal hypertension → splenomegaly → hypersplenism. The enlarged spleen sequesters and destroys platelets (and other blood cells). The bone marrow shows megakaryocyte hyperplasia = compensatory response to increased platelet destruction. This confirms peripheral destruction rather than production failure. The spleen is destroying platelets faster than the marrow can produce them.
subject: Upper gastrointestinal surgery

stem: A surgeon is carrying out an elective splenectomy for congenital spherocytosis. Which structure will be divided in order to mobilize the spleen from the posterior abdominal wall?
explanation: The lienorenal (splenorenal) ligament connects the spleen to the left kidney and contains the splenic vessels and the tail of the pancreas. It must be divided to mobilise the spleen from the posterior abdominal wall. The gastrosplenic ligament (containing short gastric vessels) connects the spleen to the stomach and is also divided, but the lienorenal ligament is the key posterior attachment.
subject: Anatomy

stem: A 50-year-old man is admitted with epigastric pain and a rigid abdomen. He is diagnosed with a perforated duodenal ulcer. Ulceration due to excessive gastrin activity may be caused by increased levels of:
explanation: Adrenaline (via β-adrenergic receptors on G-cells) can stimulate gastrin release. Somatostatin INHIBITS gastrin release. Secretin INHIBITS gastrin. However, the question is about what increases gastrin activity — in clinical practice, a gastrinoma (Zollinger-Ellison) is the classic cause. Among the options, adrenaline is the only one that stimulates gastrin release.
subject: Upper gastrointestinal surgery

stem: A 66-year-old woman with known tumour of her spine has started to retain urine and is experiencing decreased anal and rectal tone. The tumour is pressing directly on the conus medullaris. At which one of the following vertebral levels is the tumour most likely to be located?
explanation: The conus medullaris (terminal end of the spinal cord) lies at approximately the L1/L2 vertebral level in adults. It may extend from T12 to L3 but L1/L2 is the most common level. Cauda equina syndrome from compression at this level causes urinary retention, decreased anal tone, saddle anaesthesia, and lower limb weakness.
subject: Colorectal surgery

stem: A 26-year-old man presents with a two-month history of unilateral testicular swelling. An ultrasound scan shows a heterogeneous mass within the testis with surrounding fluid. His blood test shows an elevated alpha fetoprotein level. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Elevated alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) with a testicular mass in a young man indicates a non-seminomatous germ cell tumour — most likely a teratoma. Seminomas produce β-hCG (not AFP). AFP is produced by yolk sac elements within teratomas. Testicular lymphoma is more common in older men (>50). LDH may be raised in both types.
subject: Urology

stem: A 50-year-old woman presents with a history of faecal incontinence over the past few years. She had a prolonged and difficult first stage of labor 20 years previously. Physical examination reveals a relatively lax anal sphincter. Which nerve is likely to have been damaged in labour?
explanation: The pudendal nerve (S2-S4) innervates the external anal sphincter and the pelvic floor muscles. Prolonged/difficult labour causes stretch injury to the pudendal nerve (pudendal neuropathy), leading to denervation of the external sphincter and progressive faecal incontinence. This is the most common nerve injury causing post-obstetric faecal incontinence.
subject: Anatomy

stem: A 70-year-old man is admitted to hospital with a 12-hour history of a painful white leg. A femoral artery embolus is shown on angiography. He is an insulin-controlled diabetic and takes ibuprofen for longstanding osteoarthritis. Twenty-four hours after emergency embolectomy his blood pressure is 90/60 mmHg and he passes very dark brown urine. A dipstick shows myoglobin and traces of blood. His blood glucose is 15 mmol/L, urea 12 mmol/L, and creatinine 180 mmol/L. What is the most likely cause of his abnormal renal function?
explanation: Dark brown urine with myoglobin on dipstick after reperfusion of an ischaemic limb = rhabdomyolysis. Prolonged limb ischaemia (12 hours) causes muscle necrosis. Upon reperfusion, myoglobin is released into the circulation → myoglobinuria → acute tubular necrosis. The elevated creatinine and urea confirm acute kidney injury. Treatment is aggressive IV fluid resuscitation and alkalinisation of urine.
subject: Breast and endocrine surgery

stem: An 86-year-old woman, with a history of partial gastrectomy, is in the high dependency unit for a chest infection that is being treated with antibiotics. She complains of difficulty swallowing. Endoscopy shows multiple white plaques on the mucosal surface of the oesophagus. Biopsy is most likely to show:
explanation: Multiple white plaques on oesophageal mucosa in an elderly, immunocompromised patient (on antibiotics, in HDU) is classic oesophageal candidiasis (Candida albicans). Broad-spectrum antibiotics disrupt normal flora allowing Candida overgrowth. The white plaques are pseudomembranes of fungal hyphae, desquamated epithelial cells and inflammatory debris. Treatment is fluconazole.
subject: Upper gastrointestinal surgery

stem: A 65-year-old woman has been given a total of 15 mg of morphine over a 30-minute period for pain relief following a femoral neck fracture. The following observations are found: SpO2 on 80% oxygen is 80%; blood pressure 90/60; respiratory rate 6 breaths/minute. The immediate intervention should be:
explanation: Respiratory rate of 6/min, SpO2 80% despite 80% oxygen, and hypotension following 15mg morphine = opioid toxicity causing respiratory depression. The IMMEDIATE treatment is IV naloxone (opioid antagonist). Naloxone has rapid onset (1-2 minutes IV) and will reverse the respiratory depression. Oxygen alone won't help if the patient isn't breathing adequately.
subject: Head and neck surgery

stem: The following drugs are used to treat patients with peripheral vascular disease. They all reduce the rate of myocardial infarction and stroke except:
explanation: Oxypentifylline (pentoxifylline) is a methylxanthine derivative that improves blood flow by reducing blood viscosity and improving red cell deformability. While it may help claudication symptoms, it has NOT been shown to reduce the rate of MI or stroke. ACE inhibitors, antihypertensives, aspirin, and statins all have proven cardiovascular mortality benefits.
subject: Vascular surgery

stem: A 4-year-old boy is brought to the Emergency Department with a painful right elbow. His father states that he was swinging his son by his arms when the pain came on suddenly. An X-ray shows that the radial head is displaced from its usual position. What is the ligament (of the proximal radio-ulnar joint) that holds the radial head in place?
explanation: The annular ligament encircles the radial head and holds it in the radial notch of the ulna at the proximal radio-ulnar joint. 'Pulled elbow' (nursemaid's elbow/radial head subluxation) occurs when sudden traction on the forearm pulls the radial head partially through the annular ligament. It is common in children aged 1-4 years.
subject: Anatomy

stem: A 35-year-old man presents with a three-week history of low back pain and a three-day history of pain and weakness in his left leg. Physical examination demonstrates numbness over the posterior aspect of the left calf extending to the lateral aspect of the foot. Left ankle reflex is absent. A magnetic resonance scan shows compression of the left S1 nerve root. What is the most likely responsible structure?
explanation: The nucleus pulposus herniates through a weakened annulus fibrosus (disc prolapse) to compress the nerve root. At L5/S1, a posterolateral disc prolapse compresses the S1 nerve root. The nucleus pulposus is the gelatinous core of the intervertebral disc that herniates. The posterior longitudinal ligament is thin laterally, allowing posterolateral herniation.
subject: Upper gastrointestinal surgery

stem: A 26-years-old man motorcyclist loses 1 L of blood secondary to an open fracture of the femur sustained in RTA. Which of the following is the most likely earliest compensatory response in hypovolemia in this patient?
explanation: The earliest compensatory response to hypovolaemia is baroreceptor-mediated venoconstriction. Baroreceptors detect reduced arterial pressure within seconds and trigger sympathetic venoconstriction, which shifts blood from the venous capacitance vessels into the central circulation, increasing preload. Capillary fluid shifts take minutes-hours. RAAS activation takes longer.
subject: Emergency medicine and trauma

stem: Histology of a discrete palpable lump in the breast of a 34-year-old woman has shown apocrine metaplasia, epithelial overgrowth and papillary projections. What is the most likely pathological process?
explanation: Apocrine metaplasia with epithelial overgrowth and papillary projections in a discrete breast lump of a 34-year-old describes fibrocystic change — specifically a benign breast cyst. Apocrine metaplasia is the hallmark of benign cystic disease. Fibroadenomas show fibroepithelial proliferation. Phyllodes tumours show leaf-like stromal growth.
subject: Pathology

stem: A 32-year-old man presents with a painful torticollis. There is no past medical history and his only complaint is that he has been feeling rather tired over the last 4 nights. On examination, he has large rubbery mass in the lateral aspect of his neck as well as a few smaller masses along his internal jugular vein. You correctly assume that the muscular neck spasm and the large mass are connected. The most likely cause of his torticollis is due to pressure on?
explanation: Large rubbery lymph nodes along the internal jugular vein causing torticollis (neck muscle spasm) suggests pressure on the spinal accessory nerve (CN XI). This nerve crosses the posterior triangle superficially and is closely related to the deep cervical lymph node chain. Lymphoma (B symptoms: tiredness/night sweats + rubbery nodes) compressing CN XI → sternocleidomastoid spasm → torticollis.
subject: Anatomy

stem: A thin menopausal 52-year-old woman is diagnosed with breast cancer. Her menarche was at the age of 14. She had her first child at age 40 years. During lactation, she developed breast abscess that necessitated surgical intervention. She has no family history of breast cancer. Which of the following is the most significant risk factor for this patient?

options.text: Age at first full term pregnancy

explanation: Late age at first full-term pregnancy (40 years) is the most significant risk factor here. First pregnancy after 30 significantly increases breast cancer risk because breast tissue is exposed to oestrogen for longer without the protective differentiation that early pregnancy provides. Menarche at 14 is normal. No family history excludes familial risk. Breast abscess does not increase cancer risk.
subject: Breast and endocrine surgery

stem: A 30-year-old woman is sent to the outpatient clinic with weight loss of 5 kg over the last 6 months. She also complains of anxiety, panic attacks and palpitations. On examination, there is a swelling in the anterior neck which moves on swallowing. Which of the following is most likely pathology underlying this presentation?
explanation: Weight loss, anxiety, panic attacks, and palpitations in a 30-year-old woman with a thyroid swelling = hyperthyroidism. Graves' disease is the most common cause of hyperthyroidism in young women (autoimmune, anti-TSH receptor antibodies). The diffuse thyroid swelling that moves on swallowing is a goitre. Hashimoto's causes hypothyroidism. Carcinomas rarely cause hyperthyroidism.
subject: Breast and endocrine surgery

stem: A 69-year-old man has been admitted to the high dependency unit following an anterior resection under general anesthesia. He was given 2 mg of intrathecal morphine. On examination, he looks pale and drowsy. Arterial blood gases results are: pH 7.28, pCo2 8.1 kPa, pO2 10.2 kPa, Base Excess -2.1, Glucose 21 mmol/L, Lactate 4.0 mmol/L. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: pH 7.28 (acidosis) with elevated pCO2 8.1 kPa = respiratory acidosis. Base excess -2.1 is borderline normal (no significant metabolic component). The high glucose and lactate are concerning but the primary acid-base disturbance is respiratory. Intrathecal morphine causes respiratory depression → CO2 retention → respiratory acidosis. The patient is pale and drowsy = classic opioid effect.
subject: Perioperative care

stem: A 32-year-old woman has a pigmented lesion excised from her left calf. The histopathological diagnosis is melanoma in situ, which is completely excised with a 1 cm margin. What is the next most appropriate management?

options.text: Education about skin self-examination and discharge from follow up
Removal of any other pigmented lesions

explanation: Melanoma in situ (Stage 0) is confined to the epidermis with NO dermal invasion. A 1 cm excision margin is not standard (5mm is recommended for in situ), but if completely excised, the prognosis is excellent with virtually no risk of metastasis. No sentinel node biopsy is needed (no dermal invasion = no lymphatic access). Patient education and surveillance is appropriate.
subject: Skin and wound management

stem: A 60-year-old man with a past history of angina undergoes an uncomplicated operation for an inguinal hernia. Postoperatively he is found to be hypotensive, tachycardic, and has a raised jugular venous pressure. What is the most likely underlying cause of his hypotension?
explanation: Hypotension + tachycardia + RAISED JVP in a patient with angina history = cardiogenic shock, most likely from a perioperative MI. The raised JVP indicates the heart cannot pump effectively (pump failure), so blood backs up. This causes reduced stroke volume. In hypovolaemia, JVP would be LOW. Reduced stroke volume from poor cardiac contractility is the cause.
subject: Emergency medicine and trauma

stem: A 34-year-old man is admitted to the Emergency Department with a head injury. On examination his Glasgow coma scale is 9. A CT scan of the brain demonstrates an extra dural haemorrhage. Which of the following arteries is the most likely source of this?
explanation: Extradural (epidural) haematoma is caused by rupture of the middle meningeal artery, typically following a temporal bone fracture. The classic presentation is a lucid interval followed by rapid deterioration. The middle meningeal artery runs in a groove on the inner surface of the temporal bone, making it vulnerable to injury from skull fractures in this region.
subject: Neurosurgery

stem: A 65-year-old man has a history of transient ischemic attacks. He is due to undergo carotid endarterectomy. Which one of the following is true of the internal carotid artery?

options.text: Begins at the level of the sixth cervical vertebra
Divides into the anterior, middle and posterior cerebral arteries
Is accompanied within the skull by preganglionic sympathetic nerves

explanation: The internal carotid artery gives off the ophthalmic artery as its first major branch after entering the skull. It begins at the bifurcation of the common carotid at C3/C4 (not C6). It divides into the anterior and middle cerebral arteries (NOT posterior). It is accompanied by postganglionic (not preganglionic) sympathetic fibres. It enters the skull via the carotid canal (not foramen ovale).
subject: Anatomy

stem: A 25-year-old male athlete is in training. At rest, how many liters of blood per minute does his heart pump out?
explanation: Resting cardiac output is approximately 5-6 L/min in a healthy adult (stroke volume ~70 mL × heart rate ~70-80 bpm). Athletes may have slightly lower resting heart rates but larger stroke volumes, still giving approximately 5 L/min at rest. During exercise, cardiac output can increase to 20-25 L/min in trained athletes.
subject: Physiology

stem: A 26-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department after sustaining a glass cut to his arm. On examination there is a 10 cm longitudinal laceration on the anterior aspect of his upper arm. He has symptoms suggestive of ulnar nerve injury. On exploring the upper part of the arm we would expect the ulnar nerve to be:

options.text: Anterior then medial to the brachial artery
Medial then anterior to the brachial artery
Posterior then medial to the brachial artery

explanation: In the upper arm, the ulnar nerve runs medial to the brachial artery in the anterior compartment. It then pierces the medial intermuscular septum at the mid-arm level to enter the posterior compartment, passing behind the medial epicondyle. In the proximal upper arm, the relationship is consistently medial to the brachial artery.
subject: Critical care

stem: A 55-year-old man presents with acute back pain following a severe road traffic accident. Neurological examination reveals lack of sensation of the umbilicus and below. What is the spinal level of the neurological deficit likely to be?
